Attorney General Jay Jones

RICHMOND, Va. – Attorney General Jay Jones, as part of a coalition of 21 attorneys general, filed an amicus brief in the U.S. Court of Appeals for the D.C. Circuit in support of litigation challenging the U.S. Department of Homeland Security’s (DHS) policy and practice of conducting warrantless civil immigration arrests.

Under federal law, immigration officers conducting warrantless civil immigration arrests must have probable cause to believe that an individual is unlawfully present in the United States and is likely to escape before a warrant can be obtained.

“The Trump Administration is creating and stoking fear in our communities through these unlawful arrests that aim to make a political statement and sow mistrust between law enforcement and the communities they serve,” said Attorney General Jones. “Threats to our neighbors, friends, teachers, and families have resulted in widespread fear. President Trump’s DHS continues to strip people of their humanity and dignity, and it continues to exacerbate mistrust when we should be strengthening relationships and transparency between law enforcement and communities. My office will keep using every legal power and tool at our disposal to stand up for our communities and Virginians.”

The brief was filed in Escobar-Molina v. DHS, a case challenging DHS’s policy and practice of conducting unlawful warrantless civil immigration arrests in the District of Columbia. On December 2, 2025, the U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia granted in part a motion for a preliminary injunction.

In filing the brief, Attorney General Jones joins the attorneys general of Arizona, California, Colorado, Connecticut, Delaware, District of Columbia, Hawaii, Illinois, Maine, Maryland, Massachusetts, Michigan, Minnesota, Nevada, New Jersey, New Mexico, New York, Oregon, Rhode Island, Vermont, and Washington.

title: Deportations climb under Trump but fall short of White House target, a new report finds
description:
The report by the Migration Policy Institute shows deportations increased from 620,000 during the first year of Trump’s second administration.
Trump, a Republican, returned to power last year promising to stanch crossings at the southern border and crack down on immigration.
More people being deported, but not at all-time highs The analysis found that the Department of Homeland Security carried out 980,000 deportations during the first 18 months of the second Trump administration.
Despite the surging arrests, the report details some of the challenges to the Trump administration reaching its deportation targets.
Figures the Trump administration has released are inconsistent and unverifiable.
text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — President Donald Trump’s administration is on track to deport about 660,000 people over the past year, a new report released Thursday shows, as arrests ramp up across the country fueled by billions of dollars meant to supercharge his immigration agenda.

The report by the Migration Policy Institute shows deportations increased from 620,000 during the first year of Trump’s second administration. The numbers fall short of previous highs in the early 2000s and fail to meet the Trump administration’s promise, made when it received the billions from Congress, that the money would allow for 1 million deportations annually.

The report, based on publicly available data obtained through Freedom of Information Act requests, comes after the Trump administration in January 2025 stopped publicly releasing similar figures compiled by the Department of Homeland Security.

Trump, a Republican, returned to power last year promising to stanch crossings at the southern border and crack down on immigration. His administration has pushed through restrictions on both legal and illegal immigration and launched high-profile arrest operations in its bid to force migrants out.

More people being deported, but not at all-time highs

The analysis found that the Department of Homeland Security carried out 980,000 deportations during the first 18 months of the second Trump administration.

During the last fiscal year — when the Trump administration’s immigration enforcement mechanisms were shifting into high gear — an estimated 660,000 people were deported.

According to MPI’s analysis, that’s a 26% increase from the yearly average from 2021 to 2024 during the administration of President Joe Biden, a Democrat, but well below the 1.86 million deportations recorded in 2000, under President Bill Clinton, another Democrat.

Despite the surging arrests, the report details some of the challenges to the Trump administration reaching its deportation targets.

Historically, many immigrants living in the U.S. without authorization were from Mexico and didn’t often seek asylum. But in recent years, migrants have come to the U.S. from a wide range of countries, which can make it more complicated to deport them. And immigration courts, which ultimately decide whether someone can be removed from the country, face more significant case backlogs.

Voluntary departures are increasing as are interior arrests

The report said voluntary departures — when people give up their cases in immigration court and agree to leave the country — were at an “all-time high,” with 170,000 choosing to do so since Trump returned to office in January 2025. People who choose voluntary departure could one day return to the U.S. But some immigrant advocates and lawyers say that people give up their court fight and agree to leave simply to get out of U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement, or ICE, detention.

The Trump administration was also increasingly deporting people it arrested in the country’s interior, the report said, reflecting how it was stepping up enforcement against migrants who have been in the country for a long time. In 2025, about 28% of the people deported were arrested inside the country, but by July of this year that had risen to 39%.

Migrants arrested at the southern border still make up a large number of deportations, the report said — 69% of all deportations between Jan. 20, 2025, and July 31, 2026, were of people initially intercepted at the border.

People in the country longer may have more opportunities to contest their removal while the government typically has greater authority to fast-track deportations for people arrested at the border.

The analysis said most people deported have never been convicted of a crime, despite the Trump administration claiming to be targeting the “worst of the worst.” Previous data has showed the same.

In response to the MPI report, White House spokesperson Lauren Bis said: “President Trump has delivered the largest reduction in illegal immigration in modern history.”

Trump administration no longer regularly releases immigration data

Homeland Security stopped releasing similar data when Trump took office, making it difficult to track one of his key campaign promises. Figures the Trump administration has released are inconsistent and unverifiable.

The administration says it is transparent. On Tuesday, it released some of its own figures as part of a document boasting of its achievements on immigration, including that 1.2 million migrants have been deported or removed during Trump’s second term. The discrepancy could not immediately be reconciled.

In the absence of regular data, analysts and activists interested in immigration trends have relied on information obtained through lawsuits or limited and sporadic information released by federal agencies to track deportation data.

title: Trump Suffers Legal Loss In Bid To 'Reset' Migrant Detention Clock - Newsweek
description:
A federal appeals court has rejected the Trump administration's argument that it can restart a six-month detention clock when immigrants are detained again after being released.
The court sent the case back to the district court to reconsider his detention claim without applying that presumption.
Abedi filed a habeas corpus petition in July 2025, challenging the legality of his detention, but a district court denied his petition that October.
What The Court Decided The appeals court found that the district court had made legal errors in assessing Abedi's claims on two central issues.
The case will now return to the district court for further proceedings.
text:
A federal appeals court has rejected the Trump administration's argument that it can restart a six-month detention clock when immigrants are detained again after being released.

The U.S. Court of Appeals for the Tenth Circuit ruled Wednesday in the case of Kavah Abedi, an Iranian national who was detained by Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) in June 2025, more than two decades after he was released from immigration custody.

The court found that the government could not treat the first six months of Abedi's re-detention as presumptively reasonable under a Supreme Court ruling governing prolonged detention while the government seek to remove a person from the United States.

Read More on News

The appeals court also ruled that immigration officials violated federal regulations by failing to provide Abedi with a prompt interview after revoking his release, denying him an opportunity to challenge the basis for his detention.

The decision reverses parts of a lower court ruling and sends the case back for further proceedings.

Why Does This Matter?

The ruling addresses the limits of the federal government's authority to detain immigrants who have final orders of removal but cannot be deported in the reasonably foreseeable future.

In its 2001 decision in Zadvydas v. Davis, the Supreme Court established a six-month period of presumptively reasonable detention following the removal period.

After that, if a detainee provides good reason to believe there is no significant likelihood of removal in the reasonably foreseeable future, the government must respond with evidence sufficient to rebut that showing.

The Trump administration argued that the six-month presumption should restart when a person is released from immigration detention and later detained again.

The Tenth Circuit rejected that interpretation, concluding that the six-month presumption applies only to the first six months after the removal period begins and should not be applied again to Abedi's re-detention.

The court sent the case back to the district court to reconsider his detention claim without applying that presumption.

The ruling does not automatically require the release of all immigrants who are detained again. Instead, it establishes how the six-month presumption must be applied when courts assess the legality of detention in circumstances like Abedi's.

What Happened To Kaveh Abedi?

Abedi was 10 when his family fled Iran and entered the United States in 1991, where they were granted asylum, according to the court's opinion.

After he was convicted of a drug possession offense in California, he was placed in removal proceedings.

In September 2002, an immigration judge granted Abedi deferral of removal under the Convention Against Torture.

He was later released under an order of supervision because his removal was not considered reasonably foreseeable.

Over the following two decades, Abedi complied with the conditions imposed by immigration officials, including attending required check-ins and seeking permission before traveling outside his state of residence, the court said.

Abedi married a U.S. citizen in 2016 and had been his wife's primary provider and caretaker since 2020, as her chronic health conditions prevented her from continuing to work as a chef.

In 2025, the couple moved from California to Kansas for financial reasons after receiving approval from ICE.

On June 23, 2025, ICE officers detained Abedi outside his home while one told his wife that he was being deported to Iran, according to the court's account.

Abedi had previously been granted protection under the Convention Against Torture, which had resulted in the deferral of his removal.

While in detention, he received a notice stating that his release had been revoked because "removal to a country other than Iran is now a possibility". The notice also said he would "promptly be afforded an informal interview" at which he could respond to the reasons for the decision.

However, the government did not dispute that Abedi had not received the promised interview by the time the case was briefed on appeal.

The court noted that documents from a following case suggested an interview may eventually have taken place in January 2026, more than six months after his re-detention.

Abedi filed a habeas corpus petition in July 2025, challenging the legality of his detention, but a district court denied his petition that October.

In January 2026, he filed a second petition arguing that his detention had exceeded six months and that there was no real likelihood of his removal in the reasonably foreseeable future.

The district court granted that petition in February and he was released under an order of supervision on February 25, but the government then argued that his release meant the original appeal should be dismissed.

The Tenth Circuit rejected that argument, finding that the dispute could recur and evade judicial review.

What The Court Decided

The appeals court found that the district court had made legal errors in assessing Abedi's claims on two central issues.

First, it ruled that the government had violated its own regulations by failing to provide the required prompt interview after revoking his release.

The court said the interview requirement was designed to allow a detained person to challenge the reasons for their detention, but it rejected the government’s position that it should not be held to a particular time frame for providing that process.

The court said that accepting that argument would make the promptness requirement meaningless and effectively insulate administrative decisions from judicial review.

The government had not explained why it could not have interviewed Abedi within the four weeks before he filed his first habeas petition or the three months before the district court ruled on it.

The appeals court also rejected the lower court's conclusion that Abedi had not demonstrated sufficient prejudice from the failure to provide the interview.

It found that the regulatory safeguards protected fundamental due process rights and that the government's failure to follow them warranted relief.

Second, the court found that the district court had applied the wrong legal standard to Abedi’s claim under Zadvydas v. Davis by treating the first six months of his re-detention as presumptively reasonable.

The Supreme Court’s decision limits post-removal-period detention to a period reasonably necessary to secure a person’s removal, while its six-month presumption is intended to help courts assess when continued detention may no longer be lawful.

The Tenth Circuit also rejected the government’s interpretation that the presumption could begin again following re-detention.

The appeals court’s decision does not itself establish that every instance of re-detention is unlawful, instead it requires courts to assess the legality of detention without automatically treating the first six months after re-detention as presumptively reasonable.

The case will now return to the district court for further proceedings.

Updated at 13.20 EDT

How do Trump voters feel about his immigration policies?

Anonymous reader, Maryland asks in a callout question:

How do prior Trump and/or MAGA voters assess his administration’s immigration policies and actions and what effect will this have on their mid-term voting choices? Why?

double quotation markMaanvi: Donald Trump ran on immigration as a top issue – but since taking office, voter support for his immigration crackdown has flagged. A Reuters/Ipsos poll released on 21 September found that only 36% of voters approved of Trump’s handling of immigration. According to Pew research, half of Americans see the administration’s immigration tactics as too aggressive. Voters who self-identify as “Maga” still seem to strongly support Trump’s immigration policies, but fissures have appeared among Republican voters overall. This is especially clear in Republican districts that Trump easily carried during the presidential election. In deep-red Texas, for example, a poll by the New York Times and Siena University found voters there evenly split on which Senate candidate they trusted more to handle immigration – a striking shift in a state that hasn’t elected a Democratic senator in almost 40 years. Republican candidates are now trying to distance themselves from the most extreme parts of the administration’s crackdown. Republican senator Roger Marshall – who had once vehemently backed Trump’s immigration agenda – recently softened his hardline rhetoric, saying ICE should coordinate with local law enforcement. We’ve already mentioned here how this is playing out with Latino Republicans in Florida. Overall, an October NBC News/Telemundo poll of registered Latino voters found that two-thirds believe his enforcement policies have gone “too far”. Of those polled, 17% said that they or someone close to them had considered not voting in person this year because of concerns about ICE.

Share

How can assisted living facilities survive without immigrant workers?

Anonymous reader, Massachusetts asks in a callout question: Assisted living facilities for the elderly and disabled are grossly understaffed due to Trump’s policies. The lifting of Temporary Protected Status (TPS) is a major contributor to short-staffing, as Haitians filled the majority of these roles. This has put the elderly and disabled at risk. What will politicians do to right this wrong?

double quotation markMaanvi: Indeed, of the 330,000 Haitian TPS holders who suddenly lost their legal status this summer, about 13,000 work daily as nursing assistants, caring for 65,000 patients, according to a report commissioned by Democratic senators. But Trump’s immigration policies appear to have impacts across the healthcare system. According to the Association of American Medical Colleges, nearly one in four doctors in the US was trained abroad – and have been crucial to addressing medical staff shortages in rural areas, where few American doctors want to move.

In terms of legislative solutions – short of broad overhaul of immigration policies, legislators have tried approaches help immigrants in the healthcare workforce. This month, for example, Democratic representatives Adam Smith (Washington) and Raja Krishnamoorthi (Illinois) introduced two bills that would open grants for programs that provide training, licensing, certification, etc for immigrants interested in entering the health care field and allow non-US-citizen immigrants to work for the National Health Service Corps.

Share

Have Trump's immigration strategies on the border and within the US been effective?

Simon Rowell, Florida asks in a callout question: With the Trump administration claiming total success in halting unauthorized immigration-citing a drop in border encounters, does ICE’s current interior focus function as a targeted, effective strategy to address the remaining unauthorized population, or has it devolved into a high-visibility PR exercise that relies more on tactical theater than measurable policy results? Does it really achieve anything useful or is it simply a point scoring mechanism for the electorate?

double quotation markJose: I think it is important to clarify what “border encounters” mean in the context of immigration enforcement. A border encounter does not only take place when someone is caught crossing the border between ports of entry. A border encounter can also be Customs and Border Protection (CBP) officials interacting or processing an immigrant who arrives to the US and requests asylum. Previously, the vast majority of border encounters were at ports of entry with asylum seekers. Trump, during his first day in office, filed a proclamation that essentially shut down the border — what observers call an “asylum ban.” Earlier this year, the D.C. Circuit Court of Appeals ruled the asylum ban was unlawful, prompting the Trump administration to ask the Supreme Court to review it (we’re not sure if the Supreme Court will take up the case).

There are lots of factors why border encounters are at an all-time low, including the asylum ban and Mexico’s role in immigration enforcement efforts. But also, people might still be trying to cross into the US between ports of entry, in terrain that is extremely difficult and dangerous that may not be hyper-surveilled, like through the Sonoran desert. It’s also important to remember that ICE is a massive agency. Not only does ICE carry out deportation work (through its Enforcement and Removal Operations teams), but they also enforce and investigate around 400 federal statutes (through Homeland Security Investigations), including drug trafficking, child exploitation, human trafficking, internet/deepweb crimes, etc.

double quotation markJose continues: However, there have been internal and public criticisms of the Trump administration for putting so many resources in its immigration/deportation work, leaving other crimes untouched. There are Homeland Security Investigations special agents who have been frustrated that their work (child exploitation investigations, drug trafficking, etc.) is being pushed to the side, while they are forced to do the ERO deportation work. The first year of the Trump administration saw massive, large-scale “surge” operations around the country (Los Angeles, Chicago, Minneapolis), where federal officials entered cities, puffing out their chests as a show of force to carry out the “mass deportation” campaign promise. However, those operations were deeply unpopular, especially after the shooting deaths of Renee Good and Alex Pretti. Now, ICE has shifted tactics, engaging in quieter arrests and operations that have, arguably, been more effective in terms of arresting, detaining and deporting immigrants.

In terms of PR exercises and tactical theatre, I would like to add the following: the Trump administration has time-and-time again equated undocumented immigrants and asylum seekers with crime. They have repeatedly claimed that immigrants are the “worst of the worst” and are wreaking havoc throughout the US. ICE’s own statistics, however, do not show that to be the case — it seems their claims of immigrants being the “worst of the worst” is crumbling as they continue with their operations.

Share

Updated at 13.19 EDT

What is the Democratic party's position on immigration?

Bruce, Maryland asks in a callout question: What is the Democrats’ policy on immigration? Why is the party (not individual candidates) so afraid of publicizing its position on major issues (DEI, immigration, climate change, etc.)?

double quotation markSam: On the campaign trail, immigration has not been a major talking point of many Democratic candidates, and I think it remains to be seen what their specific policy priorities would be if they regain control of Congress. I’m chatting with a politics colleague about it now, and she pointed out that many Democrats have largely avoided the subject other than condemning Trump’s crackdown and agreeing there must be controls at the border. Democrats have not been aligned and put forward a clear, proactive vision on what they would do differently.

Share

Will there be justice for US citizens killed or injured by immigration enforcement officers?

MJ Upham, Colorado asks in a callout question: Will there ever be justice for Renee Good and Alex Pretti? Will changes in the House and Senate do anything for all of the innocent people being held in detention centers?

double quotation markSam: It is historically very rare for officers in the US, whether local or federal, to face criminal charges for shooting or killing civilians and even rarer that they are convicted. The Trump administration has defended officers’ actions in nearly all high-profile cases, and the Minnesota Star Tribune reported today that the DoJ has halted cooperation in the ongoing state investigations into the killings of Renee Good and Alex Pretti, according to Minnesota officials. So even if Democrats regain a majority in Congress, the federal government will continue to have significant power in these cases, which will make it difficult for families and communities to get the accountability they are demanding.

If Democrats take control, I expect we may see more hearings where DHS officials are forced to answer questions about these cases and about detention conditions, and Democrats would have more leverage in disputes about the funds going to ICE and detention, which could have some impact on Trump’s agenda.

Share

How are US farms surviving without immigrant workers?

Cheryl Bath, Wisconsin asks in a callout question: During covid I was surprised to learn how many foreign workers, especially from Mexico, worked in the Wisconsin farm fields. And now, I was more surprised to learn that these workers would also be deported and not allowed to work any longer at these fields even though it was all legal with paperwork. These foreign workers paid into the federal government taxes and social security system which was a plus for U.S. social security. I’ve been wondering how these Wisconsin farms are dealing with the absence of these workers seeing how it is harvesting time right now. Propublica had a article a year or so ago about the effects of this immigration sweep on the workers and the farms but that was still when the workers were still here. I can’t find any follow up or information on this anywhere. I think the farmers really feel left out to deal with this on their own and no one is asking questions. Maybe you can?

double quotation markMaanvi: Cattle ranchers and dairy farmers have indeed been pushing for immigration reform, not only recently, but for years – because the industry relies so heavily on immigrant labor. In September, the the Texas Cattle Feeders Association, Kansas Livestock Association, and Oklahoma Cattlemen’s Association issued a joint warning that ICE operations were threatening their industy, and would have “a massive chilling effect on the legal, documented, skilled workers that put beef on the table and keep the supply chain moving”. I recently spoke with Matt Teagarden, CEO of the Kansas Livestock Association, who said that the US cattle herd has shrunk to its lowest numbers in 75 years – and ranchers are struggling to keep up with consumer demand. Farms aren’t able to expand operations without immigrant labor – and Teagarden said that this could mean that US consumers will increasingly be eating imported beef. He also noticed that ICE crackdowns are having a systemic impact on agriculture – it’s not only dairy or cattle industry workers who are impacted, but also farmworkers who grow the feed for cows, and immigrant workers who process the dairy and meat before it gets to grocery stores. Two-thirds of farm workers are non-citizen immigrants. As the administration targets these workers, food producers could struggle to keep up operations, and prices are expected to increase steeply, according to a study by the thinktank Fwd.us.

double quotation markJosé: Many people caught up in the Trump administration’s dragnet are workers in the US — they pay taxes and contribute to Social Security, while receiving almost none of the benefits. The process to gain asylum or remain in the US can be long and arduous — oftentimes, as undocumented people go through the process, they will receive work permits, Social Security numbers and, in certain states, driver’s licenses. Now, many people with those legal work permits have been arrested by federal immigration officials and sit in detention centers, waiting for their immigration cases to proceed.

Share

¿Hasta qué punto las deportaciones y las políticas migratorias de Donald Trump están influyendo en el voto de los estadounidenses?

Catalina Beleña Martinez, España, nos envió una pregunta por callout:

¿Hasta qué punto las deportaciones y las políticas migratorias de Donald Trump están influyendo en el voto de los estadounidenses? ¿Se está votando por seguridad, por miedo o por convicción?

double quotation markJose: Para cada persona que ha sido arrestada por ICE, hay docenas de personas afectadas. No solamente afecta a los familiares — hijos, hijas, parejas, etc. — pero también a la comunidad que posiblemente han cultivado en los Estados Unidos. Gracias a esto, y también con los métodos agresivos que hemos estado viendo, hay algunas comunidades que apoyaron a Trump en el 2024 (principalmente cubanos en Florida), que están poco a poco abandonando y dejando de apoyar a la política migratoria de la administración. Esto se puede ver con la campaña de la congresista María Elvira Salazar, una republicana de Florida, que tuvo una ruptura muy pública con Trump y su política migratoria. En un comercial de su campaña, la congresista le dijo a Trump que “los mismos hispanos que te ayudaron llegar a la Casa Blanca en el 2024 se sienten traicionados hoy en día.” Una encuesta de NBC News y Telemundo de votantes latinos encontró que el 2/3 de ellos piensan que la política migratoria de Trump está fuera de control (“too far”). El 17% de los que participaron en la encuesta dijeron que ellos, o algún conocido, están considerando no votar en persona este año, por preocupación de ICE. Vamos a tener que ver realmente cuáles serán los resultados de estas elecciones y de ahí podremos ver cuáles comunidades y cuántas personas votaron por el partido Demócrata gracias a la poítica migratoria. Pero después de eso, si ganan los Demócratas, hay que ver realmente lo que van a hacer para oponerse a la política migratoria de Trump. Por ejemplo, muchas personas que trabajan con migrantes estuvieron sumamente decepcionados con la administración de Biden, porque después del primer mandato de Trump, él decidió continuar muchas de las políticas agresivas de Trump.

Share

How many ICE agents are in the field, and do they have working body cameras?

Paul, Texas asks in a callout question: How many ICE agents are there in the field? What percentage of ICE agents have verified working cameras?

double quotation markSam: ICE launched an extraordinary and rapid hiring push last year after the agency received an unprecedented $170bn in funding for immigration and border enforcement activities. With DHS lowering its standards for new recruits and reducing training, there have been significant concerns about the quality of hires, as I reported last year.

At the start of 2026, ICE said it had doubled the number of its officers and agents from 10,000 to 22,000, though as my colleagues have reported, the department has extensively relied on local, cooperative police to support their deportation efforts.

In terms of body cameras, ICE in recent weeks has said it now has enough of the devices for all officers, though it’s unclear how widely the cameras have been distributed and used.

The agency has also at times signaled its reluctance to release footage, so the impact of this deployment, particularly in terms of accountability for alleged misconduct, remains to be seen.

Share

Why can’t local law enforcement monitor ICE?

Richard Wolfe, Maine asks in a callout question: Why can’t local law enforcement be assigned to monitor ICE?

double quotation markMaanvi: Across the US, local police, highway patrol, sheriffs departments, even Fish and Wildlife Services actually work directly with ICE – helping the federal government find and arrest immigrants as part of what’s called the 287(g) program. In many regions, it’s unclear whether local cops are conducting routine police work (pulling someone over for speeding, or conducting a drug operation) or engaging in immigration enforcement. Sometimes, it’s both at the same time.

I recently wrote about an operation at the El Corralón bar in Memphis on 29 August. It began as a police raid targeting illegal gambling and drugs turned into one of the largest sweeps of undocumented immigrants in Tennessee – 120 people were detained. Initially, search warrants at the bar related to drugs and gambling targeted the bar’s owner. But agents also arrested a number of patrons on immigration charges.

Share

Updated at 12.37 EDT

How often has DHS targeted US citizens?

Nola67 from comments: After Ilhan Omar’s house was raided, I’m wondering if there’s any kind of statistic that shows how much ICE/DHS has come after US citizens or tried to fake evidence?

double quotation markSam: The federal government has said it was working to carry out the “largest denaturalization effort in history,” and there have been isolated DoJ announcements of cases to strip people of citizenship based on their criminal records or claims that they illegally procured their naturalization. Denaturalization cases have been brought under previous administrations, and it’s unclear if the scale of this administration’s efforts match its rhetoric. We do know that US immigration agents in the field have frequently detained US citizens. The Trump administration has repeatedly downplayed this problem, but ProPublica recently did great reporting documenting reports of 506 citizens detained by DHS between January 2025 and September 2026.

double quotation markWill Craft, data editor at the Guardian US:

It’s hard to know how often us citizens are being arrested, the impact from immigration enforcement goes way beyond just the person getting arrested. We know for a fact that immigration is impacting US citizens across the country and there are lots of families with mixed statuses. When a person is arrested, the impacts reverberate throughout a family and a community. We sued the Trump administration for records on the people being arrested, and found that the data had a column for the citizenship of the person’s children. Thousands of parents, nearly 7,500 fathers and 1,000 mothers in the first 7 months of the Trump admin, had a different nationality than at least one of their children. In about half of these families, siblings had different citizenships from each other. That means that those families faced incredibly difficult decisions about how they might get split up. Taken together, it really seems like a new family separation crisis created by the US government.

Share

Updated at 12.37 EDT

Has Trump's immigration agenda contributed to a drop in visits to the US?

Mr_202 from comments: Has there been a drop in visitor numbers to America either as tourists or migrant workers and if so, are US voters and businesses feeling the economic pinch?

double quotation markMaanvi: It’s hard to pin down exactly how much US tourism has been affected by Trump’s immigration crackdown. But various Trump policies have certainly made it more difficult for people from certain countries to visit the US – either as tourists, or academics and students, or business visitors.

Earlier this year, union leaders in the hospitality industry said that the immigration crackdown has not only scared immigrant workers in the tourism indosuty, but also discouraged international tourism.

The number of employed hospitality workers dropped by 98,000 from December 2024 to December 2025, according to a report from Unite Here, which represents 300,000 workers across the hospitality, food and tourism industries in the US and Canada.

double quotation markJosé Olivares: The Welcome Corps refugee program, like all refugee programs in the US, was canceled and shut down by the Trump administration in early 2025. This was then compounded with further constraints on refugee communities and their ability to enter the US via travel bans — all through executive order. We recently reported on how the US is admitting only 17,500 refugees for Fiscal Year 2027, but they will “primarily” be white Afrikaners from South Africa. The administration’s refugee policies are now leaving thousands of vetted and approved refugees stuck in refugee camps or in dangerous conditions, including relatives of US citizens. It is hard to speculate, but a Democratic majority in congress would have a very challenging time reinstating the refugee and resettlement programs. Congress would have to introduce and then pass new legislation to override Trump’s refugee and “travel ban” executive orders, which would be a lengthy and difficult battle. At the moment, there is a major lawsuit playing out in a federal court that is challenging the administration’s refugee policies and executive orders. Maine, where polling indicates a deadlocked Senate race(link is external), is seeing depressed exports(link is external), canceled foreign investment projects, and decreased tourism(link is external) amid the U.S. trade war with Canada. The Republican Senate candidate in that race, Susan Collins, has criticized the president’s levies on the bordering country and spoke of her work in Congress to exempt key Canadian products(link is external) like road salt and cement. Trump, meanwhile, said he is close to a trade deal with Mexico in an October 19 rally in Kansas(link is external), a traditionally Republican state with an atypically close Senate race that counts Mexico as its top trade partner(link is external).

Trump has made immigration enforcement and border security centerpieces of his presidency. In his second term, daily immigrant encounters at the southern border have dropped 95 percent(link is external) compared with during the Biden administration(link is external). A March survey by the Civic Health Institutions Project recorded support for Trump’s immigration policy at 37 percent, but just 11 percent of Democrats support it, compared with 78 percent of Republicans(link is external). Democrats’ disapproval is driven by their objection to Trump's aggressive tactics(link is external), such as pausing visa and asylum applications, increasing immigrant detentions, and expanding ICE actions.

As part of his immigration strategy, Trump has struck bilateral deportation deals with countries in Latin America while also ending migrant protections known as TPS for Haitians, Hondurans, Nicaraguans, and Venezuelans. On the ground. Immigration is animating campaigns on both sides of the aisle(link is external). Two of Trump’s most decisive foreign policy in Latin America actions have been his January removal of Venezuelan leader Nicolás Maduro(link is external), leaving interim President Delcy Rodríguez to govern in his stead, and his ongoing oil embargo on Cuba. text:
Temporary Protected Status (TPS) continues to evolve as the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) reviews country designations and courts weigh in on the agency’s authority to terminate protections.

Recent TPS terminations, court challenges and agency guidance have created uncertainty for employers and foreign nationals navigating changing work authorization requirements.

As the TPS landscape continues to shift, Jennifer Yeaw, Managing Attorney, breaks down frequently asked questions, explains recent developments and highlights what employers and affected individuals should know moving forward.

What Is Temporary Protected Status?

TPS is a temporary humanitarian immigration benefit that allows eligible nationals of designated countries to remain and work in the U.S. when conditions in their home country prevent a safe return. DHS may designate a country for TPS due to armed conflict, environmental disasters or other extraordinary and temporary conditions.

Individuals granted TPS may:

Remain lawfully in the U.S. during the designation period;

Apply for employment authorization;

Obtain a Social Security number and work authorization documentation; and

Be protected from removal while TPS remains in effect.

TPS does not provide a direct pathway to lawful permanent residence or U.S. citizenship.

Additionally, TPS designations are temporary and may be extended, redesignated or terminated by DHS depending on evolving conditions in the designated country.

Why Has TPS Been in the News?

Over the past 18 months, DHS has moved to terminate TPS designations for several countries while courts have reviewed challenges to those decisions.

As a result, TPS beneficiaries, employers and immigration professionals have had to navigate a series of agency announcements, court orders and temporary extensions affecting work authorization and employment eligibility verification requirements.

While some TPS designations have been terminated, others remain subject to ongoing litigation, making it important for employers to stay informed about the latest developments.

Employer Obligations and I-9 Reverification Considerations

Employers should closely monitor TPS-related developments and maintain processes for tracking employees who rely on TPS-based work authorization. When a TPS designation is terminated, an automatic extension expires or a TPS-related Employment Authorization Document (EAD) is no longer valid, employers may need to complete Form I-9 reverification to confirm an employee’s continued authorization to work in the U.S.

To remain compliant, employers should:

Maintain accurate records of employees’ work authorization expiration dates;

Monitor DHS, USCIS and E-Verify guidance for changes affecting TPS beneficiaries;

Reverify affected employees when required under Form I-9 rules; and

Ensure reverification is conducted consistently and without discrimination.

Because TPS-related developments can change quickly, employers and foreign nationals should regularly review USCIS, DHS and Envoy Global updates for the latest country-specific guidance.

Frequently Asked Questions about TPS

What happens if a TPS designation is terminated?

DHS must publish a termination notice with an effective date typically 60 days from the date of publication. Please note that ongoing litigation can impact the effective date and grace period. Once TPS ends, the TPS holder is no longer protected from removal based on the TPS alone.

Can TPS holders switch to a different work visa or immigration status?

Yes, if they are eligible for another category. We highly advise seeking an assessment from immigration legal counsel to explore possible options.

Does ending TPS affect pending visa or green card applications?

Options here are case-specific. A TPS holder may still be able to pursue permanent residency if they have alternative eligibility not based on the TPS category that was terminated.

Does TPS count as lawful status?

While an individual is protected under TPS, they are in a “lawful” status and authorized to stay in the U.S. and/or pursue alternative immigration status pathways if eligible.

text:
Months after training thousands of Minnesota residents to observe ICE operations, a local group has shifted to training voters in what they call democracy defense. Trainers aim is to prepare voters to respond if federal officials interfere with people’s ability to cast their ballots next month.

On a recent Sunday, about two dozen people filtered into a mostly windowless room at a library in the southern suburbs of the Twin Cities to get trained on election protection. Jessi Meliza, one of the volunteer trainers for the day, got active this winter during the ICE surge into Minnesota with the Unidos project Monarca, which trained tens of thousands of Minnesotans about their rights to observe and document the actions of federal agents.

“Constitutional observer [training] is very straightforward. There's a triggering action. You know what to do. You do it, and then you go home,” Meliza said. “With election defense, it's much more nebulous, much more conceptual. So we're really focusing on what mechanisms allow things like fascism to take hold, and then what does that look like to combat it in a meaningful way?”

The trainers walk participants through basic steps they can take: voting early, driving neighbors to the polls, or identifying misinformation. They ground the training in Constitutional language, but Meliza said they also emphasize how important it is to build trust and relationships with your neighbors.

“Nobody really knows the right way to do it, but [we want to] dispel some of the hopelessness, show people they do have power, and then give some actionable things they can do toward feeling better in general,” Meliza said.

Participants also consider how they’d react in what may seem like far-fetched scenarios, like the collapse of communication networks. How would they stay informed and in contact with allies?

“What the other side is counting on is that we're not going to react in an organized manner, that we're just going to descend into chaos, and everyone's going to bump into walls and be screaming, ‘Everything is on fire!’” Meliza said. “That's really what we're trying to combat.”

Residents already wary of federal intervention after Metro Surge

Minnesota residents have been on edge following the federal government’s surge into Minnesota this winter, which included two fatal shootings of civilians by federal agents. The Trump administration has also pressured election officials across the country by seeking access to voter rolls, including in Minnesota, although federal judges have so far batted down those efforts.

According to reporting from NPR, the Department of Justice plans to monitor elections in Ramsey and Hennepin Counties. State officials say the federal government also sent monitors during primary elections in August, but the monitors did not interfere with the process.

The group’s election protection trainings have already been going on for months and will continue until the election. Unidos Minnesota Executive Director Emilia Gonzalez Avalos said Monarca was launched in 2025 to help provide infrastructure for people to organize themselves.

“Monarca is like a vertebrate. It expands when it needs to expand, and it contracts when it needs to contract,” Avalos said. “These are basic organizing lessons that sometimes we forget: You support people making a choice, sometimes you get out of the way.”

The groups shifted their focus to elections partly to ensure people are prepared if the ICE observer trainings during the surge gave Minnesotans the tools to help protect their immigrant neighbors, Avalos said. The next stage is for people to realize that they also have a personal stake in this democracy and that elections need to be protected to maintain anyone’s rights. She said it’s also a way to be sure that the grassroots muscles Minnesotans exercised during the surge don’t atrophy.

Minnesota Secretary of State Steve Simon wants to reassure voters that the state has strong laws governing elections, including limits on how federal law enforcement can interact with voters. Law enforcement can’t preemptively be placed at the polls, but can be summoned to a precinct if there’s a disruption. But, generally, no one who isn’t an election volunteer, voter or worker in the building is allowed within 100 feet of the entrance.

“I'm confident not only that we have really good and precise laws in place, but that our partners at local units of government will enforce those laws,” Simon said.

Simon urges anyone who sees anything inappropriate at their voting place to talk to the head precinct judge and contact his office. If US Department of Justice observers do visit precincts, as they did during the primaries, state officials would investigate to ensure they are following the rules.

As the election approaches, Simon said voters should be wary of disinformation and seek out credible sources. But if something unexpected does happen, he said Minnesota and other states will be ready at the institutional level. They’ve been planning with election officials and attorneys general from across the country.

“Sadly, this year one of the hazards potentially is that the federal government will do something that will interfere directly or indirectly with the election,” Simon said. “It may not happen. I hope it doesn't happen. But we have to drill and war game those things, and we have been doing that now for months.”

Moriah O’Malley, now a leader with the group, said she considered herself just a bit of an activist before the surge. She’d call her congresspeople or attend a protest. But these sorts of trainings have opened her up to the possibility that people organizing their own neighborhoods and communities can be a transformative force in a democracy.

“I recognize that the skills and experience that I have is valuable to contribute,” O’Malley said. “When we all combine those, we can create a much better solution than the world that we have been given so far, and we can really craft the future that we deserve.”

description:

text:
The U.S. Department of Defense has reportedly decided to conduct test operations of a non-lethal "heat-ray weapon" that causes skin pain through high temperatures. The department is also developing tactics to deploy this weapon for immigration enforcement along the southern border. Controversy has arisen over the inhumane treatment of migrants as if they were enemy combatants.

CNN reported on the 21st that U.S. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth approved the test operation of the heat-ray weapon, the "Active Denial System (ADS)," to the Department of Homeland Security last month. The agreement involves lending the ADS for seven months, with the Department of Homeland Security taking full responsibility for developing operational tactics and equipment management. Details such as the test location remain unconfirmed.

The ADS, initially developed by the U.S. Air Force Research Laboratory and the Joint Non-Lethal Weapons Directorate, fires a 100kW electromagnetic beam at targets up to approximately 800 meters away, inducing intense heat sensation on the skin. The outermost layer of skin, containing microscopic moisture and fat molecules, heats up, causing individuals to instinctively move away after just 1-2 seconds of exposure. The pain lasts 10-15 minutes, but no side effects such as cancer or corneal damage were reported during development. At specific frequencies, the absorption depth is shallow, penetrating only about 0.4mm into human skin tissue—sufficient to reach pain receptors on the skin’s surface without affecting subcutaneous fat or internal muscle layers.

The weapon is mounted on tactical trucks or large transport vehicles and operated using optical/electronic targeting cameras and joysticks. It can sweep wide border areas or target specific sections of a crowd. The U.S. military deployed the ADS on M977 military trucks in Afghanistan during wartime in 2010 but never used it in combat, reportedly due to concerns that enemy forces might label it an "inhumane microwave device" in propaganda. In 2018, during the first Trump administration, the U.S. Customs and Border Protection (CBP) considered using the ADS to disperse undocumented immigrants, but the plan never materialized.

Critics warn of potential safety risks if the weapon is used for immigration enforcement. For instance, migrants near rivers or streams might flee into deep water, risking drowning. Firing the weapon on individuals in Mexican territory before they cross the border could also spark diplomatic disputes. Additionally, international agreements discourage treating migrant groups as enemy combatants.

A federal appeals court has dealt another setback to state efforts to restrict how federal immigration officers conduct enforcement operations, permanently blocking a California law requiring officers, including Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agents, to visibly display identification while on duty.
The appeals court concluded that California’s identification requirement improperly regulated the federal government’s operations, violating principles of federal supremacy, and doing so without approval from Congress.
The decisions underscore the legal challenges states face when attempting to impose new transparency and accountability requirements on federal immigration officers.
In Maryland, the state’s 2026 law, enacted through Senate Bill 1, restricts face coverings for law enforcement officers and establishes identification requirements, including provisions affecting federal immigration officers.
The dispute also highlights an important distinction for county governments that challenges to requirements imposed on federal officers do not invalidate rules governing state, county, and local law enforcement.

In a recent ruling, following an appeal by the US Department of Justice, the Ninth Circuit Court of Appeals has struck down a California law requiring Immigration and Customs Enforcement officials to wear identification.

A federal appeals court has dealt another setback to state efforts to restrict how federal immigration officers conduct enforcement operations, permanently blocking a California law requiring officers, including Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agents, to visibly display identification while on duty. The October 14 ruling by the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit follows an earlier decision by a federal judge blocking California’s ban on law enforcement officers wearing face coverings.

The appeals court concluded that California’s identification requirement improperly regulated the federal government’s operations, violating principles of federal supremacy, and doing so without approval from Congress. The decisions underscore the legal challenges states face when attempting to impose new transparency and accountability requirements on federal immigration officers.

The California decision follows a similar ruling in New York, where U.S. District Judge Mae D’Agostino issued a preliminary injunction on August 3 blocking enforcement of provisions banning federal immigration officers from wearing masks and requiring them to display identification. As previously reported on Conduit Street, the judge found that the federal government was likely to succeed in arguing that the requirements improperly interfered with federal authority. Together, the California and New York cases provide significant legal precedent for the federal government’s challenges to similar state policies.

In Maryland, the state’s 2026 law, enacted through Senate Bill 1, restricts face coverings for law enforcement officers and establishes identification requirements, including provisions affecting federal immigration officers. The U.S. Department of Justice filed a lawsuit on October 1 challenging Maryland’s law, arguing that state and local governments cannot directly regulate federal officers carrying out their official duties. The California and New York rulings strengthen the federal government’s legal arguments and raise questions about whether Maryland’s requirements for ICE officers would withstand judicial review. However, the precise effect will depend on the Maryland litigation and the scope of any court order. The dispute also highlights an important distinction for county governments that challenges to requirements imposed on federal officers do not invalidate rules governing state, county, and local law enforcement.

title: A Philosopher Makes the Case to Call Trump Evil | The New Republic
authors: Samuel Clowes Huneke, hitmakers Samuel Clowes Huneke, AFTERMATH Laura Marsh, muskworld David Klion, Swedish Meatball Alex Shephard, Mark Krotov
description:
More surprisingly, Democratic congressmen and senators largely stayed mum in the face of administrative evil.
In her new book, the philosopher Susan Neiman, recently retired director of the Einstein Forum in Berlin, takes Americans to task for failing to call Trump and his administration what they are: evil.
Evil isn’t what you think it is, but rather the inability to recognize evil.
Neiman’s account of actual evil is thus strangely bloodless, the many atrocities of the last two years glossed over.
Neiman’s definition of evil as an absence of moral reasoning also makes it difficult for her to recommend solutions.
text:
On the evening of March 15, 2025, while government lawyers haggled in a D.C. courtroom, three airplanes delivered 238 chained prisoners to the Terrorism Confinement Center in El Salvador. Better known as CECOT, the center is little more than a twenty-first-century concentration camp, where conditions are tantamount to “torture,” in the words of a Salvadoran jurist. According to Kilmar Ábrego García, a U.S. resident who was sent there for three months in early 2025 as the result of an “administrative error,” inmates are subjected to “severe beatings, severe sleep deprivation, inadequate nutrition, and psychological torture.”

A grotesque abuse of human rights, the administration’s illegal deportations to CECOT caused a furor across the country. Despite the outrage, however, most elected officials remained silent. Republican lawmakers, perhaps unsurprisingly, either demurred or supported the president. Then–Secretary of Homeland Security Kristi Noem visited the facility, posing in front of a cage brimming with prisoners while sporting a $50,000 watch.

More surprisingly, Democratic congressmen and senators largely stayed mum in the face of administrative evil. “Democrats cannot say a word, apparently,” ex-Republican Bill Kristol seethed on March 31, “without going through some filter of what pollsters have been telling you.” Of the 47 members of the Senate Democratic caucus, only a handful criticized the deportations (and in April, Maryland Senator Chris Van Hollen visited Ábrego García in El Salvador). In May, a group of centrist senators introduced a milquetoast fact-finding bill—while deportees languished in the prison.

Their fecklessness was, unfortunately, not an anomaly. Despite Democrats’ eagerness to point out the economic missteps of Trump’s second term, the party’s leaders and most prominent figures rarely denounce its worst human rights violations (which have primarily targeted immigrants and trans people, two groups that most Democratic politicians avoid talking about like the plague). And while the party has spent over a decade warning American voters about the threat Trump poses to democracy, it has done little to actually defend it: Senate Democrats routinely vote to confirm Trump nominees (every one of the party’s senators voted to confirm Marco Rubio as secretary of state), favor arming the executive branch with authoritarian powers such as warrantless wiretapping, and have approved slates of Trump-nominated judges.

In her new book, the philosopher Susan Neiman, recently retired director of the Einstein Forum in Berlin, takes Americans to task for failing to call Trump and his administration what they are: evil. Declining to do so, in her view, is not merely a moral failing but has real-world ramifications. “Our culture’s reluctance to trade in moral ideas,” she writes, “has left them to right-wing demagogues and brought us to this pass.” A demand for moral clarity in an amoral world, Call It Evil: Understanding the Trump Era urges us to face “the moral ideas that Donald Trump embodies and reinforces, ideas that are destructive enough to warrant the word evil.”

In making a case to think about the Trump administration in these terms, Neiman offers a potent rebuke to those who would rather talk about “kitchen table issues” than torture. Yet her peculiar definition of evil makes it difficult to actually face the worst cruelties of this administration and to pin down who, precisely, she is talking about when she suggests that “we’ve lost confidence in moral conviction.”

“Make America moral again,” Joe Biden stated on April 30, 2019, when asked if he had a motto to contrast with Trump’s, “Make America great again.” It is not controversial to state, however, that after four years in power, numerous legislative accomplishments, and every effort to restore a measure of comity to American politics, Biden failed in his goal.

Some would undoubtedly point to the genocide in Gaza, mass slaughter that Biden’s administration did nothing to halt, besides throwing off a few tepid rebukes. Others might point to economic insecurity. As the celebrated economist Isabella Weber took to saying in those years, “Inflation kills governments.” While Neiman is unlikely to disagree with these assessments—a chapter of the book is devoted to Gaza, naming it “the moral watershed of our time”—she argues that the true culprit of our present malaise is the neoliberal ideology of self-interest; that, in the words of Gordon Gekko, “Greed is good.”

Neoliberalism is a word thrown around so freely that it has lost much of its meaning. But it did once refer to a specific political agenda that sought not only to unshackle the “free” market, but also to apply market logic to all spheres of life, hence the all-too-common refrain that governments or universities or other public goods should be “run like a business.” In Neiman’s view, this ideology arose from a bastardized reading of Adam Smith: a free market regulated only by the self-interest of its actors. This belief in a “rational” market was, Neiman adds, complemented by similar misreadings of Charles Darwin, which developed “increasingly baroque explanations of human behavior” to show that this self-interest is evolutionary in its origins. The terminus of this ideology is nihilistic: In a world where everyone is out to maximize profit, “moral concepts are for suckers.”

The more we are convinced that people are “rational” actors motivated only by greed, in short, the more likely we are to act that way. We live in a country where we’re told to look out for ourselves alone, to get ahead whatever the cost. In the process, Neiman contends, “the very idea of social rights,” by which she means everything from housing to education to health care, has become “anathema,” precisely because it infringes on the sovereign self-interest of the individual. But depriving citizens of these rights—or passing them off as “a safety net”—has real consequences. “The undercurrent of anger,” which Neiman contends characterizes American society, arises from the subconscious knowledge that it’s nigh impossible to get by this way, that the American dream is little more than a “mirage.” Trump is an expression of that rage, a symptom of a broken system and a bankrupt ideology, rather than its cause.

Neiman is certainly not the first to make this diagnosis. The book departs from other recent works on neoliberalism and twenty-first-century fascism in its focus on evil, which Neiman movingly defines as the “idea that arises whenever the gap between the way the world is and the way the world ought to be becomes too big to bear alone.” Pointing to Hannah Arendt’s formulation of the “banality of evil,” she insists that in order to recognize evil in our own time, we must get away from the assumption that it only appears “as demons in jackboots.” Anyone can do evil. Thus, “the worst kind of evil” is not any particular expression of it, but rather “the refusal to recognize morality at all.”

It’s a beautifully simple formulation. Evil isn’t what you think it is, but rather the inability to recognize evil. It echoes Franklin Delano Roosevelt’s stirring dictum that “the only thing we have to fear is fear itself.” And yet, if prompted, most of us would likely come up with rather a different definition. We might arrive at a definition closer to that offered by Judith Shklar, a Harvard philosopher who was intrigued by the role of emotions in rational government. “Human cruelty,” she wrote, is not only “a distinct and unmitigated evil,” but is the “most evil of all the evils.” In Shklar’s view, the hallmark of a civilized society was its intolerance of cruelty.

Disdain for cruelty is precisely what has gone missing in the Trump era and what sits behind the fanaticism of the president’s most ardent supporters. What, after all, is “owning the libs” if not an indulgence in cruelty for cruelty’s sake? The protesters at No Kings marches and anti–Immigration and Customs Enforcement demonstrations know this. Adam Serwer knew it when he wrote in 2018, “The cruelty is the point.”

Neiman certainly gestures to the everyday atrocities of the last two years, acknowledging that Trump “reflects a culture that sells cruelty as entertainment.” Still, in her view, “faith in the tyranny of self-interest” is “far more significant than vicious or malicious cruelty” because it has allowed “cruelty to become ordinary.” Yet, that logic, as much as we might wish to believe it, doesn’t sustain the barest interrogation. There are plenty of neoliberal societies in which cruelty has not become normalized in the way that it has in the United States. There have been plenty of cruel societies that were not neoliberal in nature. And history is littered with examples of evil committed in the name of morality.

Neiman’s account of actual evil is thus strangely bloodless, the many atrocities of the last two years glossed over. “Counting crimes,” in her view, “is pointless.” A reader will search in vain for descriptions of the CECOT deportations, mentions of Alligator Alcatraz, or the number of innocents who have died in ICE custody. The so-called “Department of Government Efficiency,” which wrecked swathes of the government, putting thousands of dedicated public servants out of work and leading to the deaths of at least seven hundred thousand recipients of U.S. aid, is likewise nowhere to be found. And if you’re looking for sympathy with trans people, whose rights are being systematically shredded, forget it. Neiman tiptoes up to the line of blaming them for their own predicament, writing that a 2019 ACLU questionnaire, which asked if candidates would “ensure that transgender and nonbinary people who rely on the state for medical care—including those in prison and immigration detention—will have access to comprehensive treatment,” was “a thumb in voters’ eyes.”

That kind of slippage is, unfortunately, more a feature than a bug in Neiman’s writing. With a fondness for dramatic claims, she often invokes straw men. “Why aren’t more of us in the streets?” she asks, apparently unaware that more Americans are protesting now than in Trump’s first term. Likewise, she suggests that the word fascist “fell into disuse after Trump began his second term.” Really? Perhaps most egregiously, she contends that the famous gender theorist Judith Butler recently said, “Of course there has been progress in my lifetime; now people can change their pronouns.” In Neiman’s view, “A clearer statement of woke bankruptcy has yet to be made.” The only problem? I’ve found no evidence that Butler ever said such a thing.

In fact, “the woke” (a term that Neiman does not define, instead arguing that “woke eludes definition because it’s an incoherent concept”) feature prominently in the book’s concluding section. In her view, “the woke” embraced an identity politics that, much like the reactionaries they claimed to oppose, abandoned morality in favor of tribalism. Because of their insistence on a radical kind of social justice that equated progress with “oppression” and reason with “domination,” this amorphous group of figures (Biden, Neiman assures us, “was woke but not left”) “clearly played a role in the second election of Donald Trump.”

Neiman’s fascination with wokeness (three years ago, she published a book titled Left Is Not Woke) means that although she has indeed identified real flaws in American politics and diagnosed a real inability to speak about them in moral terms, the book is criticizing the wrong people. Why, one might reasonably ask, does it not take aim at the centrists, at the politicians, journalists, and intellectuals who for years stoked fears of cancel culture and wokeness, who compared leftist efforts at social justice to fascism? Where is Bari Weiss, who in a few short years has evolved from “a self-styled free speech martyr” to propagandist-in-chief at CBS News? It is these same figures who breathlessly warned about the danger from the left but have gone silent in the face of state efforts to censor the media, shred academic freedom, intimidate political opponents, punish those who have protested Israel’s genocide in Gaza, and strip migrants of even a vestige of rights or dignity. Senator Chuck Schumer, whose main objection to the administration’s deportation regime seems to be its lawlessness rather than its cruelty, is never mentioned. Nor is John Fetterman, who has become Israel’s greatest cheerleader on Capitol Hill throughout its atrocities in Gaza. Why are these figures—rather than “the woke”—not the ones whom Neiman chastises?

Neiman’s definition of evil as an absence of moral reasoning also makes it difficult for her to recommend solutions. While contending we could all learn “impatience with clichés,” she resorts to her own clutch of them, arguing that we ought to start “defending truth” and “renewing the moral concepts the right has trampled.” I’m not sure moral handwringing is worth much to the hundreds of babies and toddlers who have been disappeared into ICE custody since the administration took office.

Instead, we could start by acknowledging the truth that a great many ordinary Americans have been moved to action by the moral atrocities they are witnessing each and every day. Communities from Minneapolis, Minnesota, and Portland, Oregon, to Austin, Texas, and Cambridge, Massachusetts, have banded together against federal overreach and to protect their neighbors from ICE. State governments have passed measures protecting access to abortion and gender-affirming care. More and more progressives are winning elections, speaking not only about economic justice but also with equal fervor about the moral stain that this administration has visited upon the American people and in which the American people are, to our everlasting shame, complicit.

text:
Pete Hegseth, the US secretary of defense, reportedly signed a memo last month permitting the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) to test a non-lethal “heat ray” for potential use at the US southern border.

The “heat ray”, known as the Active Denial System, is a military-grade weapon that shoots an energy beam causing “a sensation of intense heat on the surface of the skin”, according to a 2009 National Defense University case study on the weapon.

The sensation “creates an intolerable sensation and reflexive movement” such as ducking or running.

In a memo, first obtained by CNN, Hegseth authorized a “temporary loan” of the Active Denial System to the DHS for seven months beginning in September. The DHS can request further use of the Pentagon system if needed.

A spokesperson for Customs and Border Protection (CBP) said in a statement it was “continually evaluating new technology, especially technology that can save lives while simultaneously enhancing national security effectiveness”.

When asked for comment, the Pentagon referred the Guardian to the DHS, which shared the CBP statement.

It is unclear what the DHS plans to use the Active Denial System for exactly, but the memo permits the department to use it for potential operations at the US-Mexico border.

The US military initially brought the system to Afghanistan nearly 20 years ago, but it was quickly returned home without ever being used, the Washington Post reported.

Previously, CBP officials reportedly considered using the Active Denial System in areas with a large number of illegal crossings or for crowd dispersal, but it was never deployed.

When used, the Active Denial System can produce an invisible beam of 95 gigahertz that penetrates about 1/64th of an inch into the skin, causing a burning sensation. (The system is technically not a “heat ray” because it uses millimeter waves, not infrared, Forbes reported in 2020.)

Pentagon officials have compared the feeling to a blast of heat when opening a hot oven, according to CNN. The feeling is temporary, lasting between 10 and 15 minutes.

In 2012, the Marine Corps announced that the system was compliant with international legal obligations of the US, and officials said they felt “comfortable” that it was safe.

The new memo, seen by CNN, states that the DHS will be solely responsible for the system’s “employment, use and development of tactics, techniques and procedures”. It also states that no Department of Defense personnel shall operate it.

What to know:

Republican Mike Rogers and Democrat Abdul El-Sayed traded sharp criticism during a debate less than two weeks before Election Day.

Rogers highlighted manufacturing job losses and high utility and auto insurance costs, while El-Sayed emphasized lowering living costs and expanding access to health care.

El-Sayed criticized Rogers’ alignment with President Donald Trump’s policies. Rogers countered that El-Sayed repeatedly invoked Trump in his answers.

Rogers accused El-Sayed of wanting to defund law enforcement, an allegation El-Sayed denies.

Rogers defended Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE), while El-Sayed criticized the agency’s tactics.

Rogers called El-Sayed’s health care proposal too expensive. El-Sayed accused Rogers of being too closely aligned with the pharmaceutical industry.

Rogers warned of economic consequences if Iran obtained a nuclear weapon, while El-Sayed accused Rogers of repeatedly advocating for war.

El-Sayed opposed the Safeguard American Voter Eligibility (SAVE) Act, calling it voter suppression. Rogers supported requiring photo ID to vote.

The candidates also debated education, cybersecurity and Michigan’s future.

SOUTHFIELD, Mich. — U.S. Senate candidates Mike Rogers and Abdul El-Sayed traded sharp criticism during a debate less than two weeks before Election Day, making their closing pitches to Michigan voters on issues including the cost of living, immigration enforcement, and the war in Iran.

Rogers focused on the loss of Michigan manufacturing jobs and high utility and auto insurance costs.

He also accused El-Sayed of wanting to raise taxes. El-Sayed emphasized lowering living costs and expanding access to health care, while accusing Rogers of closely aligning with President Donald Trump’s policies.

“You’re gonna hear a form of MAGA bingo, because the thing about MAGA is whenever they’re talking, they are trying to distract you,” El-Sayed said. “They’re going to use buzzwords.”

Later in the debate, Rogers countered: “The bingo game ought to be how many times can he put the word Trump in any answer that he has given.”

El-Sayed and Rogers clashed about public safety, with Rogers accusing El-Sayed of wanting to defund law enforcement, which El-Sayed denies, and other topics ranging from how to improve education in Michigan to cybersecurity.

The candidates also clashed over immigration enforcement. Rogers defended Immigration and Customs Enforcement, saying it has pursued “rapists and murderers, and gang bangers, and drug dealers, and human traffickers” and has had “a tremendous impact on crime.”

El-Sayed criticized the agency’s tactics, saying, “He supports ICE running through your streets. They don’t have to tell you who they are. They don’t have to tell you why they’re there.”

The candidates also again clashed over El-Sayed’s Medicare for All plan. Rogers said other Democrats wouldn’t support the plan because “it’s outrageously expensive.”

“We cannot afford to have a United States Senator who is in bed with big Pharma,” El-Sayed said during his rebuttal.

On Iran, Rogers warned that allowing the country to obtain a nuclear weapon could mean voters would “pay $8 a gallon of gas.”

El-Sayed accused Rogers of promoting war for years, saying, “He’s got a war for everything, and he won’t back off the war now.”

When asked about the Safeguard American Voter Eligibility (SAVE) Act, which would require voters to show a photo ID at the polls, El-Sayed said he opposed the bill, calling it voter suppression.

Rogers said he would support it, calling it “reasonable and rational” to ask for voter ID.

TROY — Rensselaer County Sheriff Kyle Bourgault and County Executive Steven F. McLaughlin say this week’s arrest of a 25-year-old Guatemalan man accused of raping a 16-year-old girl is an example of why the county must be allowed to continue its cooperation agreement with U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement.

Troy police said they arrested the suspect, Kovy B. Carillo-Flores, on Monday and charged him with four counts of third-degree rape, a felony, for allegedly having sexual contact with the girl, who was unable to legally consent due to her age. Deputy Police Chief Steven Barker said in a news release Tuesday that Carillo-Flores bit an officer trying to arrest him on Fifth Avenue and that another officer sustained a wrist injury during the struggle.
