Barker said Carillo-Flores was familiar with the alleged victim, but would not disclose further details of their relationship to protect her privacy. Carillo-Flores was arraigned Tuesday morning and is being held at the Rensselaer County jail.

During a news conference Wednesday, Bourgault and McLaughlin framed Carillo-Flores’ case as a reason they have joined a lawsuit that was filed in federal court challenging a new state law that bans law enforcement agencies from having formal agreements with ICE. Their lawsuit targets Gov. Kathy Hochul and state Attorney General Letitia James, who are both strong proponents of the ban.

It’s unclear whether Rensselaer County sheriff’s officials verified Carillo-Flores' citizenship using federal immigration databases.

Rich Crist, a spokesperson for the county, said their agreement with ICE enables the county to access a federal database known as Person Centric Query Service that was developed by U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services. It allows authorized government officials to view an immigrant’s or nonimmigrant’s history across multiple federal, state, and private databases.

Advertisement

Article continues below this ad

The county’s agreement was put in place in 2018 under a congressionally authorized statute. It states that it is “designed to identify and process removable aliens” within Rensselaer County’s correctional facilities. The recently passed state law prohibiting those agreements prompted 15 sheriff’s departments, including Rensselaer County’s, to file the lawsuit challenging the ban. According to the lawsuit, the 287(g) agreements must be canceled by Nov. 25.

Hochul’s prior public statements and the language of the new statute make clear that the law was intended only to prevent state and local police agencies — and other government workers — from assisting in civil immigration enforcement under formal agreements with ICE. But according to the sheriffs' court filings, virtually none of the local sheriff’s departments involved in the case conduct civil immigration enforcement that is not tethered to a person charged with a crime.

The state law banning the formal agreements is also being challenged in an ongoing lawsuit filed by the U.S. Department of Justice against the state of New York in June.

McLaughlin claimed that without an ICE agreement, their county would have more difficulty communicating with the federal agency and finding information about suspects' criminal histories.

Advertisement

Article continues below this ad

“If we can’t use that 287(g) database and that person is in our jail, we don’t know what other crimes he is wanted for,” McLaughlin said.

At the news conference, Bourgault would not disclose whether the county used the federal database to perform a background check on Carillo-Flores.

McLaughlin called Carillo-Flores an “illegal alien” and said he admitted to being a citizen of Guatemala.

“We are 100% confident that (Carillo-Flores) is here illegally,” McLaughlin said.

Advertisement

Article continues below this ad

Asked how local authorities verified Carillo-Flores' citizenship status, Bourgault said the man “admitted” he was from Guatemala and that law enforcement used “investigative efforts” to confirm the information, but declined to provide further information. Bourgault would not say if authorities used the federal database to inspect his background when he was taken to the county jail.

According to McLaughlin, ICE issued an immigration detainer for Carillo-Flores shortly after he was taken to the Rensselaer County jail. The detainer requests the county hold an “alien” in custody for up to 48 hours beyond the time they would normally be released, according to ICE’s website.

Bourgault said Carillo-Flores, who is being held without bail, is expected to appear in court Friday. If he is released, “ICE is going to be there,” the sheriff noted.

Formal cooperation agreements between localities and ICE have for 30 years enabled the federal agency to train local officers to conduct some immigration enforcement in exchange for federal funding. Bourgault has previously said Rensselaer County does not receive funding in exchange for its participation.

Advertisement

Article continues below this ad

The federal statute that authorizes the agreements — Section 287(g) of the Immigration and Nationality Act — was added to the Illegal Immigration Reform and Immigrant Responsibility Act of 1996, which was adopted during President Bill Clinton’s administration. The legislation was amended in 2002 to authorize the secretary of the Department of Homeland Security to enter into written agreements with state and local agencies “so that qualified personnel can perform certain functions of an immigration officer.”

Hochul has for years suggested that state and local law enforcement agencies could still assist federal agencies in matters involving “serious crimes,” but the new state statutes — and policies already implemented by State Police — do not define a “serious” crime. The governor has also said repeatedly that crossing a U.S. border without authorization is “a civil violation” and “not a crime,” but that is misleading. People who cross a U.S. border while evading a checkpoint are routinely prosecuted for the misdemeanor in U.S. District Court.

Hochul has also drawn a distinction between law enforcement agencies assisting ICE and other federal agencies with civil enforcement or matters involving criminal conduct.

In August, she reiterated that the law banning the agreements applies only to “civil” immigration enforcement. She added: “Once they’re convicted and do their time, we work with ICE to ensure they’re deported.”

title: When denying a stay denies the rule of international law | SCOTUSblog
description:
Yet the D.V.D.
It’s news that spells trouble for anyone concerned with immigrant rights and the rule of international law.
*** D.V.D.
But even more disturbing was any apparent engagement with international law, much less international human rights.
So too with D.V.D.
text:
Just as the 2026-27 term was getting underway, the Supreme Court once more sided with the Trump administration with a stay order in what has been variously called the emergency, shadow, interim, or equity docket. The case, Department of Homeland Security v. D.V.D., involved the government’s plan to deport undocumented persons without a hearing to third countries where they might be subject to torture or other persecution.

Though the stay generated some publicity, the court permitting a Trump policy plausibly seen as violating fundamental rights pending further review is, by now, hardly news. Yet the D.V.D. order is newsworthy in another regard. It brings together the court’s now familiar emergency docket leanings with another tendency – its increasing disregard, if not antipathy, to international human rights law. That combination is not only news. It’s news that spells trouble for anyone concerned with immigrant rights and the rule of international law. Still less does any of this bode well given that the court has now granted cert to consider the merits.

***

D.V.D. involves a class action on behalf of undocumented aliens subject to a February 2025 Department of Homeland Security policy mandating immediate removal from the United States to a third country. Immediate means just that. Those subject to the new initiative would have no opportunity to argue that they have a valid fear of torture or other forms of mistreatment to the new destination, so long as DHS received “credible,” non-individualized “diplomatic assurances that [any person being deported] will not be persecuted or tortured.” For all other countries the detainee would have 24 hours to demonstrate that it would be “more likely than not” that she or he would be subject to persecution or torture. If so, the case would be referred to an immigration judge. If not, Immigration and Customs Enforcement must “consider” filing a motion to reconsider or select another country.

The named plaintiffs demonstrate the dangers the third-country policy poses. Each one goes by only initials. D.V.D. is a Cuban national with severe mental illness who is afraid of deportation to a country where he will be deprived of psychiatric treatment and be imprisoned on arrival. O.C.G is a gay man from Guatemala who already “has faced multiple death threats on account of his sexual orientation" in his home country and “was kidnapped and raped” in Mexico. M.M., a citizen from Honduras, had been severely beaten by her husband and dreads him finding her in a “third country,” as he already did once. As members of a certified class, they, by definition, share common questions of law and fact with countless others.

The key common question of law and fact for the current stay centers on whether DHS must provide persons it intends to remove to a third country: 1) notice of which third country to which it intends to remove the individual; as well as 2) a meaningful opportunity to show the basis for a fear of likely being subject to torture or persecution.

Those challenging the DHS policy rely on two federal statutes. In particular, section 241(b)(3)(A) of the Immigration and Nationality Act, codified as 8 U.S.C. section 1231(b)(3)(A), provides that “the Attorney General may not remove [a noncitizen] to a [third-country] if the Attorney General decides that the [noncitizen’s] life or freedom would be threatened in that country because of the [non-citizen’s] race, religion, nationality, membership in a particular social group, or political opinion.” Likewise, section 2242(a) of the Foreign Affairs Reform and Restructuring Act, codified as a statutory note to 8 U.S.C. section 1231, states that that it shall be the policy of the United States “not to expel, extradite, or otherwise effect the involuntary return of any person to a country in which there are substantial grounds for believing the person would be in danger of being subjected to torture, regardless of whether the person is physically present in the United States.” The regulation implementing this policy provides that “[i]f the immigration judge determines that the alien is more likely than not to be tortured in the proposed country of removal, the alien is entitled to protection under the Convention Against Torture.”

Neither statute expressly requires notice and an opportunity to be heard. Nor do the related regulations to implement the statutes, which provide for individualized consideration of persecution and torture claims, but do not expressly prescribe prior notice nor an opportunity of such.The U.S. District Court for the District of Massachusetts and the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 1st Circuit nonetheless held that they are best read as implicitly requiring those protections. These holdings asserted that the two laws, together with associated regulations, are most sensibly read to require procedural protections giving a person notice of which third country to which they will be removed and an opportunity to demonstrate that they would face torture or persecution there. Bolstering these interpretations was the venerable cannon of constitutional avoidance: Not to require notice and an opportunity would risk interpreting the two statutes in a way that would violate procedural due process under the Fifth Amendment. As Justice Louis Brandeis perhaps most famously articulated the canon, “it is a cardinal principal that the Court will first ascertain whether a construction of [a] statute is fairly possible by which the question [of its constitutionality] may be avoided.”

The Supreme Court subsequently granted a stay on the ground that the government would likely succeed on the merits. The court’s lack of any substantive explanation for its ruling, which has become commonplace on the emergency docket, was troubling enough. But even more disturbing was any apparent engagement with international law, much less international human rights. Even as background, that body of law would appear to be relevant to a situation involving one country detaining asylum speakers claiming to escape severe persecution from their nation, only to send them to another potentially authoritarian state without any opportunity to demonstrate that their removal would subject them to the same type of mistreatment that caused them to flee their home country to begin with. As it happens, this case invites and even compels consideration of international law as a matter of well-settled U.S. legal doctrine.

***

A cornerstone of both international refugee and human rights law goes under the French term, non-refoulment. Under this doctrine, a nation may not oblige a person to return – refoule – to a territory where “where his life or freedom would be threatened on account of his race, religion, nationality, membership of a particular social group or political opinion." This prohibition appears in several landmark treaties, including the 1951 Refugee Convention, its 1967 Protocol, and the 1987 Convention Against Torture and Other Cruel, Inhuman or Degrading Treatment or Punishment. It is also widely accepted that the principle of non-refoulment has attained the binding status of customary international law. Through both its treaties and international custom, this obligation applies to the United States.

International non-refoulement also implicates corollaries directly relevant to the Supreme Court’s consideration. The UN Committee Against Torture, which implements CAT, has stated that diplomatic assurances from a state are not sufficient to justify refouling an individual where there is clear evidence that the receiving state would engage in torture or other mistreatment. More generally, the Executive Committee of the UN Office of High Commissioner for Refugees has set out extensive procedural protections to enable a person to argue against deportation to a state likely to engage in persecution, including some, like the right to consult a UNHCR representative, that go well beyond the opportunity sought by the asylum seekers in D.V.D. These bodies, like the district court and 1st Circuit on domestic grounds, concluded that the right against non-refoulement would mean little unless the person facing persecution had some opportunity to contest the removing government’s say-so.

How a nation’s international law obligations do or do not come down into its domestic legal system could well fill up a year of columns. Suffice is to say in the present case several well-settled American legal doctrines invite, if not mandate, their application.

The most obvious route involves FARRA and congressional intent. In 1988 President Ronald Reagan, with the advice and consent of two-thirds of the Senate two years later, made the U.S. a party to CAT. Congress enacted FARRA in particular to incorporate CAT’s provisions with respect to non-refoulement. Indeed, the statute tracks CAT’s language closely, making it the policy of the United States “not to expel, extradite, or otherwise effect the involuntary return of any person to a country in which there are substantial grounds for believing the person would be in danger of being subjected to torture, regardless of whether the person is physically present in the United States.”

Both the lower federal courts in D.V.D. noted FARRA’s general purpose to incorporate CAT’s non-refoulement prohibition en route to holding that the substantive limit on removal would have little practical meaning without the procedural protection of a deportee’s opportunity to be heard. They could have gone even further. A more powerful argument would have been to emphasize Congress’ intent to bring the U.S. in line with not just CAT, but with the global legal commitment to non-refoulment – a commitment at least worth a mention by name.

Then there is the Charming Betsy. In that celebrated 1804 case, Chief Justice John Marshall proclaimed that “an act of congress ought never to be construed to violate the law of nations, if any other possible construction remains.” Applying the Charming Betsy canon, any ambiguities in the INA, which is not directly tied to CAT, or for that matter FARRA itself, should be interpreted in a way that avoids placing the U.S. at risk of violating evolving customary international law. Among other things, that means not naively relying on a state’s diplomatic representations that it is not repressive. No less importantly, it also confirms that argument that the right not to be refouled means little without an opportunity to contest the refoulement.

Finally, there is the federal court’s authority to effectively fashion national common law rules to draw upon even those international standards that have yet to achieve the near universal status of international custom. Here the precedent is the court’s landmark 1964 decision in Banco Nacional de Cuba v. Sabbatino. In that case, the court applied that act of state doctrine, which holds that the courts of one nation state will accept the official acts of another undertaken within its own borders, to side with a Cuban state bank over a U.S. corporation. This it did even though the majority held that the doctrine had not achieved the status of binding customary international law. But the court applied the doctrine in any event using its Article III judicial power to fashion rules out of respect for international comity and widespread practice.

So too with D.V.D. Even if one views the procedural protections against non-refoulement as not quite a matter of binding international custom, Sabbatino affords the federal courts a rationale to mandate them nonetheless. Doing so, moreover, would have the further basis of the well-established power of the federal courts to fashion common law rules to fill, in the words of Judge Henry Friendly, the “interstices” of federal statutes.

text:
WASHINGTON – The United States Department of Homeland Security (DHS) released the following statement after a U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) facility was firebombed in Atlanta, Georgia.

On the evening of October 20, 2026, a male suspect threw an improvised incendiary device toward the ICE Enforcement and Removal Operations (ERO) Field Office in Atlanta. Miraculously, the device did not reach the facility, as it became caught on the top of the perimeter fence.

“This latest attack is part of a dangerous and unacceptable escalation of violence against the men and women of ICE who are simply enforcing the laws of the United States,” said DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin. “Irresponsible rhetoric from sanctuary politicians and radical activists has contributed to a massive increase in violence and threats against federal law enforcement officers performing their Congressionally-mandated duties. ICE officers are facing a more than 1,600% increase in assaults against them. Assaults on our officers and facilities will not be tolerated. Anyone who targets federal law enforcement will be prosecuted to the fullest extent of the law.”

At approximately 9:00 p.m. EST, the subject threw a bottle, later identified as an improvised incendiary device, toward the facility. The device failed to clear the perimeter and became caught on top of the fence. An Atlanta Police Department (APD) officer in the immediate vicinity observed the incident and attempted to apprehend the subject by chasing him on foot. The suspect fled the scene.

Image

The improvised incendiary device

Image

The perimeter fence that the device got caught on after it was thrown

Law enforcement partners, including the Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI), Homeland Security Investigations (HSI), and APD, are actively investigating the incident.

This incident follows a pattern of escalating violence against ICE facilities and personnel nationwide. The brave men and women of ICE continue to put their lives on the line every day to arrest criminal illegal aliens, including murderers, rapists, gang members, and terrorists, and make our communities safer.

text:
During the early months of President Donald Trump’s second term, the federal government detained and sought to deport several students and academics because of their support for Palestine. The Supreme Court could soon take up the cases of two of those detainees, Mahmoud Khalil and Badar Khan Suri, both of whom have since been released. The issue at the center of these cases is whether federal trial courts have the power to consider challenges to the two men’s detentions, or whether (as the Trump administration argues) those challenges are instead barred by federal immigration law.

The Trump administration has urged the Supreme Court to grant both petitions, telling the justices that the court’s “review is warranted to resolve” a conflict among the federal courts of appeals “over a question of immigration jurisdiction that affects tens of thousands of cases.” “Left unchecked,” U.S. Solicitor General D. John Sauer wrote, “such suits risk producing an overwhelming litigation burden on both the government and the courts.”

Sauer made that claim in the case of Suri, an Indian national with a Ph.D. in Peace and Conflict Studies who came to the United States in 2022 for a postdoctoral fellowship at Georgetown University. Sauer’s wife is a U.S. citizen of Palestinian descent; her father once served as an adviser to a leader in the Palestinian militant group Hamas.

In March 2025, Suri – who contended that he had “never even been to a protest” – was approached outside his suburban Virginia apartment by masked officers who told them that they were from DHS, that he was being arrested because of his “social media,” and that the government planned to deport him that day. (An analysis by The Hoya, the Georgetown University student newspaper, found that Suri’s social media posts “frequently express support for Palestine, especially since the Oct. 7, 2023, attack on Israel by the Palestinian militant group Hamas and Israel’s subsequent invasion of Gaza,” but that Suri “has never openly advocated breaking U.S. law.”) Secretary of State Marco Rubio had determined that Suri’s “Hamas associations and advocacy compromised the United States’ foreign-policy interests, thereby rendering him deportable.”

Suri’s attorney went to federal court in Virginia to seek his release. He argued in a habeas petition, which is a brief asking a federal district court to review the legality of his detention, that (among other things) Suri had been detained in retaliation for his speech. The district court issued an order on March 20 that barred the government from deporting Suri, and in May it instructed the government to release him on bail.

The U.S. Court of Appeals for the 4th Circuit turned down the government’s request to pause the district court’s ruling while it appealed, and in an opinion on July 23, 2026, that court upheld the district court’s decision.

The Trump administration came to the Supreme Court on Sept. 21, asking the justices to decide whether a noncitizen like Suri who is placed in immigration detention while the government seeks to deport him can challenge his detention in a habeas petition when his claims are also related to whether he can be removed. Sauer wrote that federal immigration law generally requires all challenges “arising from” deportation proceedings or the decision to begin such proceedings to go first to a federal appeals court, rather than a district court. “That naturally includes claims raised by an alien that reduce to the assertion it is illegal to detain him for all of the same reasons that it is ultimately illegal to remove him.”

Sauer told the justices that, in addition to granting the Trump administration’s petition for review in Suri’s case, they might also want to take up the case of Mahmoud Khalil, an Algerian citizen who was born in a Palestinian refugee camp in Syria and became a lawful permanent resident of the United States in 2024. Doing so, Sauer said, “would guard against the possibility that either case might become moot” – that is, no longer a live controversy – if, for example, either man leaves the United States.

Khalil was arrested on March 8 at his apartment building in New York City, where he had recently received a master’s degree from Columbia University. Khalil, who is married to a U.S. citizen, describes himself as a “lifelong advocate for Palestinian human rights” who has also “condemned anti-Semitism.” In the wake of the Oct. 7 attacks in Israel, Khalil participated in the pro-Palestinian protests at Columbia.

The government sought to deport Khalil based on Rubio’s determination that Khalil’s “participation and role[] … in antisemitic protests and disruptive activities” would “compromise a compelling U.S. foreign policy interest.” On March 19, a federal district court in New Jersey barred the government from deporting Khalil to give that court time to consider his habeas petition. Khalil alleged, among other things, that his detention violated both the First Amendment, because it was intended to retaliate against him for his support of Palestine and to deter others from expressing that same support, and the Fifth Amendment, because it was intended to punish him. Approximately three months later, the New Jersey district court ordered Khalil’s release on bail.

In January of this year, a divided three-judge panel of the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 3rd Circuit ruled that the district court did not have the authority to consider Khalil’s challenges. “The scheme Congress enacted governing immigration proceedings provides Khalil a meaningful forum in which to raise his claims later on—in a petition for review of a final order of removal,” the majority wrote.

After the full 3rd Circuit declined to weigh in, Khalil came to the Supreme Court on Monday, asking the justices to take up his case. He stated that federal law “channels most challenges to the validity of a final order of removal through the administrative process and” petitions for review “of a final removal order to the court of appeals. But it does not, and could not, consistent with the U.S. Constitution, strip habeas courts of” the power to hear “constitutional challenges to executive detention that is retaliatory in violation of the First Amendment and punitive in violation of the Fifth Amendment.”

Suri’s response to the government’s petition for review is due on Nov. 20; the government’s response to Khalil’s petition will also be due in late November. The justices will likely consider both petitions at a private conference sometime early next year.

description:

Where a beneficiary will work in multiple locations, the lowest qualifying wage level applies; where more than one registration is submitted for the same beneficiary, the lowest wage level among them applies.
Level IV wages receive four entries in the selection pool, Level III three, Level II two, and Level I one.
On March 27, 2026, DOL published anotice of proposed rulemaking covering H-1B, H-1B1, E-3, and PERM cases.
Under the order, agencies may look at how a filing's job description, wage level, and stated business need line up with the employer's recent workforce decisions.
text:
Within twelve months, the H-1B program has moved from an unweighted random lottery to a lottery weighted by wage level. A six-figure payment restriction has been extended by proclamation, while courts have blocked enforcement of the agency policies used to implement it. A separate six-figure fee remains proposed. Since September, an executive order has also directed agencies to consider specified workforce reductions in H-1B-related decisions.

These developments have different legal status. Some are in effect, others remain proposed, and agency implementation of the proclamation-based payment is currently blocked by court orders. Together, they affect cap selection, potential sponsorship costs, prevailing-wage methodology, and agency review.

From Random Selection to Wage-Weighted Registration

A central change concerns how registrations are selected for the annual H-1B cap.

A Department of Homeland Securityfinal rule published on December 29, 2025, and effective February 27, 2026, replaced unweighted random selection with a wage-level-weighted random selection process beginning with the FY 2027 cap season.

When properly submitted registrations exceed projected demand, USCIS assigns each unique beneficiary a weight based on the highest Occupational Employment and Wage Statistics (OEWS) wage level that the offered wage meets or exceeds for the occupation and area of intended employment. Where a beneficiary will work in multiple locations, the lowest qualifying wage level applies; where more than one registration is submitted for the same beneficiary, the lowest wage level among them applies.

Level IV wages receive four entries in the selection pool, Level III three, Level II two, and Level I one. The annual numerical limits are unchanged: 65,000 under the regular cap and 20,000 under the U.S. advanced-degree exemption.

The distinction matters. A higher wage does not guarantee selection, and a lower wage does not make a registration ineligible. The offered wage changes the odds of reaching the petition stage.

The September 2026presidential proclamation extending the entry restriction also reported changes in the selection pool. According to the proclamation, registrations for beneficiaries with at least a U.S. master’s degree rose from 45.1% of FY 2026 registrants to 66.1% for FY 2027. Offers at the two highest wage levels accounted for approximately 46.3% of selections, compared with 17.8% at the lowest level. The proclamation attributes these shifts to the “combined effect" of the $100,000 payment and the weighted selection process. It does not attempt to separate the effect of either measure, and the figures are the administration's own assessment.

Sponsorship Costs Become a Separate Point of Uncertainty

Selection is not the only development affecting employers. The cost of sponsorship is now the subject of two separate measures that operate through different legal mechanisms. One is the $100,000 payment tied to presidential proclamations restricting entry of certain H-1B workers. The other is DHS’s proposed $103,265 filing fee for cap-subject petitions.

The two measures should not be treated as interchangeable. The proclamation-based payment has been extended, but court orders currently block enforcement of the agency policies used to implement it. The $103,265 fee remains only a proposal and would have no effect unless DHS issues a final rule. Together, they create uncertainty about whether, and through what authority, additional sponsorship costs may apply in future H-1B cases

The $100,000 payment and the court challenges

Proclamation 10973, signed September 19, 2025, and effective September 21, 2025, restricted the entry of certain H-1B workers unless their petitions were accompanied or supplemented by a $100,000 payment, subject to specified exceptions. Proclamation 11069, signed September 18, 2026, extended the restriction until September 21, 2027.

The payment and its implementation have been challenged in at least three federal courts, with conflicting results so far.

On June 8, 2026, the U.S. District Court for the District of Massachusetts vacated the agency actions implementing the payment in State of California v. Mullin, No. 1:25-cv-13829-LTS (D. Mass. June 8, 2026). On July 24, the First Circuit denied the government’s request to stay that ruling pending appeal.

A separate ruling followed on September 30. In Global Nurse Force v. Trump, No. 4:25-cv-08454-HSG (N.D. Cal. Sept. 30, 2026), the court granted in part a motion for a preliminary injunction, vacating the agency policies that implement the payment and barring their enforcement under both the 2025 proclamation and the 2026 extension until the agencies complete notice-and-comment rulemaking and Regulatory Flexibility Act analyses. The court did not vacate or enjoin the proclamations themselves and did not decide the claims against the President. The district court denied the government's request for a stay pending appeal in its September 30 order. The district court denied the government's request for a stay pending appeal in its September 30 order. The government filed a notice of appeal to the Ninth Circuit on October 9. As of October 15, no stay had been granted.

Not every court has ruled against the payment. In an earlier decision, Chamber of Commerce v. DHS, No. 1:25-cv-03675 (D.D.C. Dec. 23, 2025), the district court upheld the proclamation and its implementing policies as within the President's authority under INA § 212(f). The Chamber's expedited appeal (D.C. Cir. No. 25-5473) was argued on March 9, 2026, and remained undecided as of October 15, 2026.

As of October 15, 2026, the proclamations remain in effect, but the agency policies used to collect the payment are blocked by court orders. Appeals are pending in the First, Ninth, and D.C. Circuits. The distinction between the proclamations and the policies implementing them is central to the current legal position.

A separate $103,265 fee proposal

A separate regulatory proceeding also bears on sponsorship costs.

On August 25, 2026, DHS published aproposed rule that would impose a $103,265 fee at filing for H-1B petitions subject to the annual cap, including those eligible for the advanced-degree exemption.

As proposed, the fee would apply to 'all H-1B cap-subject petitions' and would not apply to cap-exempt petitions, which DHS identifies as including petitions covered by INA § 214(g)(7). Because § 214(g)(7) generally prevents workers already counted against the cap from being counted again, extensions, amendments, and change-of-employer petitions for those workers would ordinarily fall outside the fee, although the NPRM does not list those petition types. The proposed text also does not distinguish by the beneficiary's location; read as written, it would reach cap-subject petitions for individuals already in the United States, including change-of-status requests. That differs from the proclamation-based payment, which applies to beneficiaries outside the United States.

DHS describes the proposal as a way to recover a portion of the costs that multiple federal agencies incur in administering the lawful immigration system. It estimates the fee would generate about $8.8 billion annually. The comment period closed on September 24, 2026. The fee is not in effect unless DHS issues a final rule.

The proposed fee and the disputed $100,000 payment are separate measures with different legal bases and procedural histories. Neither is currently a universally applicable, collectible charge on H-1B petitions.

Prevailing Wages Could Also Change

Sponsorship costs are only part of the picture. The Department of Labor has separately proposed changing how prevailing wages are calculated.

On March 27, 2026, DOL published anotice of proposed rulemaking covering H-1B, H-1B1, E-3, and PERM cases. The proposal would raise the percentile thresholds behind the four wage levels: Level I from the 17th to the 34th percentile, Level II from the 34th to the 52nd, Level III from the 50th to the 70th, and Level IV from the 67th to the 88th. According to DOL, the change would align prevailing-wage levels more closely with wages paid to similarly employed U.S. workers.

The comment period closed on May 26, 2026, but the proposal has not become a final rule. The existing methodology remains in effect unless and until DOL finalizes a change.

If finalized, the proposal could increase applicable prevailing-wage levels and therefore affect the wage obligations employers must meet for covered positions. Any practical interaction between revised prevailing-wage levels and the weighted-selection process would depend on the final text of any DOL rule and subsequent agency implementation.

Layoffs Enter the H-1B Review Framework

The most recent development shifts attention from the offered position to the employer's broader workforce decisions.

On September 18, 2026, the President signedExecutive Order 14431, Enhancing Program Integrity and Interagency Coordination in the Administration of the H-1B Nonimmigrant Visa Program.

The order directs the Secretaries of State, Labor, and Homeland Security, 'consistent with' specified INA provisions, including the LCA requirements in § 212(n), to take into account, in any H-1B labor condition application (LCA), petition, visa, and entry, whether the employer sponsor directly or indirectly engaged in layoffs within the previous year or plans future layoffs that negatively affect the employment of similarly situated United States workers. Workforce history and planned reductions therefore become relevant at several decision points, not only at the petition stage.

The order does not prohibit sponsorship after a layoff. It also does not say that a workforce reduction alone requires an adverse decision. It directs agencies to take the circumstances into account, which leaves open how the information will be weighed.

The order also calls for interagency coordination. State, Labor, and Homeland Security must coordinate and consult with Commerce, Education, and the Small Business Administration. Those agencies are directed to provide relevant wage, employment, academic, industrial, or other economic information. The order delegates the President's authority under INA § 215(a) to the Secretaries of State, Commerce, Labor, and Homeland Security, to the extent necessary to implement the order, including authority to issue or adopt rules, policies, and operational or other guidance.

Separately, within 30 days of the order, DOL’s Wage and Hour Division must begin reviewing data on previously submitted LCAs to determine whether further action is warranted under INA § 212(n)(2)(G). The order requires the review to begin. It does not predetermine the outcome.

How the New Directive Differs From Existing Layoff Rules

Layoffs were already relevant to certain H-1B cases before EO 14431.

H-1B-dependent employers and employers found to be willful violators must makeadditional attestations, including non-displacement attestations, for covered LCAs. LCAs that the employer designates for use only with "exempt" H-1B workers, meaning those paid at least $60,000 a year or holding a master's or higher degree in a specialty related to the job, are outside those additional obligations.

Existing displacement regulations prohibit covered employers from displacing a U.S. worker from an essentially equivalent job during the 90 days before or after filing an H-1B petition supported by a covered LCA. Similar restrictions apply when such an employer places an H-1B worker at another employer's worksite under circumstances indicating an employment relationship with that employer: the H-1B employer must first inquire about the other employer's displacement of similarly employed U.S. workers.

EO 14431 sets a different scope. It is not limited to H-1B-dependent employers or willful violators. It looks back one year and also reaches planned future layoffs. It uses the phrase “similarly situated” U.S. workers without defining how that standard will be applied.

The order does not say whether agencies will adopt, adapt, or depart from concepts in the existing displacement regulations. That choice will matter when the directive becomes operational guidance.

What Remains Unclear

Several practical questions remain open. The order does not define an "indirect" layoff, how agencies will identify similarly situated workers, what scale of reduction will draw closer scrutiny, or what evidence employers may be asked to provide. It also does not say how a layoff will be weighed against other facts in an LCA, petition, visa application, or entry decision.

Consider a company that eliminates certain positions and later files H-1B petitions for roles that appear similar. Whether the two decisions are connected could depend on job duties, qualifications, business purpose, location, and timing. The order directs agencies to consider such circumstances but does not prescribe how.

Future agency guidance, if issued, and any action that follows the Wage and Hour Division review may clarify how the directive will operate. The order does not set a timeline for resolving every open question.

What Comes Next

The core H-1B requirements still apply: wage obligations, the LCA where required, and the specialty-occupation standard. EO 14431 adds workforce reductions to the information agencies are directed to take into account.

Under the order, agencies may look at how a filing's job description, wage level, and stated business need line up with the employer's recent workforce decisions. A workforce reduction may be lawful and made for business reasons, and the order does not say that a layoff forecloses sponsorship.

The next phase depends on four developments: agency guidance implementing EO 14431, the Wage and Hour Division’s LCA review, the appeals over the $100,000 payment, and whether DHS and DOL finalize their fee and prevailing-wage proposals. Together, these developments may shape the FY 2028 cap season, depending on litigation outcomes, final rulemaking, and implementation guidance.

title: Rule 11's Unfulfilled Promise to Protect Noncitizen Defendants - Race, Racism and the Law
description:

Instead, several trends in Rule 11(b)(1)(O)’s application have emerged that reveal the Rule undermines the rights of noncitizen defendants in many cases.

However, this promise was unfulfilled, and the Rule has instead undermined the rights of noncitizen defendants.
text:
Abstract

Excerpted From: Allison McCarthy, Rule 11’s Unfulfilled Promise to Protect Noncitizen Defendants, 90 Missouri Law Review 1169 (Fall 2025) (257 Footnotes) (Full Document).

While President Trump’s mass deportation policies may seem unprecedented, the use of the federal criminal legal system as a mechanism for immigration enforcement is not. The federal criminal legal system has long served as a deportation pipeline. In this system, noncitizen defendants have historically been convicted at disproportionate rates. In his 1995 State of the Union Address, former President Clinton infamously stated, “We are a nation of immigrants. But we are also a nation of laws.” That year, 24.3% of all persons sentenced for federal criminal convictions were noncitizens, despite comprising less than 10% of the country’s total population.

Over the past thirty years, the degree to which the federal criminal legal system is used as a tool of immigration enforcement has grown significantly. During fiscal year 2024, the percentage of all persons sentenced for federal crimes who were noncitizens grew to 34.7%, while noncitizens still accounted for less than approximately 10% of the total population of the United States. Immigration-related crimes also accounted for the largest portion of the total federal criminal caseload.6Policy changes from early 2025 directing the United States Department of Justice to prioritize immigration-related crimes will undoubtedly drive this trend to a greater extreme.

While this data showing the prioritization of noncitizen prosecutions emphasizes the aggressiveness of federal policymakers’ choices, more troubling evidence suggests noncitizens also face unequal treatment within the federal legal system. In fiscal year 2024, noncitizen defendants were more likely than citizens to receive prison sentences, and in the past decade noncitizens’ prison sentences were on average longer than those received by similarly situated defendants who are United States citizens. Even worse, it has become increasingly recognized that two of the most prosecuted immigration-related crimes, improper entry and reentry of removed aliens, have blatantly racist origins.

Exacerbating this concerning data, the federal criminal legal system today is “for the most part a system of pleas.” Almost all convictions of noncitizen defendants result from guilty pleas, following their decision to waive the right to a jury trial among other paramount constitutional protections. The Supreme Court has interpreted the Due Process Clause of the Fifth Amendment to require that guilty pleas be made “voluntarily, knowingly, and intelligently, 'with sufficient awareness of the relevant circumstances and likely consequences.”’ Courts have long recognized that this “voluntary and knowing” requirement protects all defendants regardless of immigration status, and further implicates the interrelated right to effective assistance of counsel of the Sixth Amendment, as well as other overlapping statutory and administrative protections. Included therein is Federal Rule of Criminal Procedure 11, which, since 1966, has required the court to “address the defendant personally in open court and determine that the plea is voluntary.”

For noncitizen defendants, the decision to plead guilty can be even more fraught and complicated than for their citizen counterparts. When contemplating a guilty plea, few criminal defendants weighing the near certainty of conviction at trial against the benefit of a possible reduction of sentence as part of a plea offer would find going to trial to be an attractive option. Noncitizen defendants convicted of crimes, however, must also consider the virtual inevitability of banishment from the United States, including possibly permanent separation from their families or the risk of persecution and torture upon return to their home country. For many noncitizens, deportation is, as the Supreme Court has recognized, “an integral part--indeed, sometimes the most important part--of the penalty that may be imposed.” Given the severity and permanence of those consequences, for some noncitizen defendants “even the smallest chance of success at trial may look attractive.”

In the past several decades, changes in United States immigration law and policy have resulted in more frequent and generally automatic deportations of noncitizens convicted of federal crimes. Courts have therefore faced repeated questions about whether a noncitizen defendant’s guilty plea can be knowing and voluntary if they are not first advised about the resulting immigration consequences. Historically, courts accepted that a defendant must understand certain consequences of a criminal conviction before entering a guilty plea, such as any mandatory minimum prison sentence or fine. Courts saw immigration consequences differently, however. With subtle differences in reasoning, courts almost universally concluded such consequences were collateral to criminal convictions and therefore fell outside the scope of noncitizen defendants’ due process rights, as well as their rights to the effective assistance of counsel.

Then in 2010, the United States Supreme Court held in Padilla v. Kentucky that for noncitizen defendants making the vitally important decision to plead guilty, “the effective assistance of competent counsel” included advice about “whether [their] plea carries a risk of deportation.” In Padilla, the Court refused to characterize deportation as either a direct or collateral consequence of a criminal conviction because of its unique nature, being so severe and so closely related to the criminal process.24Padilla addressed only the issue of effective assistance of counsel for noncitizen defendants. In the years following that decision, however, many advocated for a similar departure from the direct and collateral consequences distinction in the context of due process claims as well. Litigants argued the Supreme Court’s logic in Padilla created a similar duty for courts to ensure noncitizen defendants did not plead guilty ignorant of the resulting immigration consequences.

The Padilla decision prompted the Judicial Conference Advisory Committee on the Rules of Criminal Procedure (“Advisory Committee”) to propose amending Rule 11, which requires courts to advise defendants of certain rights and consequences, including the defendant’s right to a trial and the maximum possible penalty for their crime, prior to accepting a guilty plea. Effective December 1, 2013, Rule 11(b)(1)(O) added the required advisement that “if convicted, a defendant who is not a United States citizen may be removed from the United States, denied citizenship, and denied admission to the United States in the future.” Prior to its adoption, stakeholders argued broadening Rule 11 to require an advisement about what had been traditionally considered a collateral consequence would “turn a plea colloquy into a minefield for a judge.” On the other hand, some expressed concern that the amendment did not do enough to promote fairness for noncitizen defendants and even risked undermining noncitizen defendants’ constitutional rights. Ultimately, however, the Advisory Committee determined that “a general statement of possible immigration consequences in every case” was “good policy,” even if not required by Padilla.

It has now been over a decade since the Advisory Committee implemented the amendment to Rule 11, and this Article is the first to consider whether time has validated or dispelled the original misgivings about the Rule. Unfortunately, Rule 11(b)(1)(O)’s promise to better protect the rights of noncitizen defendants has been unfulfilled. Instead, several trends in Rule 11(b)(1)(O)’s application have emerged that reveal the Rule undermines the rights of noncitizen defendants in many cases. Among other issues, the language of Rule 11(b)(1)(O) is imprecise and misleading to noncitizen defendants who mistakenly rely upon the general warning as advice. Courts also rely upon Rule 11(b)(1)(O) to deny claims of ineffective assistance of counsel, finding the warning remedies any failure by counsel or renders any error harmless. Despite the Advisory Committee’s Note to Rule 11(b)(1)(O) requiring the warning be given in every case regardless the citizenship status of the defendant, many judges continue to ask defendants on the record about their immigration status, infringing defendants’ Fifth Amendment privilege against self-incrimination. Additionally, even if courts do find a violation of Rule 11(b)(1)(O) occurred, noncitizen defendants are often unable to obtain relief for a violation of Rule 11(b)(1)(O) under the harmless-error analysis employed in appellate review of Rule 11 violations.

Given the growing use of the federal criminal legal system as a mechanism of immigration enforcement, and the increasing severity of immigration consequences to noncitizen defendants today, it is time to reimagine Federal Rule of Criminal Procedure 11(b)(1)(O). This Article suggests several practical amendments to the text of Rule 11(b)(1)(O) that would better safeguard the rights of noncitizen defendants and promote fairness in the federal criminal legal system. Additionally, this Article suggests a doctrinal shift may be necessary to truly protect the rights of noncitizen defendants and ensure just outcomes of federal criminal proceedings. Courts must recognize that a noncitizen’s understanding of the immigration consequences of a guilty plea is a fundamental due process issue rather than a merely helpful procedural requirement. This recognition is critical to ensure noncitizen defendants make knowing and voluntary guilty pleas and can obtain relief in the event they do not.

This Article proceeds in four parts. Part I reviews the historical treatment of Fifth and Sixth Amendment protections for noncitizen defendants, including those doctrines as they existed prior to Padilla, the treatment of these issues in the Padilla decision itself, and the major legal developments in these doctrines since that decision was issued. Part II discusses the history and adoption of Federal Rule of Criminal Procedure 11(b)(1)(O), including the Advisory Committee’s goals for the Rule as well as early criticisms and concerns related to the Rule. Part III identifies problematic trends in cases involving violations of Rule 11(b)(1)(O) and argues that courts too frequently undermine the knowing and voluntary nature of noncitizen defendants’ guilty pleas and other important rights. Finally, Part IV advocates for several changes to Rule 11(b)(1)(O) and the legal doctrine surrounding knowing and voluntary guilty pleas that would result in fairer and more just criminal proceedings for noncitizen defendants.

[ . . . ]

The federal-criminal-legal-system-to-deportation pipeline necessitates improving protections of the rights of noncitizen criminal defendants. The Due Process Clause requires that all defendants, regardless of immigration status, plead guilty with full knowledge and understanding of the attendant consequences. Padilla was an important first step toward ensuring noncitizen defendants possess this knowledge. Federal Rule of Criminal Procedure 11(b)(1)(O) then promised an additional layer of protection. However, this promise was unfulfilled, and the Rule has instead undermined the rights of noncitizen defendants. With the benefit of over a decade of hindsight, we must now amend Rule of Criminal Procedure 11(b)(1)(O) so it can more effectively protect the rights of noncitizen defendants. Courts must also recognize that understanding immigration consequences of a guilty plea is a fundamental due process issue rather than a merely helpful procedural requirement to ensure more just outcomes for noncitizen defendants in the federal criminal legal system.

title: Deportations climb under Trump but fall short of White House target, a new report finds
description:
The report by the Migration Policy Institute shows deportations increased from 620,000 during the first year of Trump's second administration.
Trump, a Republican, returned to power last year promising to stanch crossings at the southern border and crack down on immigration.
More people being deported, but not at all-time highs The analysis found that the Department of Homeland Security carried out 980,000 deportations during the first 18 months of the second Trump administration.
Despite the surging arrests, the report details some of the challenges to the Trump administration reaching its deportation targets.
Figures the Trump administration has released are inconsistent and unverifiable.
text:
WASHINGTON – President Donald Trump's administration is on track to deport about 660,000 people over the past year, a new report released Thursday shows, as arrests ramp up across the country fueled by billions of dollars meant to supercharge his immigration agenda.

The report by the Migration Policy Institute shows deportations increased from 620,000 during the first year of Trump's second administration. The numbers fall short of previous highs in the early 2000s and fail to meet the Trump administration's promise, made when it received the billions from Congress, that the money would allow for 1 million deportations annually.

The report, based on publicly available data obtained through Freedom of Information Act requests, comes after the Trump administration in January 2025 stopped publicly releasing similar figures compiled by the Department of Homeland Security.

Trump, a Republican, returned to power last year promising to stanch crossings at the southern border and crack down on immigration. His administration has pushed through restrictions on both legal and illegal immigration and launched high-profile arrest operations in its bid to force migrants out.

More people being deported, but not at all-time highs

The analysis found that the Department of Homeland Security carried out 980,000 deportations during the first 18 months of the second Trump administration.

During the last fiscal year — when the Trump administration's immigration enforcement mechanisms were shifting into high gear — an estimated 660,000 people were deported.

According to MPI's analysis, that's a 26% increase from the yearly average from 2021 to 2024 during the administration of President Joe Biden, a Democrat, but well below the 1.86 million deportations recorded in 2000, under President Bill Clinton, another Democrat.

Despite the surging arrests, the report details some of the challenges to the Trump administration reaching its deportation targets.

Historically, many immigrants living in the U.S. without authorization were from Mexico and didn't often seek asylum. But in recent years, migrants have come to the U.S. from a wide range of countries, which can make it more complicated to deport them. And immigration courts, which ultimately decide whether someone can be removed from the country, face more significant case backlogs.

Voluntary departures are increasing as are interior arrests

The report said voluntary departures — when people give up their cases in immigration court and agree to leave the country — were at an “all-time high,” with 170,000 choosing to do so since Trump returned to office in January 2025. People who choose voluntary departure could one day return to the U.S. But some immigrant advocates and lawyers say that people give up their court fight and agree to leave simply to get out of U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement, or ICE, detention.

The Trump administration was also increasingly deporting people it arrested in the country's interior, the report said, reflecting how it was stepping up enforcement against migrants who have been in the country for a long time. In 2025, about 28% of the people deported were arrested inside the country, but by July of this year that had risen to 39%.

Migrants arrested at the southern border still make up a large number of deportations, the report said — 69% of all deportations between Jan. 20, 2025, and July 31, 2026, were of people initially intercepted at the border.

People in the country longer may have more opportunities to contest their removal while the government typically has greater authority to fast-track deportations for people arrested at the border.

The analysis said most people deported have never been convicted of a crime, despite the Trump administration claiming to be targeting the “worst of the worst.” Previous data has showed the same.

In response to the MPI report, White House spokesperson Lauren Bis said: “President Trump has delivered the largest reduction in illegal immigration in modern history.”

Trump administration no longer regularly releases immigration data

Homeland Security stopped releasing similar data when Trump took office, making it difficult to track one of his key campaign promises. Figures the Trump administration has released are inconsistent and unverifiable.

The administration says it is transparent. On Tuesday, it released some of its own figures as part of a document boasting of its achievements on immigration, including that 1.2 million migrants have been deported or removed during Trump’s second term. The discrepancy could not immediately be reconciled.

In the absence of regular data, analysts and activists interested in immigration trends have relied on information obtained through lawsuits or limited and sporadic information released by federal agencies to track deportation data.

text:
An embrace between a husband and wife who were apart for four days after what one Bronx couple described as a horrifying situation. An immigrant father was detained by U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) and released.

Gagne Diagne, who is originally from Senegal, spoke to NY1 through a translator.

“One of my happiest moments is when I was released, and I came home and saw my baby,” he said.

The 30-year-old has an infant daughter who was born in the U.S., making her a U.S. citizen.

He says that agents approached him near his car around 7 a.m. on Aug. 14 outside his Bronx home. Surveillance video obtained from a nonprofit organization helping with his case, the Amadou Ly Foundation, shows agents approaching him next to the vehicle.

Diagne alleges the agents wore masks and did not initially identify themselves.

“I saw them with masks. I thought they were robbers,” Diagne said. “At this moment, I was shook.”

Diagne says it wasn’t until they reached a nearby gas station that ICE chained his waist, legs and hands, and he says that’s when they identified themselves.

NY1 reached out to ICE to ask about Diagne’s characterization of his arrest and detention. The agency would not respond to his specific complaints, but said in a statement, in part: “ICE officers followed all approved official procedures during the arrest, including identifying themselves as ICE law enforcement officers.”

Diagne said he was taken to 26 Federal Plaza, one of the federal immigration courts in the city, where he said he was held in a small, cold room. He alleges he was forced to sign documents he did not understand because he does not speak English. He said an interpreter was brought in later, but by then, it was too late.

He was allowed to call his wife — who up until that point had no idea her husband had been arrested. His wife, whom Diagne met in the city, agreed to be filmed and interviewed on the condition of anonymity for fear of deportation.

“I felt extreme pain,” she said. “I cried after learning that my husband was apprehended by ICE.”

Diagne said he was later transferred to an ICE detention facility in New Jersey, where he was held for four days. He was released after the Amadou Ly Foundation, which has been assisting West African immigrants in the city, filed a petition on his behalf and a federal judge ordered Diagne released.

ICE old NY1: “Ngagne has multiple arrests for felony trademark counterfeiting and public order crimes. ICE released Ngagne Aug. 19, based on a court order. He will be afforded all due process.”

Diagne said he is innocent and that all charges against him were dismissed. He showed NY1 documentation of a trademark counterfeiting case’s dismissal in June. NY1 reached out to the NYPD for more details on his arrest but has not heard back.

Diagne said he came to the United States through the U.S.-Mexico border in April 2023. He said he was detained briefly in Texas before being allowed to continue pursuing his asylum case in the United States.

He said he was involved in politics in Senegal and came to the U.S. in search of safety. Diagne has a work permit and works as a DoorDash delivery driver, but he said he has not been able to work since his release because he fears being detained again.

“It hurts seriously because if you look at someone in my situation, who’s in charge of everything in this house, because my wife doesn’t work, it is worrying to know that if I’m not there, they’re most likely going to be homeless,” Diagne said.

The Amadou Ly Foundation said it is providing temporary financial assistance to the family. Diagne said that in the meantime, he’s been taking English classes, hoping to get a commercial driver’s license to become a truck driver.

“My biggest dream is to have legal status in this country, be granted the opportunity to stay with my family, and never be separated from them,” he said.

Diagne is continuing to move forward with his asylum case.

He says the next hearing in front of an immigration judge is Dec. 17.

text:
Abstract

Excerpted From: Evelyn Marcelina Rangel-Medina and Hilary A. Symes, Blood, Soil, and Race: The Perils of Shredding the Fourteenth Amendment, 115 Geo. L.J. Online 1 (2026) (209 Footnotes) (Full Document)

Race remains a central organizing principle of U.S. citizenship. By extending birthright citizenship across racial lines, the Reconstruction Constitution established the foundations of a fragile multiracial democracy. That transformation also emerged from profound conflict. The sectional crisis was intensified by Dred Scott v. Sandford, and the Civil War culminated in the adoption of the Fourteenth Amendment’s Citizenship Clause.

However, Reconstruction did not eliminate racial hierarchy. Rather, systems of exclusion and subordination, such as citizenism, adapted to new legal and political conditions. Citizenism distributes racialized rights and belonging through immigration and citizenship status, using formally race-neutral language. Although primarily organized around immigration status, citizenism operates alongside race, nationalism, xenophobia, and religion to produce hierarchies of membership and exclusion.

Citizenism enshrined exclusionary measures in immigration and citizenship law, transmitting precarity across generations. The Naturalization Act of 1790 restricted citizenship to “free white person[s],” and Congress did not fully eliminate racial restrictions on naturalization until 1952. Other measures, including the Page Act of 1875, the Chinese Exclusion Acts (1882-1902), and the Undesirable Aliens Act of 1929, used immigration law to regulate access to civil and political rights along racial lines. For example, the Undesirable Aliens Act criminalized entry into the country by specifically targeting Mexican migrants.

is a contemporary mechanism of citizenism. By conditioning birthright citizenship on parental immigration status, the Order sought to reintroduce lineage-based restrictions into a constitutional framework that has long rejected them. The Order would have disproportionately burdened communities that are targeted by racialized immigration policies and exclusionary citizenship law. Efforts to restrict access to birthright citizenship, coupled with mass deportation campaigns, are implemented against a backdrop of demographic anxieties surrounding the increasingly multiracial composition of this country and the rise of white supremacist ideology in mainstream politics.

Since the ratification of the Fourteenth Amendment, numerous unsuccessful congressional measures have sought to re-whiten birthright citizenship by conditioning access to it based on parental immigration status. The Citizenship Clause limited such restrictions by overruling Dred Scott v. Sanford and invalidating the doctrine of partus sequitur ventrem, which used maternal lineage to deny citizenship to Black people. Consistent with the common-law principle of birthright citizenship, Supreme Court precedent, and federal statutes, the Supreme Court in Trump v. Barbara rejected the government’s argument that a child’s citizenship status should depend on the immigration status of the parent.

Trump signed the Order the day he took office a second time. The following day, lawsuits across the country challenged the Order, including in Washington, Maryland, and Massachusetts. Federal district and circuit courts consistently held that the Order conflicted with the Fourteenth Amendment, United States v. Wong Kim Ark, and federal citizenship statutes. Despite the absence of a circuit split, the Supreme Court granted certiorari before judgment and consolidated the litigation under Trump v. Barbara. The Court heard oral argument on April 1, 2026, and delivered its highly anticipated opinion on June 30, 2026.

Although the Court ultimately invalidated the Order, the litigation reveals that this country’s commitment to racial integration remains deeply contested, despite the Reconstructionists’ greatest aspirations for ending racial subordination. The majority reaffirmed the holding of Wong Kim Ark, that the Fourteenth Amendment made territorial birth, rather than parental lineage, the principal constitutional rule of birthright citizenship. The concurrence rooted its argument in “the entire point of the Second Founding: The Reconstruction Amendments were an anticaste, antisubordination reset for the Nation, not a mere spot treatment for the dark stain of slavery.” The dissents, by contrast, advanced competing understandings of allegiance and political membership that would have effectively reintroduced lineage-based restrictions into our constitutional framework.

This Article argues that the competing opinions articulated across the lengthy Trump v. Barbara decision illuminate the continuing operation of citizenism even after the Court invalidated the Order. Indeed, the Trump Administration’s continued efforts to restrict birthright citizenship, including its subsequent Executive Orders, demonstrate the fragility of our multiracial democracy. This Article then contends that the Order and similar mechanisms to curtail birthright citizenship seek to racially subordinate mixed-status families of color by perpetuating “multigenerational illegality.”

The Article’s argument proceeds accordingly. Part I briefly summarizes the historical and legal underpinnings that led to the adoption of the Fourteenth Amendment’s Citizenship Clause. Considering this context, it examines the litigation in Trump v. Barbara and the Supreme Court’s decision. This Part argues that although race-making was central to the Order, explicit mentions of race were largely absent from the litigation record, except for the Solicitor General referring to immigrants as “illegal aliens.”

Part II explores the racialized principles of birthright citizenship through the lens of citizenism. By disaggregating national origin data for undocumented and temporary-status populations targeted by the Order, the data show that restrictions on birthright citizenship primarily affect communities of color originating from the Global South. At the national level, people of Mexican origin constitute the largest affected population. At the broader regional and racial-group levels, Latinx/e populations constitute the largest affected group, while Asian-origin populations likewise comprise a significant affected population. This Part also shows that comparable congressional or constitutional restrictions on birthright citizenship would produce similar racialized outcomes upon mixed-status communities of color.

Part III examines the multigenerational harms this constitutional regression would inflict on mixed-status families of color. These harms include building inequality within the family structure, facilitating economic exploitation, exacerbating health disparities, and increasing the risk of statelessness. In outlining these harms, this Part analyzes how restricting birthright citizenship based on parental immigration status would transmit multigenerational illegality across generations for mixed-status families of color.

[ . . . ]

Trump v. Barbara resolved the immediate challenge to birthright citizenship, but it did not resolve the broader constitutional conflict over citizenship that citizenism seeks to reconstruct. The litigation itself illustrates why Reconstructionists sought to place the “great question of citizenship” beyond ordinary political contestation. The majority concluded that the Fourteenth Amendment rejected inherited legal status and reaffirmed territorial birth as the constitutional foundation of birthright citizenship. The separate opinions advanced competing historical accounts that would make parental allegiance, rather than territorial birth, constitutionally significant. Yet, as Justice Jackson’s concurrence observed, Reconstructionists did not conceive of citizenship as a zero-sum contest between formerly enslaved people and immigrants. Instead, “Freed Blacks fought for the shared humanity of all people,” and the Reconstruction Constitution ultimately linked “the fates of all” in rejecting systems of inherited subordination. That understanding reinforces the central premise of this Article: the Citizenship Clause was designed to dismantle lineage-based systems of racial subordination that would be reinstituted if restrictions on birthright citizenship are determined by parental immigration status.

Although the Supreme Court foreclosed the Order’s implementation, the broader project of citizenism remains. Indeed, the Trump Administration’s subsequent actions demonstrate that efforts to restrict birthright citizenship continue notwithstanding Trump v. Barbara. The demographic evidence presented in this Article shows that conditioning citizenship on parental immigration status would disproportionately affect communities of color. Moreover, the multigenerational harms examined in this Article--including the manufacturing of family inequality, exacerbating economic exploitation, magnifying adverse health outcomes, and increasing the risk of statelessness-- show that birthright citizenship is a structural safeguard against the perpetuation of multigenerational illegality.

The constitutional stakes, therefore, extend well beyond the Order. As the population of people of color continues to increase, citizenist projects are likely to continue relying on formally race-neutral mechanisms to reproduce racial hierarchy through immigration and citizenship status. The enduring promise of the Reconstruction Constitution and of preserving the foundations of a multiracial democracy demands vigilance to prevent the reemergence of hereditary hierarchy in new legal forms.

Evelyn Marcelina Rangel-Medina is Associate Professor of Law at Temple University James E. Beasley School of Law and a Non-Resident Fellow at the Fred T. Korematsu Center for Law and Equality, University of California, Irvine School of Law.

Hilary A. Symes holds a Ph.D. in Anthropology from Temple University and was a J.D. candidate and research assistant at Temple University James E. Beasley School of Law.

text:
The US State Department has provided asylum officers with internal assessments suggesting that violent crime in Mexico, Honduras, Guatemala and El Salvador is no worse than in some US cities, despite publicly warning Americans about security risks in parts of the same countries, CNN reported Wednesday.

The documents compare crime rates in the four Latin American countries with those in cities including Baltimore, Houston and Memphis.

CNN reported that the documents place less emphasis on human rights abuses, kidnappings and extortion than previous assessments.

Asylum seekers must prove they face persecution at home, with the assessments potentially affecting their eligibility for protection and relocation.

The assessments downplay the dangers posed by criminal groups and weak local institutions, marking a significant shift from previous evaluations despite limited changes on the ground, said Andrew Selee, president of the Migration Policy Institute.

The documents also state that Honduran police are generally willing and able to respond to requests for assistance.

Selee said the assessment overlooked alleged police links to organized crime and the risks of relocating. The State Department said regional experts prepared and reviewed the reports to help US immigration authorities assess asylum claims.

The assessments come as the State Department's annual human rights report has been delayed, leaving officers with alternative information on conditions in applicants' home countries.

Asylum denials reached 94% of cases in June compared with about 50% two years earlier, according to data from Syracuse University's Transactional Records Access Clearinghouse cited by CNN.

"People like me who were warning about this years ago have sadly been proven right, but the problems are gonna be here for a very, very long time," Farage told Fox News Digital in an interview. "Please, please don't make the same level of mistakes that we have," he said in his message to Americans.

Violent riots have erupted across parts of Europe in recent weeks, particularly in France, with Farage pointing to years of mass migration and failed political leadership as key factors fueling the unrest. The Reform UK leader singled out Emmanuel Macron, arguing that the French president should have mobilized the military to confront the violence, after education protests spiraled into riots, destruction and theft.

MACRON JETS OUT OF RIOT-TORN FRANCE FOR GULF TRIP AS POLITICAL PRESSURE MOUNTS

"Meloni's reaction was swifter and a better sign of leadership," Farage said, referring to the Italian leader deploying 500 military troops to Milan in response to recent riots. "I'm concerned that these things could happen here. And I wonder whether a British Prime Minister has got any more courage than President Macron in France," he added.

Farage contrasted Europe's failure to control its borders with President Donald Trump's immigration crackdown in the United States.

"They're crazy, these people. Look at that guy. He's a nutjob," Trump said, in reference to the protester.
