title: With midterms looming, ICE agents investigate suspected voter fraud across Missouri
description:
Federal immigration agents are investigating suspected voter fraud in Missouri as part of a nationwide effort by the Trump administration in the weeks leading up to the midterm elections.
The Department of Homeland Security is using the agency, CNN reports, in President Trump's hunt for widespread election fraud.
One photograph shows a federal agent walking in front of the St. Louis Board of Election Commissioners office.
Denise Lieberman, the director for the Missouri Voter Protection Coalition, called the efforts by HSI “unprecedented” and something she hasn’t seen over two decades on the job.
The Trump administration has faced scrutiny over its claims of voter fraud nationwide.
text:
Federal immigration agents are investigating suspected voter fraud in Missouri as part of a nationwide effort by the Trump administration in the weeks leading up to the midterm elections.

In two social media posts on Sept. 3, the Kansas City office of Homeland Security Investigations said its agents were investigating suspected unlawful voting in St. Louis, citing the agency's commitment to “protecting election integrity and rooting out voter fraud wherever it occurs.”

HSI is Immigration and Customs Enforcement’s investigative arm, which typically deals with criminal matters such as human trafficking, weapons trade and financial fraud. The Department of Homeland Security is using the agency, CNN reports, in President Trump's hunt for widespread election fraud.

One photograph shows a federal agent walking in front of the St. Louis Board of Election Commissioners office. Another shows two HSI agents outside a residential building. The agency posted that agents were “on the ground in St. Louis investigating suspected unlawful voting”; the post does not say when the photographs were taken or how many people are under investigation.

The Trump administration is making a nationwide push to investigate potential voting by people without legal status. On Wednesday, CBS News reported its investigation found that armed federal agents have been knocking on doors in several states, questioning residents about their immigration status and whether they have registered to vote or cast ballots in previous elections.

Missouri is among nine states listed in a federal lawsuit filed Oct. 15 that were targets of the large-scale investigation by Homeland Security Investigations. The suit filed by the League of Women Voters, Electronic Privacy Information Center and League of United Latin American Citizens alleges DHS illegally collected voting records from at least 47 states and combined them with other personal information to attempt to identify noncitizens accused of voting.

Voting rights advocates said HSI’s decision to publicize unfounded investigations amounts to voter intimidation even for eligible Missouri residents. Denise Lieberman, the director for the Missouri Voter Protection Coalition, called the efforts by HSI “unprecedented” and something she hasn’t seen over two decades on the job.

“This is happening now so close to the midterm because narratives about noncitizen voting rile people up and are intended to generate vitriol [and] generate divisiveness,” she said. “This is about fear tactics. This is about intimidation. This is about trying to keep ethnic minority communities from exercising their right to vote.”

A federal judge in California shared many of Lieberman’s sentiments and issued a scathing preliminary injunction late Wednesday, curtailing the DHS’ so-called “Unauthorized Voter Initiative" from executing certain investigations through Election Day.

U.S. District Judge Araceli Martínez-Olguín's decision said the Trump administration’s use of armed agents, unreliable voter data and a social media publicity campaign — specifically noting the two St. Louis posts — likely violated the Voting Rights Act’s protections against voter intimidation.

A separate suit brought against DHS by the NAACP also alleges the administration’s threats to send armed immigration agents to the polls during the November midterms equated to voter intimidation against communities of color.

While federal prosecutors in Kansas City charged at least two Green Card holders this month with voting illegally, including a Cass County man and a McDonald County woman, there is no conclusive evidence of widespread voter fraud in Missouri.

The federal government said that both people were legally authorized to live in the United States but were not eligible to vote in federal elections. The cases are pending.

Robert Patrick, a spokesperson for the Eastern District of Missouri, told STLPR they have not charged any election fraud cases, but Department of Justice policy is to neither confirm or deny when an investigation is taking place.

The Heritage Foundation, a right-wing think tank, has kept a registry of people convicted of voting illegally since 2000. Of the 30 cases in Missouri, STLPR found two tied to people without legal status. The database includes cases involving fraudulent voter registration, forged ballot-petition signatures and other election-related offenses. As of 2022, more than 4.2 million Missourians were registered to vote.

The Trump administration has faced scrutiny over its claims of voter fraud nationwide. In July, the Department of Homeland Security admitted to inflating the number of people without legal status who could be registered to vote.

Across the country, 156 people have been charged with voting-related offenses since the beginning of Trump's second administration, according to Department of Justice figures cited by CBS News. Federal data show there were more than 211 million people in the United States registered to vote in the 2024 presidential election.

ICE, which oversees HSI, did not immediately respond to requests for comment.

This story has been updated.

title: WA AG Nick Brown backs legal challenge to DHS immigration arrest practices – KIRO 7 News Seattle
description:
WASHINGTON — Washington Attorney General Nick Brown has joined a coalition of 22 attorneys general supporting a legal challenge to the Department of Homeland Security’s use of warrantless civil immigration arrests.
The coalition alleges agents routinely fail to determine whether the person poses an escape risk.
The coalition’s filing describes what it said are widespread consequences of aggressive immigration enforcement, including disruptions to public health, education, safety and local economies.
The brief asked the appeals court to consider those community harms as it reviews the challenge to the department’s arrest practices.
Washington is supporting the litigation alongside attorneys general representing states across the country and the District of Columbia.
text:
WASHINGTON — Washington Attorney General Nick Brown has joined a coalition of 22 attorneys general supporting a legal challenge to the Department of Homeland Security’s use of warrantless civil immigration arrests.

The coalition filed an amicus brief Monday in the U.S. Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit, arguing that federal immigration agents routinely make arrests without meeting requirements established by federal law.

Immigration officers making civil arrests without warrants must have probable cause to believe a person is unlawfully present in the United States and likely to escape before a warrant can be obtained. The coalition alleges agents routinely fail to determine whether the person poses an escape risk.

“The Bill of Rights protects the public from unlawful search and seizure, but the administration treats our constitutional protections as optional rather than bedrock requirements,” Brown said. “Checks and balances are essential if we want a country that is both governed and policed fairly.”

Coalition alleges warrantless immigration arrests harm communities

The brief supports litigation in Escobar-Molina v. DHS, which challenges the department’s policies and practices involving warrantless civil immigration arrests in the District of Columbia.

The U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia partially granted a motion for a preliminary injunction in the case on Dec. 2, 2025.

The coalition’s filing describes what it said are widespread consequences of aggressive immigration enforcement, including disruptions to public health, education, safety and local economies.

In Washington, Brown’s office said enforcement tactics have kept students out of school, disrupted agricultural work and discouraged people from seeking medical care. The office also said those practices have hindered access to courts, libraries and grocery stores.

The coalition argued that enforcement activities have weakened families’ financial stability and damaged relationships between immigrant communities and local law enforcement.

Federal agents’ use of ski masks, dark sunglasses, plainclothes, and unmarked vehicles has contributed to fear and uncertainty, according to Brown’s office. It also cited agents’ refusals to identify themselves during enforcement operations.

The brief asked the appeals court to consider those community harms as it reviews the challenge to the department’s arrest practices. Washington is supporting the litigation alongside attorneys general representing states across the country and the District of Columbia.

Joining Brown are the attorneys general of Arizona, California, Colorado, Connecticut, Delaware, the District of Columbia, Hawaii, Illinois, Maine, Maryland, Massachusetts, Michigan, Minnesota, Nevada, New Jersey, New Mexico, New York, Oregon, Rhode Island, Vermont and Virginia.

The filing supports the challenge; it does not itself establish the coalition’s allegations.

text:
Woodland, CA – On Tuesday, Rep. Mike Thompson (CA-04) contacted Acting Director of U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) David Venturella to demand answers following reports that a vehicle operated by ICE personnel struck a pedestrian in Woodland.

“I demand that ICE immediately investigate this incident, fully cooperate with local law enforcement, and ensure that any individuals found to have engaged in misconduct or unlawful behavior are held accountable,” wrote Thompson.

“ICE is not above the law. Its actions have contributed to growing distrust and fear within our communities, making transparency and accountability all the more critical. Federal law enforcement officers must be held to the same standards of accountability as those they are sworn to enforce. Anything less undermines public trust and the rule of law,” he continued.

Thompson also demanded ICE immediately provide the following information to Thompson and his office’s counsel:

A preliminary account of the incident, including the circumstances surrounding the reported collision and whether the pedestrian sustained injuries.

Confirmation that ICE has initiated an investigation and referred the matter to the appropriate oversight authorities.

A description of the steps ICE has taken to cooperate with local law enforcement and preserve relevant evidence.

An explanation of the policies governing the operation of ICE vehicles during enforcement activities and how compliance with those policies will be evaluated in this case.

In addition to contacting Acting Director Venturella, Thompson remains in close communication with local law enforcement and local elected officials as more information becomes available.

Read the full text of Thompson’s letter here and below.

--

The Honorable David Venturella

Acting Director

U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement

500 12th Street, SW

Washington, D.C. 20536

Dear Mr. Venturella:

I write to convey my serious concern regarding reports that a vehicle operated by U.S.

Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) personnel struck a pedestrian in Woodland, California, on October 20, 2026. I demand that ICE immediately investigate this incident, fully cooperate with local law enforcement, and ensure that any individuals found to have engaged in misconduct or unlawful behavior are held accountable.

The safety of our communities must always come first. Federal law enforcement officers have a responsibility to protect public safety, exercise sound judgment, and uphold the law. When an incident involving federal personnel potentially endangers or injures a member of the public, the American people deserve a thorough, impartial investigation and a clear accounting of what occurred.

Accordingly, I request that ICE immediately refer this incident to the appropriate independent investigative authorities. ICE must also fully cooperate with the Woodland Police Department, the Yolo County District Attorney's Office, and any other state or local authorities with jurisdiction over this incident. This cooperation must include making relevant personnel available for interviews and providing access to evidence, including vehicle recordings, bodyworn camera footage, communications, and incident reports, as legally appropriate.

I also expect ICE to take immediate steps to preserve all evidence related to this incident and ensure that its personnel do not interfere with any independent investigation. If the investigation determines that a federal agent violated the law, departmental policy, or applicable standards of conduct, appropriate disciplinary action must follow, including referral for criminal prosecution where warranted.

To that end, I request that ICE provide my office with the following information:

A preliminary account of the incident, including the circumstances surrounding the reported collision and whether the pedestrian sustained injuries.

Confirmation that ICE has initiated an investigation and referred the matter to the appropriate oversight authorities.

A description of the steps ICE has taken to cooperate with local law enforcement and preserve relevant evidence.

An explanation of the policies governing the operation of ICE vehicles during enforcement activities and how compliance with those policies will be evaluated in this case.

ICE is not above the law. Its actions have contributed to growing distrust and fear within our communities, making transparency and accountability all the more critical. Federal law enforcement officers must be held to the same standards of accountability as those they are sworn to enforce. Anything less undermines public trust and the rule of law.

I request an initial response within seven days and continued updates as the investigation proceeds. I expect ICE's full cooperation in establishing the facts and ensuring accountability. To coordinate a response to this letter, please contact my counsel, Eric Hoffman, at eric.hoffman@mail.house.gov in my Washington, D.C., office.

Sincerely,

Mike Thompson

Member of Congress

title: Attorney General Jones Supports Litigation Challenging Unlawful Immigration Arrests
description:
Circuit in support of litigation challenging the U.S. Department of Homeland Security’s (DHS) policy and practice of conducting unlawful warrantless civil immigration arrests.
Under federal law, immigration officers conducting warrantless civil immigration arrests must have probable cause to believe that an individual is unlawfully present in the United States and is likely to escape before a warrant can be obtained.
However, DHS officers routinely carry out warrantless arrests without determining if the individual is an escape risk.
“The Trump Administration is creating and stoking fear in our communities through these unlawful arrests that aim to make a political statement and sow mistrust between law enforcement and the communities they serve,” said Attorney General Jones.
The brief was filed in Escobar-Molina v. DHS, a case challenging DHS’s policy and practice of conducting unlawful warrantless civil immigration arrests in the District of Columbia.
text:
RICHMOND, Va. – Attorney General Jones, as part of a coalition of 21 attorneys general, filed an amicus brief in the U.S. Court of Appeals for the D.C. Circuit in support of litigation challenging the U.S. Department of Homeland Security’s (DHS) policy and practice of conducting unlawful warrantless civil immigration arrests.

Under federal law, immigration officers conducting warrantless civil immigration arrests must have probable cause to believe that an individual is unlawfully present in the United States and is likely to escape before a warrant can be obtained. However, DHS officers routinely carry out warrantless arrests without determining if the individual is an escape risk. It is important to uphold the law and protect public safety, but this does neither. We must adhere to the law when we enforce the law, and so must DHS. There is no justification for the widespread harms of the Trump Administration’s unlawful immigration enforcement practices and the damage it is inflicting on our nation, our Commonwealth, and the rule of law.

“The Trump Administration is creating and stoking fear in our communities through these unlawful arrests that aim to make a political statement and sow mistrust between law enforcement and the communities they serve,” said Attorney General Jones. “Threats to our neighbors, friends, teachers, and families have resulted in widespread fear. President Trump’s DHS continues to strip people of their humanity and dignity, and it continues to exacerbate mistrust when we should be strengthening relationships and transparency between law enforcement and communities. My office will keep using every legal power and tool at our disposal to stand up for our communities and Virginians.”

Across the country, federal immigration agents have escalated their enforcement activities, disrupting communities and undermining public health, safety, education, and local economies. Virginia has seen these harms firsthand, as aggressive immigration enforcement tactics have kept students out of school, disrupted agricultural work, discouraged people from seeking medical care, undermined families’ financial stability, and weakened the relationship between immigrant communities and local law enforcement. Federal agents’ use of ski masks, dark sunglasses, plainclothes, and unmarked vehicles, and refusals to identify themselves while carrying out operations, has further contributed to fear and uncertainty in affected communities.

The brief was filed in Escobar-Molina v. DHS, a case challenging DHS’s policy and practice of conducting unlawful warrantless civil immigration arrests in the District of Columbia. On December 2, 2025, the U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia granted in part a motion for a preliminary injunction.

In filing the brief, Attorney General Jones joins the attorneys general of Arizona, California, Colorado, Connecticut, Delaware, District of Columbia, Hawaii, Illinois, Maine, Maryland, Massachusetts, Michigan, Minnesota, Nevada, New Jersey, New Mexico, New York, Oregon, Rhode Island, Vermont, and Washington.

text:
U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) confirms to 7News Reporter Nick Minock that the agency lodged an immigration detainer against Naim Arrak, an illegal immigrant from Tunisia, who has a lengthy criminal history in Northern Virginia.

Arrak is currently booked at the Arlington County Adult Detention Center.

“ICE is calling on the Arlington County Sheriff’s Office to prioritize the safety of our Northern Virginia communities and honor our detainer, after having lodged numerous detainers against this dangerous criminal illegal alien over the past several years,” ICE told 7News in a statement. “This administration will not ignore the rule of law.”

7News reported on Monday that Arrak has been arrested more than 30 times for more than 90 felony and misdemeanor charges in Fairfax County, Prince William County, Loudoun County, Fauquier County, and Arlington County. The charges include felony abduction, felony assault, aggravated assault with a gun, hit-and-run, larceny, felony larceny, felony burglary, multiple felony weapons charges, multiple felony drug charges, felony fraud, felony vehicle theft, stolen property with intent to sell, flight to avoid prosecution, failure to appear, and release violation.

SEE ALSO | Repeat offender walks after Fairfax prosecutor 'botched' prosecution at trial

Somehow Arrak has had most of his charges dropped by prosecutors throughout Northern Virginia. In some cases, he has served short sentences but then returned to Northern Virginia communities.

On Monday, 7News reported how Fairfax County Commonwealth’s Attorney Steve Descano’s office botched a prosecution against Arrak last week. Arrak was facing felony drug charges that carried a potential sentence of 5-40 years in prison and fines of up to half a million dollars.

Last week, the jury was seated, opening statements were delivered, but then the jury was sent home. That’s because Descano’s office did not publish a witness list of who was expected to testify 14 days before the beginning of the trial, as required by a judge’s order.

Therefore, a judge ruled that certain witnesses were not allowed to testify and the charges were dropped because of Descano’s office’s error.

SEE ALSO | County in Virginia won't work with ICE on gang members and accused terrorists

Arrak is currently facing gun charges, drug charges, and fleeing officer charges in Arlington County.

ICE told 7News that Arrak entered the United States on June 6, 2013, during the Obama Administration on a lawful temporary basis. However, ICE said he “violated the terms of his lawful admission when he failed to depart the country by August 6. He has remained in the United States illegally ever since. He will remain in custody pending removal proceedings and will receive due process.”

But it’s uncertain if the Arlington Sheriff will honor ICE’s detainer against Arrak. The Arlington Sheriff has a policy not to honor ICE detainers.

If the Arlington jail releases Arrak without notifying ICE, ICE will have to search for Arrak in the community as the agency has done in numerous other cases, which ICE has warned can endanger ICE agents and the public.

SEE ALSO | Arlington County sets aside $50K to aid families of ICE detainees

ICE is urging the Arlington and Fairfax County Sheriffs to work with immigration officials.

“7 of the top 10 safest cities in the United States cooperate with ICE,” ICE added. “Partnerships with law enforcement are critical to having the resources we need to arrest criminal illegal aliens across the country. We have had tremendous success when local law enforcement work with us, including 40,000 arrests in Florida and a two-week operation in West Virginia that resulted in the arrest of over 650 illegal aliens. Under President Trump and Secretary Mullin, if you break the law, you will face the consequences. Criminal illegal aliens are not welcome in the U.S.”

title: Pentagon grants DHS permission to test heat ray weapon for potential use at border - WBAL
description:
The energy beam causes a burning sensation when it comes into contact with the human skin — which Pentagon officials have previously compared to feeling a blast of heat when opening a hot oven.
The Pentagon referred CNN to DHS when asked for comment.
Customs and Border Protection officials have previously entertained the idea of using the system in areas where there’s a high concentration of illegal crossings.
Border officials have occasionally discussed potentially using the system as a crowd dispersal tool, but it has never been deployed.
In 2018, prior to midterms, CBP officials also weighed using it against migrants, but then-Homeland Security Secretary Kirstjen Nielsen shot it down.
text:
The Pentagon has given the Department of Homeland Security permission to test a military-grade heat ray and develop tactics to potentially use it in operations at the southern U.S. border, according to a memo signed by Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth last month and obtained by CNN.

The heat ray, officially known as the Active Denial System, is a nonlethal weapon that shoots an invisible beam of electromagnetic waves that can reach a little more than half a mile away, according to the U.S. military.

The energy beam causes a burning sensation when it comes into contact with the human skin — which Pentagon officials have previously compared to feeling a blast of heat when opening a hot oven. Military officials have said the resulting “tingling effect” lasts between 10 and 15 minutes but also generates “an instinctive and irresistible urge to run from the effect.”

Deploying the heat ray at the U.S. border would be an unprecedented step, even for the Trump administration, which has made border security and clamping down on immigration a top priority.

The DHS request did not specify where or how the weapon would be tested and how it might eventually be used, but over the years, there have been internal discussions about potentially using it for crowd dispersal along the U.S.-Mexico border, according to current and former Customs and Border Protection officials.

U.S. officials had also considered deploying the system during moments of domestic unrest, including at the end of President Donald Trump’s first term when protests erupted over the murder of George Floyd, according to a former U.S. official familiar with those discussions.

The memo authorizes the “temporary loan” of one ADS system for seven months, starting in September, and states that it “shall not be operated by DoW (Department of War) personnel,” appearing to absolve the Pentagon of any responsibility for how the directed-energy system may ultimately be deployed.

It also states that DHS is solely responsible for “system employment, use and development of tactics, techniques and procedures.” At the end of the seven-month loan period, DHS can submit an additional request for further use of the Pentagon system in border operations based on need, a defense official told CNN.

“CBP is continually evaluating new technologies, especially those that enhance operational effectiveness and strengthen mission capabilities,” a Customs and Border Protection spokesperson said in a statement to CNN.

The Pentagon referred CNN to DHS when asked for comment.

The U.S. military briefly deployed the system to Afghanistan nearly two decades ago but ultimately declined to use it during active combat operations. The U.S. military also considered using the system for crowd control purposes at U.S. facilities abroad where terrorist detainees were being held at the time but ultimately declined to employ it for that purpose as well, according to a source familiar with those previous internal considerations.

Customs and Border Protection officials have previously entertained the idea of using the system in areas where there’s a high concentration of illegal crossings. Border officials have occasionally discussed potentially using the system as a crowd dispersal tool, but it has never been deployed.

Concerns over effectiveness and legality

Officials ran into hurdles over legalities, use of force, effectiveness, and potential issues over sovereignty, particularly if the system was deployed on people in Mexico who had not yet crossed into the U.S. Chief among those concerns, however, was whether people could be harmed, either directly or indirectly, by the weapon.

“Even if they’re chasing people back to the river, you don’t want them to go in and drown,” a former CBP official told CNN. “For the cost, for the training and for the policies you’re going to create, is the juice worth the squeeze?”

El Centro sector, which covers around 70 miles along the U.S.-Mexico border, evaluated the system several years ago, when Rodney Scott, who now serves as CBP commissioner, helmed that sector, according to a CBP official.

At the time, officials were discussing whether the system might help agents with an influx of illegal crossings along the nearby river by discouraging people from trying to cross in that area or pushing them to get out of the water.

One of the considerations at the time was whether the system might result in more rescues if people were incapacitated by the technology, the official said, though it’s unclear why it wasn’t deployed.

In 2018, prior to midterms, CBP officials also weighed using it against migrants, but then-Homeland Security Secretary Kirstjen Nielsen shot it down.

“The issue was treating immigrants and citizens like enemy combatants,” a former DHS official familiar with previous discussions about using the weapon against migrants told CNN. “Thematically, inhumane treatments typically get rejected.”

Some Border Patrol agents have more recently cast doubt over whether they need the tool at all amid low border crossings and an increase in personnel, according to another former CBP official.

title: Shame and Shamelessness in Migration and Refugee Law - Verfassungsblog
description:
Yet the emotional logic behind the substance and implementation of laws has been understudied in migration and refugee law.
Researching Shame Shame is not solely a private emotion; it is socially generated and instrumentalised for specific purposes .
Unfortunately, Kirchheimer does not discuss the meaning and role of shame for refugee protection any further, but he positions shame as one of the most crucial elements in the refugee protection system.
Conclusion Refugee protection in Europe faces multiple, overlapping crises, including a crisis of refugee protection and an epistemological crisis in refugee law expertise.
The combined crisis of law and rationality cannot be explained without examining the emotional logic underpinning refugee law and state refugee policies.
text:
Emotions such as compassion, fear, and shame play a central role in developing and implementing migration and refugee policies and laws: they guide both the adoption of laws and their interpretation. Understanding the emotional reasoning behind laws and policies is therefore essential for explaining why particular policies are adopted, how they are justified, and whom they benefit. Emotions can help us understand, in particular, the increasing attempts by States to renegotiate the fundamental principles of refugee protection, including the right to seek asylum and the principle of non-refoulement. Yet the emotional logic behind the substance and implementation of laws has been understudied in migration and refugee law. While existing scholarship has focused on humanitarianism linked to compassion and securitisation linked to fear, research has largely omitted the role of law in relation to shame. In this post, I show how shame, shaming, and shamelessness shape the development and implementation of the international refugee protection system. I show in particular how shame acts as a moral guide for the system, but also how it is used to sustain racialised and gendered hierarchies within the system.

Researching Shame

Shame is not solely a private emotion; it is socially generated and instrumentalised for specific purposes . Most recently, David Keen, in his book Shame: The Politics and Power of an Emotion , analysed shame as a political emotion, focusing on its functions and role in relation to large-scale human suffering. Keen shows, in particular, how shame can be mobilised, manipulated, and instrumentalised, and how these uses and abuses have been central to modern politics. Keen, for instance, showed how shaming individuals or groups can help maintain unequal power relations; how calls to restore dignity or respect as an escape from shame can be used strategically for political mobilisation; and how shame about one’s own weakness can generate violence towards others.

In the context of refugee protection, emotional reasoning in general and shame in particular have been studied primarily in international relations rather than in international, EU, or national law. To be sure, the international system of refugee protection has been driven from the start by emotional reasoning, such as Fridtjof Nansen’s 1921 appeals to compassion to support refugees from Russia. Beyond humanitarian motives, other emotions have also shaped the development of the modern system of refugee protection.

In my own research and based on existing literature, I have identified at least four roles that shame, shamelessness, and shaming play in the context of refugee protection: as a basis for international refugee protection, as a strategy to press for change in state policies, as a strategy to offload shame for human rights violations onto the victims, and as an emotion that is part not only of the experience of being a refugee but also of the refugee determination procedure.

Shame as a Basis for International Refugee Protection

British migration scholar and practitioner Emma Haddad has argued that post-WWII international refugee law has constructed Western states as “moral international actors” seeking to alleviate guilt linked to their earlier neglect of Jewish refugees. German lawyer and political scientist Otto Kirchheimer has argued in his 1959 text “Asylum” that shame, as a moral stance against national self-interest, has been one of the foundations of refugee protection. Kirchheimer juxtaposes shame with raison d’état and considers shame as a collective political emotion felt by governments and political communities, an important basis for the functioning of the asylum system:

“Asylum – Herodotus already knew it – has its flaws. It is likely to remain mostly inoperative unless safely anchored in man’s propensity for shame.”

In the same text, Kirchheimer also highlights tensions between emotions and geopolitical and legal considerations, such as national vs. international law (e.g. sovereign discretion in decision-making v. international legal obligations as regulated in the Refugee Convention); compassion vs. self-interest (e.g. humanitarian basis for protection v. political aims such as embarrassing states by granting protection to their political opponents); and raison d’état vs. shame (e.g. protection of own interests v. avoiding morally questionable actions such as returning the persecuted to their countries of persecution). Unfortunately, Kirchheimer does not discuss the meaning and role of shame for refugee protection any further, but he positions shame as one of the most crucial elements in the refugee protection system. In light of the juxtapositions and tensions behind the politicisation of asylum, it is clear that national law cannot itself guarantee protection. Other factors, such as shame felt by state authorities (alongside compassion) as well as international legal standards, can therefore act as a moral and normative guide that prevents states from acting in a self-interested way.

The Strategy of “Naming and Shaming” for Violation of Human Rights of Refugees and Asylum Seekers

In line with Kirchheimer’s argument, shame and shaming have been considered to play a role also in attempts to change the behaviour of states violating human rights. In particular, shaming has been a strategy for international actors to press states to change their domestic policies. Shame here relies on highlighting the discrepancy between state behaviour, the international community’s moral standards, and the identity states aspire to. One example is EU criticism coupled with sanctions against Belarus for instrumentalising migrants and exposing them to human rights violations at the EU Eastern Border . However, the practice of “naming and shaming”, including in relation to migration, is often considered ineffective and can trigger a counterproductive backlash or counter-blaming, such as Belarus accusing Polish security forces of violence towards refugees at the border and pushing them back to Belarus . States may engage in shame offloading behaviours and use various coping styles. For instance, states may seek alliances to support each other’s rights-violating behaviour. Through such behaviour, states may engage in what is called a quasi-projection coping style , where they cite similar behaviour by other states to minimise their own immoral action. In the context of refugee protection, recent developments at the EU’s Eastern border show such collaboration between Poland and Finland. Both countries have recently adopted legal changes significantly limiting the right to apply for asylum for those applying for protection at the EU Eastern Border and considered as “instrumentalised migrants”. This limitation violates Article 18 of the EU Charter of Fundamental Rights, which guarantees the right to seek asylum, and Article 33 of the Refugee Convention, which guarantees protection from refoulement. Eastern border states have also been accused of violating multiple articles of the European Convention on Human Rights, including the prohibition of torture and the prohibition of collective expulsion . Analysis of parliamentary discussions in both countries shows that Poland and Finland have provided each other with mutual support and cited each other’s legal developments to justify adopting their own national laws, arguably to avoid the so-called hypocrisy costs linked to behaviours that run counter to officially held values.

The Perverse Distribution of Shame

Another example of projection as a coping mechanism to deal with shame for violations of human rights of migrants is what David Keen calls a “perverse distribution of shame”. Keen studied the function of suffering in the Calais refugee camp in 2016, where refugees suffered violence and different forms of humiliation induced by police, such as raids, destruction of shelters and personal belongings, contamination of food and water, racist abuse or attacks on religious symbols, among others. The authorities constructed very poor living conditions in the camp and created an image of “in-fighting, disease and desperation”. Ultimately, the camp was closed. Keen shows that the authorities thus removed shame from human rights violators (the state) and projected it onto the victims of human rights violations (the migrants). The liquidation of the camp could then be rationalised as a humanitarian act itself. As Marie-Luisa Frick analysed, this dehumanisation violated the migrants’ human dignity, consequently affecting their other rights , and made many residents of the camp internalise this shame as well. These practices of perverse distribution of shame – blaming migrants themselves for the disastrous conditions in the Calais camp, and portraying them as “fanatically determined or even crazy” , in other words, constructing migrants as an enemy – have further enhanced the perpetrators’ shamelessness and a sense of impunity for their actions .

Shame as an Emotion Linked to Refugee Status

While the development of refugee protection may be motivated by a collective sense of shame and affected by strategies to offload it, receiving protection can also cause shame. As Hannah Arendt writes in We Refugees, “[i]f we are saved, we feel humiliated, and if we are helped, we feel degraded” . To be sure, shame has been part not only of the experience of being a refugee but also of the refugee determination procedure in various ways, not to mention the internalisation of shame as a result of its perverse attribution, as discussed above. One example of an asylum procedure where shame plays an important role is the credibility assessment. For instance, Karin Åberg shows how shame has become an implicit legal requirement for LGB refugees to be found credible and therefore granted refugee protection in Sweden and the Netherlands. This is based on an understanding that fleeing the homophobic countries of origin, LGB asylum seekers necessarily internalise this homophobia and are required to provide detailed accounts of their emotions, in particular shame, about their sexual orientation.

Another example: to justify late disclosure of some acts of persecution, such as rape, in the early stages of the asylum procedure, women are expected to give a legitimate reason, such as shame or trauma. At the same time, in relation to sexual violence as a basis for persecution, women are considered less credible overall, compared with men. In the case of men, sexual violence is considered more shameful and stigmatising and therefore mentioning it during the refugee status determination procedure makes the claim more credible . Finally, being a subject of refugee procedure or receiving a negative decision on refugee status (being a “fake case” ) can cause shame.

The legal implications of shame, as an emotion experienced by protection seekers, are therefore twofold. First, shame may become an obstacle to applying for protection or to disclosing certain bases for persecution. Second, shame has become integrated into the refugee status determination procedure as an indicator of the existence of the grounds for persecution and of persecution itself. This is particularly problematic because it excludes the possibility of feeling pride or joy in one’s sexual orientation among LGBTQ+ asylum seekers, but also, importantly, it disregards the complexity of assessing emotions due to cross-cultural differences in emotional responses.

Conclusion

Refugee protection in Europe faces multiple, overlapping crises, including a crisis of refugee protection and an epistemological crisis in refugee law expertise. The combined crisis of law and rationality cannot be explained without examining the emotional logic underpinning refugee law and state refugee policies. In particular, without understanding shame’s crucial role in developing and implementing refugee protection, legal academia will struggle to understand the reasons behind refugee rights violations and propose adequate legal and policy solutions.

text:
The Ceuta migration crisis put human rights at the bloc’s external borders to the test, the EU Agency for Fundamental Rights warned in a report Thursday.

The Vienna-based agency warned that there are serious risks to fundamental rights at the bloc’s external borders and the sudden arrival of thousands of migrants to the Spanish exclave of Ceuta in July “put the balance between protecting fundamental rights and safeguarding the EU’s external borders to the test.”

In late July, more than 70,000 migrants crossed from Morocco into Ceuta in the space of 48 hours, leading to questions about how the EU should deal with sudden mass movements that may be engineered or used against the bloc. In her State of the Union address, Commission President Ursula von der Leyen promised a European emergency response framework, which she said should allow for “time-limited and strictly defined flexibility in standard procedures.”

Greece has called for a measure suspending asylum applications in emergency situations — something that could amount to pushbacks, which are banned under international law. Several countries have thrown their support behind the idea, while others question whether this type of measure should be taken at the level of the EU, rather than in national capitals.

In its report, the agency said any emergency measure should comply with EU and international law, both of which guarantee the right to seek asylum and the principle of non-refoulement — a “cornerstone of refugee protection,” it added.

At a meeting of EU leaders last week, von der Leyen said the Commission would come up with a proposal for the emergency framework before the end of the year.

“We will always uphold our values and fundamental rights, but we will never compromise on protecting our borders,” she said.

The agency’s report also highlighted other fundamental rights concerns at the EU’s external borders, including the implementation of rights monitoring mechanisms as part of migration reforms, restrictions on search and rescue organizations, and investigations into rights violations at the borders.

According to the agency’s numbers, 12 EU countries opened 322 preliminary criminal investigations between 2020 and 2025, but only nine of those resulted in a conviction.

Gaps in those investigations “lead to a perception of impunity, which risks undermining the rule of law, one of the fundamental values on which the Union is founded,” the report stated.

text:
LOS ANGELES (KABC) -- A federal claim seeking $50 million has been filed on behalf of Carlitos Ricardo Parias, a social media influencer known online as "Richard LA," one year after federal agents shot him while attempting to arrest him.

Civil rights attorney Denise Gastelum announced the claim Tuesday, describing it as a precursor to a lawsuit against the Department of Homeland Security, U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement and other agencies involved in Parias' arrest.

Parias, described by his attorneys as a popular online influencer and community journalist, was shot in the elbow during the arrest in October 2025 in South L.A. According to attorneys, the round ricocheted and also struck a U.S. marshal in the hand.

Gastelum criticized the actions of federal agents, saying, "What we see through body camera... is the indiscriminate attack by an ICE agent... shooting at a human being who's in his vehicle with his hands up, simply asking, 'Why are you detaining me?'"

Federal prosecutors charged Parias with assault on a federal officer, alleging he used his vehicle as a weapon. However, a federal judge dismissed the case late last year, finding that Parias, who was being held at the Adelanto ICE Processing Center, had been denied access to his attorneys.

In a statement, a Department of Homeland Security spokesperson said: "DHS strongly disagrees with decision to dismiss this case for assaulting a federal officer. All illegal aliens in detention have access to their lawyers. No one is denied access to counsel."

The federal government is appealing the dismissal.

Parias, a Mexican national, remains in custody, which his attorneys contend is unlawful.

"He should not be detained... whatever criminal charges they brought against him have been dismissed," said Carlos Jurado, Parias' immigration attorney.

The appeal is now before the Ninth Circuit Court of Appeals. Oral arguments are scheduled for next Friday, with a decision expected sometime in November.

text:
Voters have record low trust in Republicans' ability to handle their top issues like immigration and rising prices, according to the latest Strength In Numbers/Verasight poll shared with NPR.

The poll also finds a strong majority of voters want the next Congress to undo President Trump's agenda — or act as a check on his power — on policies like tariffs and trade, health care and immigration.

Less than two weeks out from Election Day, voters say they'd prefer to elect a Democrat to Congress over a Republican by a double-digit margin among registered voters (52% to 41%) and likely voters (54% to 42%).

The survey of 2,028 respondents was conducted Oct. 13-19 and has a margin of sampling error of 2.2 percentage points, meaning results could be about 2.2 points higher or lower.

Trump's job approval sits at near-record lows for his second term, with just 34% approving of his performance and 62% disapproving, with 50% strongly disapproving.

G. Elliott Morris, author of the Strength In Numbers newsletter and CEO of polling company Wave Polling and Research, said the latest poll explains the current challenges with the political landscape Republicans face.

"Trump's ratings hit new lows on seven of the 10 issues we've tracked since May 2025, from jobs and trade to immigration and border security, and he's now underwater on every issue we ask about," Morris said. "The president's policies have even harmed Republicans, with voters now more likely to say they trust Democrats to handle the issues of immigration and the economy."

Among adults, prices and inflation are collectively mentioned far and away as the most important problem facing the country today, with 63% of respondents saying it was one of their top three most important problems and 39% listing it first. Other top issues include jobs and the economy, health care, elections and democracy and immigration.

Taken all together, the sentiment of the electorate explains why Democrats and Republicans are spending big in House and Senate races stretching deep into conservative territory where Trump performed well in 2024.

Americans have soured on Trump and Republicans

Voters chose to give Republicans control of the White House and Congress in the 2024 election, and at least some of them say they regret their choice. According to the poll, nearly one in 10 people who said they voted in the 2024 presidential race regret their choice, including almost 15% of self-described Trump voters and 15% who backed a third-party candidate.

In May 2025, the Strength in Numbers/Verasight poll found voters trusted Republicans more than Democrats on immigration and deportations by an average of 15 points. Now, they trust Democrats by a narrow one point margin.

In every measure that the poll has tracked, Republicans have lost ground in the last year and a half, and only hold a slim advantage on crime and public safety issues and border security.

When asked which party voters trust to handle their personal top issue, Democrats hold a 47-35 advantage, a nearly 10-point jump since May 2025 and the widest gap measured.

The midterms are a referendum

Many polls, including the September NPR/PBS News/Marist survey, find that the 2026 midterm choices are best viewed in relation to Trump rather than a pure binary vote of support for the Democratic or Republican candidates.

Only 25% of respondents said it was more important to elect a Congress that will help Trump pass his agenda, compared to 58% who said it was about electing a Congress to act as a check and balance on Trump.

Two of every five voters surveyed said their decision would mostly be a statement against Trump and his agenda, compared to one in five who said it would be a statement of support. For 20% of voters surveyed, their choice would be about specific issues and candidates in their district.

On the issues of tariffs and trade, health care, foreign policy, elections and voting, government spending and social programs, immigration and deportations and artificial intelligence, a majority of those surveyed want a Congress to roll back or act as a check on Trump's stances.

More voters think the Democratic Party cares more about people like them than Republicans, and 20% say neither party does.

title: 78-year-old priest carried out of Colorado ICE facility by fellow detainees after judge orders release
description: A 78-year-old Ugandan priest, Edward Nalwamba, was released from ICE detention in Aurora after a federal judge ordered his release, but the circumstances sparked criticism after he was reportedly denied
text:
Edward Nalwamba, who has lived in Colorado for more than two decades, was released after a federal judge granted his petition challenging his continued detention and ordered immigration officials to free him by Tuesday.

Click here for updates on this story

AURORA, Colorado ( KCNC ) -- A 78-year-old Ugandan priest, who spent more than a year in immigration detention, was released from an Aurora facility Tuesday, but he was unable to walk out on his own.

CBS Colorado cameras captured two fellow detainees carrying Edward Nalwamba from the GEO-operated ICE detention facility to his ride after staff reportedly refused to allow him to use a wheelchair beyond the facility's gate.

Nalwamba, who has lived in Colorado for more than two decades, was released after a federal judge granted his petition challenging his continued detention and ordered immigration officials to free him by Tuesday.

His release comes after 13 months in ICE custody, during which his attorney says his health deteriorated dramatically.

"I was walking. I was exercising. I was playing ping pong," Nalwamba said shortly after his release, describing his physical condition before he was detained in September 2025.

Now, he says he cannot walk without assistance. Nalwamba told CBS Colorado that staff initially brought him toward the facility's exit in a wheelchair, but would not allow him to take it the rest of the way to his transportation.

"They get me outside and say we can't go beyond this," Nalwamba explained. "And I'm asking, 'Can't the car come here?' They say, 'No.' I say, 'So how am I going to get the car?'"

Nalwamba said two other detainees stepped in and offered to carry him. He knew one of the men from his housing unit but said he did not know the other.

"Those friends offered to carry me, and, I mean, I'm so grateful to them," he said.

The circumstances of his release have drawn criticism from Colorado U.S. Sen. John Hickenlooper.

In a social media post Tuesday, Hickenlooper said members of his staff visited the detention center earlier in the day and specifically requested that GEO staff allow Nalwamba to call his caretakers before his release and provide a wheelchair to take him to his ride home.

The senator said GEO staff assured his office that both requests would be honored.

"They failed to deliver on either," Hickenlooper wrote. "No phone call. No wheelchair. No human decency."

Hickenlooper called the incident an act of cruelty and pledged to continue holding those responsible accountable.

CBS Colorado has reached out to the U.S. Department of Homeland Security seeking an explanation for the wheelchair restrictions, the circumstances surrounding Nalwamba's release and allegations concerning his medical treatment.

DHS responded to CBS Colorado with this statement, "On September 18, 2025, ICE arrested Edward Nkugwa Kironde Nalwamba, an illegal alien from Uganda, in Lakewood, Colorado. Nalwamba legally entered the country on January 1, 2002, but chose to overstay his welcome in violation of our nation's laws. He was granted voluntary departure by an immigration judge on March 2, 2007, and still refused to depart. On June 2, 2009, the Board Immigration Appeals dismissed his appeal and on April 8, 2010, following a dismissal of his appeal in the 10th Circuit, he was issued a final order of removal. On October 20, ICE was forced to release Nalwamba after an activist judge ordered his release. He remains in the country illegally."

Nalwamba's attorney, Joy Athanasiou, says her client entered into ICE custody in good health but has experienced serious medical problems while detained.

"When he came to the detention center a year ago, he was extremely healthy. He was very fit. He exercised regularly. He could do 15 to 20 push-ups. Now, he is wheelchair-bound. He is extremely weak," Athanasiou said.

Athanasiou said Nalwamba was diagnosed with pneumonia in January, lost more than 30 pounds and collapsed while detained. She also says he has suffered from an ongoing respiratory illness since June, and accuses ICE of failing to provide adequate testing and treatment.

Nalwamba described experiencing chest pain, coughing, dizziness and weakness in his legs.

His attorney says his supporters are working to arrange a medical appointment and hope he can begin physical therapy and rehabilitation.

In a statement provided to CBS Colorado in June, the Department of Homeland Security defended the medical care available to people in ICE custody.

"It is a longstanding practice to provide comprehensive medical care from the moment an alien enters ICE custody," a DHS spokesperson said. According to the agency, that includes access to medical appointments and 24-hour emergency care.

Nalwamba previously served as a priest at Resurrection Anglican Fellowship in Greenwood Village for approximately 15 years. He arrived in the United States from Uganda in 2002 and remained in the country after his tourist visa expired.

Nalwamba and his supporters have said he fears returning to Uganda because of persecution connected to his pro-democracy political activities.

In its June statement, DHS said Nalwamba had overstayed his visa, was granted voluntary departure in 2007 and received a final order of removal in 2010. ICE detained him on Sept. 18, 2025.

Before that arrest, Nalwamba says he had been living under an immigration order of supervision.

His attorneys challenged his prolonged detention through a federal habeas corpus petition, arguing the government could not continue holding him indefinitely.

Athanasiou says she is concerned that ICE could attempt to detain Nalwamba again.

On Monday, a judge granted the petition and ordered Nalwamba released no later than Oct. 20. Despite that ruling, his underlying immigration case remains unresolved.

"I am back to where I was when they first arrested me," Nalwamba said. "So I was asking myself, 'Why did they arrest me in the first place?'"

text:
A federal judge ruled late Wednesday that the U.S. Department of Homeland Security's practice of knocking on doors and asking people about their immigration status — and whether they have voted in recent elections — likely violates the Voting Rights Act.

The ruling took aim at an operation that was documented by a CBS News investigation earlier Wednesday. Homeland Security Investigations has posted photos and videos of agents approaching homes in multiple states. The Trump administration says the practice is part of an effort to crack down on voting by noncitizens, but critics say it could intimidate legal voters.

In her ruling, U.S. District Judge Araceli Martinez-Olguin ordered federal immigration authorities to stop carrying out "elections-related field operations and field interviews" in nine states, including California and New York, if the operations are likely to involve people who government officials "know, suspect, or should reasonably know or suspect are U.S. citizens."

Her order will remain in effect until polls close on Election Day. She stayed the ruling until 5 p.m. on Friday, which will give the government a chance to seek appeal.

Martinez-Olguin sided with groups that sued over the noncitizen voting investigation surge, including the California Nurses Association and National Nurses United. She found the policy likely ran afoul of a section of the Voting Rights Act that makes it illegal to "intimidate, threaten, or coerce" those who assist people with voting or engage in voter mobilization efforts.

"Plaintiffs do not claim, nor does the Court find, that it is unlawful for federal officials to undertake investigations into unlawful voting in federal elections," the judge wrote. "Rather, Plaintiffs seek to stop DHS from continuing to investigate U.S. citizens, who have a legal right to vote, in a way that intimidates and threatens the participation of CNA/NNU members from urging or aiding others to vote."

Martinez-Olguin also pointed to the "high likelihood of error" in the government's process for assembling a list of potential targets, which includes data from government agencies and commercially available data.

Protect Democracy, one of the groups that sued over the policy, celebrated the ruling.

"It was clear from the start that DHS built its lists on bad data, never checked how often it was wrong, and recklessly sent agents to people's homes weeks before an election," Beau Tremitiere, counsel at Protect Democracy, said in a statement to CBS News. "Today's ruling should remind us that American citizens hold the ultimate power in our democracy, not the government–no matter what the administration says otherwise."

CBS News has reached out to DHS for comment.

President Trump has prioritized cracking down on voter fraud during his second term, although there has been little evidence to back up his claims of widespread voting by noncitizens. Just 156 people have been charged with voting-fraud related offenses since the beginning of the Trump administration, according to the Justice Department.

The Justice Department reported earlier this week that it arrested several dozen green card holders in California on allegations they illegally registered to vote in U.S. federal elections.

title: DOD Memo Greenlights DHS Use of Military 'Heat Ray' at US-Mexico Border
description:
CNN published additional details Tuesday, reporting that internal discussions have centered on using the system to disperse crowds at the southern border.
When contacted for comment by Military.com, a Pentagon spokesperson deferred comment to DHS.
A former DHS official told the network the proposal raised concerns about treating immigrants and American citizens like enemy combatants.
Border Patrol's El Centro sector in California evaluated the system several years ago under Rodney Scott, who now leads CBP.
Officials previously raised sovereign concerns about a beam that can reach across the border into Mexico, according to CNN.
text:
Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth has reportedly loaned the military's so-called "heat ray" to the Department of Homeland Security (DHS), handing civilian law enforcement a crowd-control weapon the Pentagon developed two decades ago.

The memo, signed by Hegseth last month and obtained by CNN, authorized a "temporary loan" of one Active Denial System for seven months starting in September. The system was originally sent to Afghanistan and brought home without ever being used in combat.

The memo says the system "shall not be operated by DoW (Department of War) personnel," leaving DHS solely responsible for employing the weapon and for developing the tactics, techniques and procedures governing its use.

DHS can ask to keep the system longer when the loan ends.

Former CNN correspondent Jim Acosta first reported the leaked memo Oct. 8 on his independent platform. CNN published additional details Tuesday, reporting that internal discussions have centered on using the system to disperse crowds at the southern border.

When contacted for comment by Military.com, a Pentagon spokesperson deferred comment to DHS.

A U.S. Customs and Border Protection spokesperson told Military.com the following: “CBP is continually evaluating new technology, especially technology that can save lives while simultaneously enhancing national security effectiveness.”

A Weapon the Military Shelved Without Firing

Built around an invisible beam of 95 GHz millimeter-wave energy, the Active Denial System has a range of more than half a mile, according to the military's descriptions of the weapon.

The beam heats the surface of the skin, producing a burning sensation Pentagon officials have compared to opening a hot oven, along with an effect officials say lasts 10 to 15 minutes and creates a strong urge to move away.

During testing in 2007, an airman with the 820th Security Forces Group at Moody Air Force Base in Georgia suffered second-degree burns and was treated at a hospital, according to the Valdosta Daily Times.

The military later deployed the system to Afghanistan but brought it home in 2010 without using it in combat, according to the BBC at the time. Officials considered it for crowd control at overseas detention facilities without employing it there.

It surfaced again in 2020. NPR reported that the Pentagon's lead military police officer for the National Capital Region emailed the District of Columbia National Guard asking whether it had an Active Denial System available before federal forces cleared protesters near Lafayette Square.

A Guard major later told Congress the Guard had no such system.

DHS Asked Before and its Own Secretary Said No

CBP officials weighed using the system against migrants in 2018, but then-DHS Secretary Kirstjen Nielsen rejected the idea, according to CNN.

A former DHS official told the network the proposal raised concerns about treating immigrants and American citizens like enemy combatants.

Border Patrol's El Centro sector in California evaluated the system several years ago under Rodney Scott, who now leads CBP. Those discussions focused on deterring river crossings or pushing people out of the water, according to CNN, and a former CBP official warned of drowning risks if people were driven toward the water.

Some Border Patrol agents doubt they need the tool at all, another former CBP official told CNN, with illegal crossings at low levels and staffing up.

A CBP spokesperson said the agency continually evaluates new technologies, especially those that improve operational effectiveness.

The memo does not say where or how the system would be tested or used, and the weapon has never been operationally deployed anywhere.

Federal law allows the defense secretary to make military equipment available to civilian law enforcement, and the memo's bar on military operators tracks the laws that keep troops out of direct domestic enforcement.

The loan language does not, however, guarantee how the weapon could lawfully be used against people.

DHS regulations require officers to use the objectively reasonable level of force necessary based on the totality of the circumstances. Officials previously raised sovereign concerns about a beam that can reach across the border into Mexico, according to CNN.

The loan runs into next spring, with an extension available on request. No document made public so far explains where the system is, who would fire it, or under what rules of engagement it would be utilized.

text:
A new “war on narco-terrorism” is fuelling unlawful killings and other grave human rights violations, United Nations experts warned the Third Committee (Social, Humanitarian and Cultural) today, as they sounded the alarm over mass displacement, the separation of migrant children from their families and mounting attacks on judicial independence.

‘Serial Extrajudicial Killings’ Amount to Crimes against Humanity

“In the past year, the United States has unlawfully killed at least 239 people in 71 military attacks on civilian vessels at sea”, declared Ben Saul, Special Rapporteur on the promotion and protection of human rights and fundamental freedoms while countering terrorism.

“These serial extrajudicial killings gravely violate the right to life and are a systematic attack on civilians amounting to crimes against humanity”, he said, calling for perpetrators to be held accountable.

Warning against conflating terrorism with organized crime, he reported that at least 15 countries, mostly in the Americas, have recently designated 39 criminal groups as terrorist organizations, expanding the use of exceptional security measures.

While organized crime is primarily profit-driven, terrorism involves political or ideological violence, he explained. A new “war on narco-terrorism” has led to grave human rights violations, including unlawful killings, torture and enforced disappearances. Conflating criminal and terrorist groups could also trigger travel bans, asset freezes and refoulement, he added.

He also criticized military aggression in Venezuela and Ecuador's authorization of a “shoot to kill” approach against criminal groups designated as terrorist.

“This new war on ‘narco-terrorism’ is not effective in reducing drugs or violence, and can make both worse”, he warned, noting that decades of militarized responses to drug cartels have failed to curb trafficking. Rather than pursuing “kinetic suppression of drugs”, States should invest in poverty reduction, public services, development and evidence-based prevention, he urged.

Turning to wider conflicts, he recalled earlier warnings against illegal wars justified by counter-terrorism. “Venezuela was invaded. Aggression against Iran has killed innocents and destabilized the Middle East, and energy shocks have impoverished the vulnerable worldwide”, he said. He also warned that peace in Gaza remains elusive without self-determination and justice.

Reconstruction Must Break Cycles of Displacement, Not Deepen Them

“Imagine returning home, only to find that home no longer exists”, said Paula Gaviria Betancur, Special Rapporteur on the human rights of internally displaced persons.

“For millions of internally displaced persons affected by mass devastation, this is not imagination. It is the reality awaiting them, if they can return at all”, she said, reporting that more than 82 million people are internally displaced worldwide by conflict, violence and disasters — the second-highest number ever recorded.

Reconstruction needs exceed $71 billion in Gaza, $11 billion in Lebanon, $216 billion in Syria and $588 billion in Ukraine, she reported. “The decisions taken in the first months of reconstruction will determine whether people can rebuild their lives in dignity or face new cycles of exclusion and displacement”, she warned.

Poorly designed rebuilding efforts can reward those who profit from destruction, trigger forced evictions and deepen land disputes. Yet, reconstruction also offers “a rare opportunity to confront the causes of displacement and break cycles of exclusion”.

Those who have lost everything need not only housing, but also recognition and justice, she emphasized, noting: “Reconstruction must reckon with what cannot be rebuilt with bricks and mortar: the missing whose fate is unknown, the process of mourning, the places of memory, the social bonds that held communities together.”

Delegates Clash over Gaza Reconstruction, Displacement

During the ensuing interactive dialogue, Malaysia’s representative condemned the repeated displacement of Palestinians in Gaza, accusing Israel of obstructing reconstruction by restricting building materials and equipment.

“Calling our security measures an obstruction is a moral failure”, Israel’s delegate responded, pointing to Hamas’ use of human shields. She also urged recognition of tens of thousands of Israelis displaced by attacks from Hamas, Hizbullah and Iran.

Iran’s representative rejected allegations that his country targets civilians, accusing Israel of “systematic targeting of Palestinian civilians and civilian objects” and of attacking civilian areas in his country.

Yemen’s delegate blamed Houthi militias for forcing millions from their homes, reporting that over 217,000 people had been internally displaced since September. Sudan’s representative similarly highlighted “lengthy waves” of displacement caused by conflict and militia violence, including sexual violence.

Turning to reconstruction, Azerbaijan’s delegate reported that over $16 billion had been allocated to rebuild conflict-affected towns, enabling over 100,000 people to return to newly constructed areas.

Syria's representative said Government policies had facilitated the return of approximately 2 million displaced people since the fall of the Assad regime, highlighting plans to close displacement camps through reconstruction.

‘Fossil Fuel Companies Systematically Manufacture Doubts’

Margaret Satterthwaite, Special Rapporteur on the independence of judges and lawyers, warned that justice systems seeking to enforce climate commitments face intimidation, political interference and powerful economic opposition.

“Fossil fuel companies systematically manufacture doubts about climate science, target their critics and wage war on effective climate action”, she declared.

Judges and prosecutors frequently lack adequate training in environmental law and climate science, while lawyers struggle to obtain evidence from companies refusing access to sites or environmental impact studies.

“Such restrictions undermine equality of arms and the right to a fair trial”, she warned, potentially preventing communities from challenging destructive projects before irreversible damage occurs.

The most entrenched obstacle is “hostility from powerful political and economic forces”, she said, warning that the climate crisis is unfolding alongside a global wave of “autocratization” and rising inequality.

‘Immigration Detention of Children Is Never in Their Best Interests’

Gehad Madi, Special Rapporteur on the human rights of migrants, warned that detention, deportation and restrictive border policies continue to tear migrant families apart. “Family unity saves lives and serves as an essential protective factor for children in situations of migration”, he stressed.

“Immigration detention of children is never in their best interests”, he underlined, warning of serious consequences for children's mental health and development.

Voicing further concern over “migration externalization”, he stressed that transferring migrants to third countries increases their chances of separation and protection failures. “Outsourcing migration governance does not diminish States’ obligations”, he said.

Calling for stronger family reunification measures and regular migration pathways, he urged Governments to prohibit immigration detention of children and families. “Migration status must never determine whether a child can enjoy family life”, he added.

Also briefing the Committee today were Prasad Kariyawasam, Chair of the Committee on the Protection of the Rights of All Migrant Workers and Members of Their Families, and Morris Tidball-Binz, Special Rapporteur on extrajudicial, summary or arbitrary executions.

The Trump administration has asked the Supreme Court to allow it to resume plans to build a border wall through the Big Bend region of West Texas, as part of its anti-immigration policy to strengthen security on the border with Mexico.

The Justice Department filed an emergency request on Wednesday asking the court to lift a federal judge’s injunction in a lower court that has halted construction while a lawsuit against the project, brought by an environmental group and other challengers, plays out.

The Department of Homeland Security plans include vehicle barriers, patrol roads, lighting and detection technology in and around Big Bend National Park.

Big Bend has about 805km (500 miles) of border, and, according to opponents of the project who have sued the administration, accounts for about 1 percent of migrant arrests.

Landscape, historic church

The lawsuit, filed by plaintiffs including the Center for Biological Diversity and a Big Bend-area river guide, seeks to preserve the landscape, protect a historic church, and challenge the federal government’s waivers of environmental and historical laws to fast-track the $1.7bn project.

Former Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem and current Secretary Markwayne Mullin, who issued the waivers between February and July, found the region to be an “area of high illegal entry”, requiring additional barriers to control the border.

US District Judge Kathleen Cardone issued an injunction in El Paso on October 2 halting work “until and unless Defendants comply with all applicable laws,” she wrote in her order.

In a later opinion, the judge found that the waivers exceeded the authority of Noem and Mullin.

The Justice Department in its request urged the Supreme Court to pause or overturn Cardone’s injunction.

The Supreme Court has not yet responded to this appeal.

“Even assuming that the secretary’s waiver authority implicates a question of ‘vast economic and political significance,’ Congress did clearly authorize the secretary both to build border barriers and to waive legal requirements in order to facilitate their expeditious construction,” the Justice Department wrote.

In August, the administration paused construction in Big Bend after the project drew bipartisan criticism over its potential impact on the park’s landscape and wildlife.
