title: Citizenship in a Limbo - Vidhi Centre for Legal Policy
description:
Article 11 of the Constitution has played a central role in the defence of the Citizenship Amendment Act of 2019.
It was claimed that Article 11 exempts citizenship law from any form of constitutional objection, that even encompasses part III (fundamental rights) of the constitution.
Pursuant to Article 11, it is the Parliament that is empowered to write down laws concerning Indian citizenship and the Parliament has indeed altered and modified the conditions of citizenship from time to time.
Sunali and her family are now stranded in a geopolitical limbo, having been arrested by Bangladeshi authorities for illegal infiltration.
However, the concern is, that the Court is rarely called upon to legislate in these matters of citizenship or immigration but rather to ensure that the process of determination of citizenship does not traverse due process.
text:
**Tiyasha

Introduction

The Supreme Court in Louis De Raedt and later in Sarbananda Sonowal held that the power of the Government of India to expel foreigners is absolute and unlimited and there is no provision in the Constitution fettering its discretion. Although delivered in the context of a self-admitted foreign national, years later, the constitutionally grave implications of this pronouncement are palpable.

Article 11 of the Constitution has played a central role in the defence of the Citizenship Amendment Act of 2019. It was claimed that Article 11 exempts citizenship law from any form of constitutional objection, that even encompasses part III (fundamental rights) of the constitution. Article 13 of the Constitution in clear language states that any law passed by the Parliament has to adhere to the constraints of the fundamental rights and thus citizenship laws are not outside the checks of Part III.

Despite of this seemingly straightforward proposition of what is constitutionally valid and what is ultra vires, the on-ground translation of this is rather mired with the trampling of due process, manifest arbitrariness owing to bureaucratic excess and the consequent crusade of basic rights. Pursuant to Article 11, it is the Parliament that is empowered to write down laws concerning Indian citizenship and the Parliament has indeed altered and modified the conditions of citizenship from time to time. For the purposes of this piece, the focus will be on the nascent Immigrants and Foreigners Act of 2025, the Immigration and Foreigners Order of 2025 and the May 2025 Ministry of Home Affairs letter laying down the procedure for deportation of illegal Bangladeshi nationals and Rohingyas. Before I engage with the deeper questions of constitutionality of these authorities, it is pertinent to note the current state of the process of ascertainment of citizenship in India.

What proof is enough?

Today, birth certificates, Passports or Aadhaar cards do not prove Indian citizenship. The Gauhati High Court has held that even electoral photo identity cards, PAN Cards, bank documents or land tax receipts are not sufficient to prove citizenship while a trial Court in Mumbai has held that electoral identity cards do prove a person’s citizenship.

In a press release in 2019, the Government of India stated that:

“citizenship can be proved by submitting any documents related to date and place of birth. However, a decision is yet to be taken on such acceptable documents. This is likely to include voter cards, passports, Aadhaar …….. documents relating to land or home or other similar documents issued by government officials. This list is likely to include more documents…”.

The sheer uncertainty in the language accentuates the grave vulnerability that persons, suspected of being illegal migrants, are subjected to. Justice Dhulia in one of his interviews referring to his own birth stated that during those times the idea of institutionalised registration of birth was elusive. In June 2026, the MEA stated that the Indian passport is a travel document and not a proof of citizenship. Passports are issed after a rigourous verification process conducted by the state authorities. Countries like the United States and the United Kingdom generally consider a valid passport as a strong evidence of nationality as the same is issued through a state-verified process, while the state retaining the power to revoke it in cases of fraud. In these circumstances, even minor discrepancies such as spelling errors or name changes or variations from transliteration are treated as fatal flaws that can prejudice the determination of citizenship.

On 20 June, 2025, the Delhi Police raided a slum in Rohini and detained a 25-year old Sunali Khatun, a pregnant domestic worker from West Bengal’s Birbhum district. She was detained along with her husband Danish and their eight-year old son Sabir. The family possessed localised identity cards, verified voter registration lists and official land records that dated back to 1956 tracing the last five generations of the family. However, the police demanded birth certificates, that had been lost in a recent slum fire. Bypassing a mandatory Home Ministry directive to verify citizenship claims with local authorities in her home state, the Foreigners’ Regional Registration Office (FRRO) summarily expelled the family to Bangladesh within six days based on a highly contested police “confession”. Sunali and her family are now stranded in a geopolitical limbo, having been arrested by Bangladeshi authorities for illegal infiltration. While her father has filed a habeas corpus writ petition in the Calcutta High Court, the matter may not be resolved in time, as she risks giving birth in Bangladesh before a final decision is rendered. Since May 2025, the Government of Assam has illegally “pushed-back” hundreds of persons-allegedly undocumented Bangladeshi migrants and Rohingya refugees into Bangladesh.

In this backdrop, what is the process of determining Indian citizenship? – Any person despite possessing valid documents may be suspected to be an illegal migrant on vague and remote grounds. This is exactly what the Indian Foreigner’s Act of 2025 does – it empowersthe Central Government to direct the removal of any foreigner on an “adverse security report” and the police to arrest any person without warrant against whom a reasonable suspicion of illegal migration exists. In most of these cases, the individual is neither appraised of the grounds for arrest nor furnished with the reports forming the basis of the adverse action. Veteran journalist R. Rajagopal disclosed that his application for renewal of his passport had got into a bind as his name was struck off the voter’s list during the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls in West Bengal. The Kolkata Police had sent an adverse report to the passport authorities mentioning the deletion of his name from the voter’s list. The passport office thereafter refrained from moving forward on his application.

According to the May 2025 Ministry of Home Affairs letter laying down the procedure for deportation of illegal Bangladeshi national and Rohingyas, all State Governments or UT Administrations have been empowered to detect, identify, conduct inquiry, deport illegal immigrants or detain them in holding centres. The Immigration and Foreigners Order of 2025 provides for the detention of foreigners and illegal migrants in holding centres and camps and is conspicuously silent as to the duration for which such persons are to be detained. And as empirical evidence shows, such persons have been detained for as long as ten years. It is this wide subjectivity in the exercise of discretion that renders the act arbitrary.

In May 2025, the Ministry of Home Affairs issued a circular to various states and union territories asking the authorities to accelerate the verification process of “suspected” Bangladeshis and Rohingyas illegally residing in India. This order on a plain reading is unchecked exercise of administrative discretion –no disclosure of grounds, no opportunity of constructive hearing given to the suspect, no maximum detention limits, no provision for legal assistance.

Suspicion to Expulsion: The Due Process Deficit

There are primarily two fundamental questions that arise from this context – Firstly, on what grounds will an individual be labelled as an illegal immigrant and secondly, given the extent of indeterminacy in this area, can a determination of such a magnitude be left solely in the hands of the executive with no effective scope of judicial review?

It is the uncertainty in the answer to the first question that affirms and reinforces the answer to the second question. Reflecting upon the status quo, the Parliament is yet to come up with a clear and coherent framework to ascertain Indian citizenship and therefore, the complete vesting of such powers in the executive is a precarious proposition. The Supreme Court has

held that the absence of arbitrary power is the sine qua non to rule of law with confined and defined discretion. Arbitrariness is uncanalised and unguided discretion bestowed upon the executive. Justice P.N Bhagwati had remarked that “mala fide exercise of power and arbitrariness are different lethal radiations emanating from the same vice; in fact the latter comprehends the former.”

The Apex Court in Sarbananda Sonowal reversed the burden of proof from the Government to the alleged illegal immigrant. In the former, when the burden of proof was on the government, it was exceedingly difficult to prove the illegality of the immigrant’s claims of citizenship. However, today when the burden is reversed the question that we grapple with is how does a suspected individual even prove his citizenship to the satisfaction of the government in the first place.

The enforcement of these laws by the authorities is exactly what was shunned by the Apex Court in Rahim Ali. The Court iterated that though the burden is on the foreigner to prove that he is an Indian, a mere allegation is not enough to doubt a person’s nationality. In the absence of substantial material to corroborate such claims, the Court observed, ‘it cannot be left to the untrammelled or arbitrary discretion of the authorities to initiate proceedings, which have life altering and very serious consequences for the person, based on hearsay or bald and vague allegation(s).”

In National Human Rights Commission v. State of Arunachal Pradesh, the Court held that the Indian State is obligated to protect the life and liberty of every human being, be he a citizen or otherwise. This approach of the judiciary is in line with Article 9 and 13 of the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights (ICCPR). Article 9 of the ICCPR states that everyone has the right to liberty and security of person and no on shall be subjected to arrest and detention.

Article 13 of the ICCPR reads thus:

“An alien lawfully in the territory of a State Party to the present Covenant may be expelled therefrom only in pursuance of a decision reached in accordance with law and shall, except where compelling reasons of national security otherwise require, be allowed to submit the

reasons against his expulsion and to have his case reviewed by, and be represented for the purpose before, a competent authority……”

The Human Rights Committee has commented that this protection does not extend to illegal migrants and aliens who have stayed longer than what the law or their permits allow, however, if the legality of an alien’s entry is in dispute, any decision on this point leading to his expulsion or deportation ought to be taken in accordance with article 13. Though India has made reservation to this Article in order to apply its own laws relating to foreigners, the point is to put forth the standard accepted by the international community – expulsion after the individual’s non-citizenship is conclusively decided in accordance with law.

The Foreigner’s Tribunals is now infamous for not serving notice on the suspected individuals or giving them an effective opportunity of defending their status as citizens and passing orders without adhering to the basic procedural guarantees. In July 2026, a bench comprising of Justices Vikram Nath and Sandeep Mehta set aside a series of judgements delivered by the Gauhati High Court that declared 27 individuals as foreigners. In most of these cases, the judgements had been passed ex-parte – no opportunity given to the individual to respond. The Apex Court shunned the mechanical exercise followed in determining citizenship – no service of notice, no analysis of the material forming the basis of the adjudication and no evaluation of evidence adduced by the State.

Expressly Constructing the Guardrails

The Apex Court in State of AP v. McDowell & Co. held that an enactment cannot be struck down on the grounds of it being arbitrary or unreasonable and that some constitutional infirmity has to be found before invalidating an Act. This was overruled in Shayara Bano v. Union of India. In Shayara Bano and the Association for Democratic Reforms v. Union of India, the Court pronounced that manifest arbitrariness is something done by the legislature capriciously, irrationally and/or without adequate determining principle. It is this “determining principle” that is elusive in the realm of India’s citizenship laws. As the situation presently stands, administrative actions undertaken in the course of detecting persons suspected of being illegal migrants is bereft of a discernible legal standard.

In Re: Section 6A of the Citizenship Act, 1955, (“Re Section 6A”) the Respondents argued that citizenship, external aggression, migration and other related issues are matters of foreign policy that are to be dealt by the government and thus must be excluded from the Court’s purview. In

upholding section 6A, the Court stated that Article 11 of the Constitution confers overriding powers upon the Parliament to make laws even when they are against other provisions.

The Court has taken an overtly cautious approach in not impinging on the powers of the legislature – something that is also evident in the SIR judgement (this time, with more authority in the hands of the Election Commission of India) – and correctly so. However, the concern is, that the Court is rarely called upon to legislate in these matters of citizenship or immigration but rather to ensure that the process of determination of citizenship does not traverse due process. It is imperative for the Apex Court to explicitly read certain limits, into the implementation of these laws as ex facie the law conferring the power prescribes no guardrails. In the same case, the Court held that a constitutional bench must be constituted to monitor the implementation of immigration and citizenship legislations.

The Supreme Court in Sonowal recognised illegal immigration as a threat to national security. However, unlike other areas of national security like decisions pertaining to warfare or military operations or defense acquisitions where the Executive has an upper hand, in the domain of immigration, actions of the executive are more susceptible to judicial scrutiny. This can be attributed to national security on one hand and the intersection of diversity, basic rights granted to both citizens and non-citizens, and protection against administrative excess on the other. The State machinery cannot use security as a blanket justification for deportation and detention.

In light of this, it is not appropriate to leave the responsibility of oversight in the hands of administrative or even quasi-judicial bodies (as can be deduced from the workings of the foreigner’s tribunals). The elevated standards of independence, impartiality and procedural fairness that is required in the process of this ascertainment of citizenship, is embodied only in the judiciary. However, the problem with judicial scrutiny is that such excesses are checked on an individual basis. Given the pervasiveness of these instances, the need is for the Court to clearly lay down a set of general legal principles that the administrative authorities are obligated to adhere to in the course of ascertainment of citizenship.

In Re Section 6A, the Court stated that any law pertaining to citizenship has to be congruent to Article 14, and review for intelligible differentia and manifest arbitrariness and that the Court has the authority to review the same. Executive supremacy in this domain does not preclude judicial supervision. To borrow from Mr. Gautam Bhatia, “Citizenship – like the fundamental rights, the directive principles, the federal structure, and the rest of the Constitution – were part of a coherent web of principle, not single strands floating in the air”.

**Tiyasha is a law student at Symbiosis Law School.

text:
In Yemen, fighters from Ansar Allah — commonly referred to as the Houthis — attacked a residential neighborhood in Taiz Tuesday, killing two teenage girls and wounding six others. Ansar Allah has nearly surrounded Yemen’s third-largest city and cut off most of its supply routes. Taiz is currently held by the Saudi-backed government. U.N. human rights chief Volker Türk warned that residents are in serious danger as food runs short and prices climb. This is a resident of Taiz.

Saeed Ahmed: “Citizens are struggling with gas queues, and there was no gas at the station. Only one tanker came in, and it wasn’t enough. Taiz city is now besieged by the Houthis.”

In southern Yemen, the death toll from an Ansar Allah missile strike on a government training camp has risen to 73. The U.N. Refugee Agency reports that more than 250,000 Yemenis have been displaced since the war flared up again in July between Ansar Allah and the Saudi-backed government. Meanwhile, Britain says it will step up its military support to Saudi Arabia.

Saudi Arabia executed a Bangladeshi man and woman in Mecca last week after convicting them of a supposed “indecent act” inside a mosque. Bangladesh says it was not informed of the execution. The execution has sparked public outcry in Bangladesh, since more than 3 million Bangladeshis work and live in Saudi Arabia. According to Amnesty International, Saudi Arabia has executed around 100 people this year; many of them were foreigners convicted of drug offenses.

Topics:

Saudi Arabia

In Gaza, Israeli strikes killed at least seven Palestinians Tuesday, including a married couple and a 17-year-old, in separate ​incidents across the Gaza Strip. Despite last October’s so-called ceasefire, Israeli strikes have killed at least 1,500 Palestinians in Gaza. This is a brother of a Palestinian killed in an Israeli airstrike earlier this month.

Mahmoud Yassin: “We’re supposed to be in a ceasefire period, but, honestly, we are not seeing a ceasefire or anything. The war is still going on, assassinations are continuing, and the shelling has not stopped. We are appealing to and calling on those responsible for us to put an end to these assassinations and attacks, because we are a people who want to live.”

In the occupied West Bank, Brad Lander, the Democratic nominee for New York’s 10th Congressional District and former New York City comptroller, has been detained by the Israeli military along with at least 80 rabbis, volunteers and activists accompanying Palestinian farmers.

Lander wrote on X, “We were simply harvesting olives in a grove near Nehalim in the West Bank. The occupation is a crime under international law. Harvesting olives isn’t a crime under any law I know.”

In a statement released by Rabbis for Human Rights, acting executive director Anton Goodman said, “We came to accompany farmers to land they have not been able to reach in three years, and after two hours of quiet harvesting large forces arrived and closed the area. No one could have known about this order in advance. Instead of protecting people working their own land, the army is removing them from it, and detaining those who came to stand beside them.”

Congresswoman Rashida Tlaib is calling on the Department of Justice to arrest the Israeli military commander accused of killing 5-year-old Palestinian girl Hind Rajab and six of her relatives as they hid inside the family’s car while attempting to evacuate Gaza City in 2024. The Hind Rajab Foundation has filed a legal complaint demanding the arrest and prosecution of Sean Glass on war crimes. Glass is currently in the United States. The foundation on Monday posted photos of Glass in New York City. Glass reportedly led the Israeli military’s so-called Vampire Empire Company of the 52nd Armored Battalion. The Hind Rajab Foundation’s general director, Dyab Abou Jahjah, said in a statement, “Glass is not just another man implicated in the killing of Hind Rajab. He is the man who most likely gave the order to open fire on the vehicle carrying Hind and members of her family, including other children. That Glass can walk the streets of the United States as though nothing has happened is intolerable. He must be brought to justice.”

Russia has freed a 74-year-old U.S. citizen who had been imprisoned for over four years accused of fighting as a mercenary in Ukraine. Stephen Hubbard spent decades abroad working as an English teacher. He reportedly moved to the eastern Ukrainian city of Izium in 2014. The city was seized by Russia in 2022. U.S. special envoy Steve Witkoff praised Russian President Vladimir Putin for Hubbard’s release, saying, “the whole nation sends their thanks.” Witkoff is currently in St. Petersburg meeting with Putin. This comes after President Trump reached a major energy deal with Putin to import millions of tons of Russian diesel. Trump’s surprise announcement earlier this month waives a sweeping sanctions law he signed in September targeting Russian oil and gas revenues used to fund the war on Ukraine.

In related news, The Wall Street Journal reports Elon Musk has downgraded the bandwidth speed of a military-grade version of satellite internet provider Starlink used in Ukraine. Both Trump and Musk have expressed anger at Kyiv over its recent attacks on Russian diesel refineries. Last week, Musk claimed only the Pentagon and Trump had the authority to limit the use of Starlink.

Topics:

Russia

Ukraine

France is planning a massive surge in police forces as more nationwide protests are planned for this weekend. The latest deployment announced by French Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu comes after hundreds of thousands of demonstrators marched in over 140 cities across France on Saturday demanding relief from rising cost of living, improvements to education and other issues. An estimated 2,400 protesters were arrested on Saturday. This is a lawyer representing a student.

Tristan Lawless: “Sometimes the arrests are clearly organized simply to terrify protesters and ensure that a large number of people are arrested, so that it discourages these protesters from returning to Place de la République or Place de la Bastille to assert their rights.”

Topics:

France

Protests

In Italy, the government is deploying 500 troops to Milan after days of protests against the rising cost of living. It comes as Italy’s Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni approved new security measures making it easier to prosecute minors over 14. This is Prime Minister Meloni.

Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni: “And preventive detention, which until now applied only to adults, will also be extended to minors. Fourth, Milan will receive 500 additional military personnel until the end of the year, working alongside the police and the Carabinieri, and we are strengthening the juvenile justice system with more magistrates and more places in detention facilities, so that the certainty of punishment also applies to 16-year-olds.”

Topics:

Italy

Protests

President Trump on Tuesday told reporters that Democratic Congressmember Ilhan Omar could go to jail. His comments come days after Homeland Security federal agents raided Omar’s home as part of Trump’s efforts to strip Omar of U.S. citizenship and deport her. The Trump administration has claimed, without evidence, Omar committed immigration fraud in her naturalization process. This is President Trump.

President Donald Trump: “Well, she could be. She could also go to jail. She could also go to jail. You know, they keep talking about deportation. No, she could go to jail. This is just my opinion. I think she’s a sick and very dishonest person, but — who hates our country. And she comes from a country that is essentially not even a country, Somalia. It’s a real [bleep]house.”

In California, Los Angeles election officials say a list compiled by the Department of Justice of some 20,000 alleged noncitizen registered voters includes a “high percentage” of people born in the United States. The new revelations come after a court filing by California state and local officials in response to a lawsuit filed by the Trump administration. Last week, the DOJ gave California 48 hours to segregate the ballots of those named on the list, which local officials blasted as unreliable after an early review of the voters’ records. California said in its Tuesday filing, “At best, this litigation is a reckless political stunt. At worst, it threatens to disenfranchise thousands of Californians this election.”

Topics:

California

Voting

In Texas, Democratic state representative and gubernatorial candidate Gina Hinojosa filed a lawsuit Monday seeking access to 1,200 pages of heavily redacted emails between trillionaire Elon Musk and Texas Republican Governor Greg Abbott. The governor’s office refused to release the communications last year to media outlet The Texas Newsroom, arguing they were exempted from public records laws due to “information that is intimate and embarrassing and not of legitimate concern to the public.” State Representative Hinojosa’s lawsuit accuses Governor Abbott of violating a Texas statute that grants lawmakers access to public records, including confidential information.

Rep. Gina Hinojosa: “What this is about is we have the world’s only trillionaire getting massive tax breaks from this governor after giving him over $500,000 in campaign contributions.”

Hinojosa alleges that, in return, Governor Abbott gave Elon Musk $1.6 billion in tax breaks for his planned Terafab project, a massive semiconductor manufacturing hub in Grimes County. She also pointed to Abbott’s support for tens of millions of dollars in grant funding to SpaceX and a broadband internet contract worth over $100 million that was awarded to Musk’s Starlink internet service.

This comes as FEC filings show Elon Musk was responsible for more than half of all fundraising to the Republican-aligned super PAC the Senate Leadership Fund during the third quarter of the year. Musk has spent at least $168 million on the Texas Senate race in support of MAGA Republican Ken Paxton against Democrat James Talarico.

The New York Times is reporting that a prominent Venezuelan billionaire, Julio Herrera Velutini, who was seeking clemency from the Trump administration after facing bribery charges, hired Alina Habba, Trump’s former lawyer, from the Justice Department in a $50 million deal. In exchange, Habba would serve as general counsel at a company set up by Herrera’s daughter. Weeks after Habba started her work at the company, President Trump granted Herrera a full and unconditional pardon. title: They Fled Ethiopia's War. Now, Israel May Send Them Back. - Foreign Policy
authors: Theia Chatelle, David E. Rosenberg, Shalom Lipner, Sharon Weinberger, Cullen Hendrix, Michael Poznansky, Ian Easton, Emma Ashford, Howard W. French, Daniel S. Hamilton
description:
Of the Ethiopians in Israel who are not Jewish, some—such as Habteab—fled during the Tigray war and its aftermath.
“It’s presented as giving them another chance, but in reality, they’re just being called in to be told they have to leave,” Paul Strauss said.
“She turns to me, ‘Please help me, save my life,’ and I have nothing to give her,” Paul Strauss said.
Paul Strauss spends hours filling in resettlement forms with families who cannot afford a lawyer.
Each time Paul Strauss submits a file, she said, the U.N. representative reminds her that completing it does not guarantee placement elsewhere.
text:
JERUSALEM—For 75 days starting in 2020, Luwam Habteab slept on the floor of a prison cell, given little food and no medical care. She was detained that November by Ethiopian security forces for her reporting on the Axum massacre, in which Eritrean forces killed hundreds of civilians over a weekend—one of the deadliest episodes of the 2020-22 Tigray war.

Upon her release, Habteab found that her apartment had been sealed by federal police. Her family had warned her not to return there, telling her that security forces were waiting. A local archbishop with a connection at the Israeli Embassy interceded, after which Habteab was ushered out of the country. She landed in Tel Aviv in August 2023 and applied for asylum. (Habteab is identified by a pseudonym out of fear of reprisal.)

Habteab now lives in Jerusalem’s Old City, where she spends most of her days praying. As of August, she was one of 1,334 Ethiopians with open asylum claims before Israel’s Interior Ministry, according to figures that the ministry confirmed to Foreign Policy.

Months after Habteab arrived, in January 2024, the Israeli Interior Ministry determined that the situation in Ethiopia was stable enough to send its nationals home, revoking the group protection that had shielded asylum-seekers from deportation. That stability did not last: This July, Tigray’s regional authorities declared that the 2022 peace agreement with the federal government had collapsed, accusing Addis Ababa of preparing for war.

Last month, an alliance of rebel groups launched a full-scale offensive against federal forces, seizing airports across Tigray and pushing into neighboring Afar and Amhara states. Federal forces have since retaken Tigray’s capital, though the rebels have vowed to keep fighting; Eritrea and Ethiopia have cut diplomatic ties. Explosions have been reported in Addis Ababa, which Israeli authorities say is safe for returnees.

Habteab has watched with dread as the fighting returned to her home province. Much of Tigray is under a communications blackout, reviving fears of the total siege during the 2020-22 war that starved the region and killed as many as 600,000 people. Habteab’s family in Tigray is almost impossible to reach, she said.

With Israel’s national elections set for Oct. 27, civil society advocates warn that right-wing politicians are once again casting asylum-seekers as a threat to gain a leg up. Israeli officials refer to some migrants and refugees as “infiltrators,” a term embedded in the country’s own laws, and successive governments have described their presence as a danger to Israel’s Jewish character.

Habteab and other asylum-seekers in Israel have few places left to go as domestic politics turn against them and Western governments dismantle the asylum system that was supposed to protect them.

Israel has a long history with the notion of asylum. Founded by refugees in the wake of the Holocaust as a safe haven for the Jewish diaspora, the country was among the first signatories of the 1951 Refugee Convention. Jewish jurists were instrumental in shaping the convention’s core nonrefoulement principle, the rule that no one may be returned to a country where their life is at risk.

Yet, since the Israeli government took over processing asylum claims from the United Nations in 2009, it has granted asylum status to less than 1 percent of those seeking it, according to HIAS Israel, a Jewish humanitarian nonprofit.

Israel has also long held a place in the imagination of Ethiopian asylum-seekers as the land of the ancient Israelites, in whose story of exile and return they saw themselves. In practical terms, the country was also the closest state offering asylum that they could reach without undertaking the perilous Mediterranean crossing.

Of the Ethiopians in Israel who are not Jewish, some—such as Habteab—fled during the Tigray war and its aftermath. But most have been in Israel for a decade or more, arriving on pilgrimage visas or by crossing the Egyptian border before Israel completed its fence there in 2013. They, too, are asylum-seekers: Almost all applied for protection after arriving, having fled earlier rounds of interethnic violence and state persecution, according to the Jerusalem African Community Center (JACC), a support and advocacy organization for the city’s African asylum-seekers.

On arrival, they opened asylum claims with the Interior Ministry and were interviewed about why they had come to Israel. Under Israeli law, the ministry was meant to review each claim and decide whether to grant refugee status—a process that, for most of these asylum-seekers, didn’t happen. Now, according to advocates, many Ethiopian applicants are being summoned back after more than a decade for a second interview to determine whether they can stay in Israel.

Asked for comment, Israel’s Population and Immigration Authority said, “there is no policy of deportation regarding this group” and that cases are examined individually. The authority added that it does not determine whether a country is safe for returnees, referring questions to the Israeli Foreign Ministry. (The Foreign Ministry did not respond to a request for comment.)

Anat Ben-Dor, who runs the Refugee Rights Clinic at Tel Aviv University, said the burden of proof placed on applicants for asylum to establish a credible fear of persecution is set very high and that interviewers look for inconsistencies between what an applicant says now and what they said on arrival.

“The whole interview is actually an effort not to find the truth, but to find flaws and problems in the testimony,” Ben-Dor said. “Very few people can successfully pass such an interview, particularly when the system is so slow that people are being interviewed about events that sometimes occurred 10 years earlier.”

Asked whether the system was dysfunctional or intentionally obstructive, Michal Pomeranz, another lawyer who represents asylum-seekers, said it was both. “They clearly want to make people’s lives here miserable, and that’s something even the Supreme Court has said,” she said, referring to a 2020 ruling that struck down a law requiring asylum-seekers to deposit 20 percent of their wages into a fund that they could recover only by leaving the country.

After the follow-up interview, the Interior Ministry decides whether an asylum-seeker may stay in Israel or must leave—but the outcome is almost always the same, according to Yael Paul Strauss, who runs the psychosocial department at JACC.

By her account, 90 percent to 95 percent of those summoned are rejected and given three to four months to leave the country. “It’s presented as giving them another chance, but in reality, they’re just being called in to be told they have to leave,” Paul Strauss said.

The cost of contesting a rejection is steep, running at around $4,000 to petition a denied application and another $4,000 for an appeal, according to Paul Strauss. Few employers will hire someone with a temporary permit, regardless of their profession or level of education in Ethiopia, leaving most asylum-seekers with few ways to raise that kind of money.

Paul Strauss described a message that she had recently received from a mother of three small children who had paid to appeal her asylum rejection, lost, and had no idea where she would find the money to try again. “She turns to me, ‘Please help me, save my life,’ and I have nothing to give her,” Paul Strauss said.

When he returned to office in 2025, U.S. President Donald Trump effectively dismantled the U.S. refugee admissions program and suspended the entry of all refugees into the country, including those who had already been screened. Following legal challenges, the Trump administration resumed limited admissions under a historically low cap of 7,500 refugees for fiscal year 2026—admissions that have been allocated almost entirely to white South African Afrikaners.

In December 2025, the Trump administration also terminated the temporary protected status that Ethiopians were granted during the Tigray war. Around 900 asylum-seekers in Israel—mainly Sudanese and Eritrean, along with some Ethiopians—were in the pipeline to be resettled to the United States as of early 2025, according to Sivan Carmel, the country director of HIAS Israel, which processed the cases.

Some had already cleared their medical and security checks, had departure dates, and needed only plane tickets. “They’d left their jobs; they’d already told their landlords they’d be leaving” before their entry to the United States was denied, Carmel said.

The office of the U.N. refugee agency in Israel, which referred those cases and managed resettlement out of the country, has been hollowed out as part of the same pattern of global retrenchment against asylum—its staff reduced to three and its Tel Aviv office cut. Agency staff struggle to keep up with the thousands of open asylum claims.

This has left the work to fall to groups such as JACC, which operates on a shoestring budget. Paul Strauss spends hours filling in resettlement forms with families who cannot afford a lawyer. Each time Paul Strauss submits a file, she said, the U.N. representative reminds her that completing it does not guarantee placement elsewhere.

For those who cannot leave for another country and cannot stay in Israel, the return of war to Ethiopia has taken away their last consolation: the hope that the danger that they fled might be in the past. As armed forces push toward Ethiopia’s capital and much of Tigray remains in the dark, many of the families that Israel intends to send back can’t even get in touch with their relatives.

For those working on behalf of the asylum-seekers, the bigger picture is not lost. “I want to live in a state that I’m not embarrassed by,” Pomeranz said. “I kept thinking things couldn’t get worse. They keep getting worse.”

title: The Immigration Enforcement Hydra Without a Kill Switch - Lawfare
description:
While the bill focuses on advanced AI, an apparatus already exists with the same features that make a “kill switch” attractive: today’s automated immigration enforcement infrastructure.
The impulse to call for a kill switch is natural; however, it wouldn’t work for automated immigration enforcement even if we agreed to build one.
Immigration enforcement used to be the bargain struck through federalism.
Sanctuary laws remain important because they protect a state or city’s decision not to supply officers, custody, or data to immigration enforcement.
Illinois created a state cause of action, albeit one with legal vulnerabilities, against officers who violate the Constitution while conducting immigration enforcement; the Justice Department is suing to strike it.
text:
After OpenAI’s models hacked Hugging Face in July, two members of Congress promptly proposed the AI Kill Switch Act. The bill would allow the secretary of homeland security to pull the plug on certain high-compute, high-revenue private-sector artificial intelligence (AI) models in an emergency. Since then, several frontier lab employees have resigned, citing existential safety concerns about AI. The frontier labs’ executives, for their part, have called for a government-coordinated pause.

However misguided, the instinct behind the proposal is understandable, and the problem it seeks to address is real: Powerful tools built and controlled by private companies can move faster than the institutions meant to govern them. The comparison between automated enforcement architecture and powerful, at times autonomous, frontier models may seem counterintuitive, but the same concerns underpin both. Much of the oversight available to the public is passive: a records request, mandatory disclosure, audit, or a lawsuit after a decision has already been made. The “kill switch” proposal reaches for active accountability, giving someone outside the AI company the power to stop a system in its tracks—not a request, but an intervention.

While the bill focuses on advanced AI, an apparatus already exists with the same features that make a “kill switch” attractive: today’s automated immigration enforcement infrastructure. The technology is often more mundane than foundation models, but the ecosystem of software and data flows is enormous, sophisticated, opaque, rapidly evolving, and controlled by the private sector. More than 300 million identities, Medicaid records, taxpayer addresses, TSA passenger information, and license-plate-reader networks, among other swaths of information, flow through today’s immigration enforcement apparatus.

The goal: increase the speed and scale at which the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) can target, identify, locate, detain, and deport immigrants. Vendors build databases, algorithms, and applications to specifications dictated by federal contracts—specifications that require as much data as possible to flow as seamlessly as possible between these systems. Neither courts nor Congress can match this pace.

The problem: These systems are often wrong, misused, or otherwise deleterious to our democracy. And the reasons they make a “kill switch” appealing don’t depend on bleeding-edge system capabilities.

The impulse to call for a kill switch is natural; however, it wouldn’t work for automated immigration enforcement even if we agreed to build one. There is no single database, company, or program to shut down. There are many systems held by agencies and vendors; some contracts can end and some data feeds can be stopped, but the machine’s gears would grind on. The apparatus is a virtual Hydra: Cut off a visible head—a vendor, data broker, database, or data feed—and the body of contracts, copied records, shared interfaces, and compatible tools can furnish a replacement. The point is not that resistance is futile; it is that a remedy should target the body, not merely a head.

The architecture’s resilience is a product of an intentional design feature: interoperability, or the deliberate capacity of separate systems to exchange and use one another’s data or capabilities. In practice, interoperability allows different systems to share data across systems automatically in formats the systems can both understand and process, avoiding the need for a central repository. Interoperability enables a system to benefit from the algorithmic output of another, avoiding the need for every system to build a valuable tool or capability itself. It also permits different systems to automatically flag a specific record or aggregate trend for another, avoiding the need to wait for a human to notice. The systems remain structurally separate, but their contents become mutually accessible, in real time, and without human involvement.

The term has a long technical and legal history and is often credited with promoting market inclusiveness, transparency, and ecosystem oversight. It also has a track record of benefitting the very incumbents whose power it is meant to check. Its central role in the expansion of automated immigration enforcement is underdiscussed; some scholars have exposed the rise of privatization, automation, and interagency or intergovernmental data sharing in immigration, and advocacy groups have shed light on the companies profiting off of immigration enforcement; the relevance of interoperability of procured systems remains in the shadows.

Interoperability and private vendors are one story, not two. Vendors supply the data, the integration layer, and the technical rules that determine which records can be linked and which systems are compatible. In a forthcoming law review article, Sam Adler and I examine how that role has turned vendors into intermediaries, shifting from what was once a more direct federal-state-local negotiation over immigration enforcement, and how this development has undermined state capacity to resist federal immigration policies. This article highlights the operational underpinnings of this transformation: how interoperability of vendor systems makes the problem of automated enforcement unique, not just in scale, and why addressing the new risks requires new remedies—ones that dismantle the apparatus itself.

The Architecture Hiding in Plain Sight

Litigation over Medicaid records underscores why vendor interoperability turns a one-time illegal data transfer into a cascade, proliferating sensitive information that is impossible to claw back from downstream systems. In 2025, federal health officials sent immigration officials the personal data of millions of Medicaid enrollees, with the goal of sharing data on all 79 million enrollees, interpreting their limited authority to share immigration data as expansively as possible. Twenty states sued. A federal judge responded by clarifying the scope of the department’s authority, emphasizing its limited nature, and later paused the data transfer entirely after learning the court’s orders were flouted yet again. At first blush, this looks like judicial oversight enforcing accountability.

But the states’ July filing reported that Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) had already passed a dataset of people lawfully present in the country to Palantir—data ICE should not have had in the first place. Palantir provides the government with applications, such as Enhanced Leads Identification & Targeting for Enforcement (ELITE), that aggregate data, analyze it, and generate lists of targets, investigative dossiers, and location data.

In response to the states’ discovery requests for the ill-gotten information, ICE explained that the systems’ nature made it technologically difficult to ensure it could find every file it should not have. In a declaration responding to the states’ discovery requests, ICE official Alberto Briseno said that altered file names and content made it technologically difficult to represent that every file variation had been searched for and located. Palantir reported that it deleted its copy, but removing records from one system does nothing to other copies, including those inside ICE, which later foundan overlooked copy in cloud storage and then six employees who still had the data. The court did exercise oversight, but its order could do only so much: Stopping a particular flow does not automatically identify copies, derivative records, and combinations already created elsewhere.

That pattern is not unique to Medicaid, and courts do not always bring down the hammer: In one case, the U.S. Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit permitted the Internal Revenue Service (IRS) and ICE to continue data sharing, even after a district court found the IRS had made 42,695 unlawful disclosures of taxpayer addresses to ICE. Not that ICE needed the IRS data: ICE had already purchased address data through commercial data paths, and the agency appears to be buying records related to immigrants’ taxpayer-identification numbers from a broker. A decision about one data source cannot establish that another compatible source does not give the same information.

Interoperability is not a happy accident in the government’s eyes. My companion Lawfare piece traces how the post-9/11 legal and infrastructural transformations favored interoperability over a single national warehouse: Separate systems could remain in place while their contents became accessible across institutional lines at all times. Not single records, but entire databases. Not just federal data, but also state and local records. As a governing principle for the widening network of systems, programs, and information sharing, interoperability left a durable capacity for dragnet surveillance and algorithmic monitoring that could be redirected as enforcement priorities changed. It remains the stated policy.

The apparatus operates as a hub-and-spokes model, with Palantir’s ImmigrationOS as the hub. ICE contracted Palantir to build the software in April 2025 as a roughly $30 million modification of an existing Palantir contract, without engaging in a competitive process, on the justification that Palantir’s systems “are already ingesting and processing data from multiple ICE, DHS[,] and external sources” and therefore it was the only provider that could fulfill the department’s requirements. Dependence begot dependence. Ten months later, DHS signed a department-wide purchasing agreement that essentially states any future contract with Palantir through 2031 need not go through a competitive process, at least until the $1 billion ceiling is met, invoking an exception to federal purchasing rules documented in a limited-sources justification.

The system’s significance is not just the size of a contract. Palantir’s data model—how it integrates data from different sources, classifies it, analyzes it, and presents data to enforcement officers as outputs—can shape the relationships ICE acts on. That vendor-controlled schema becomes not just a practical part of the government’s operating environment but also part of immigration governance itself. The way Palantir designs its systems, the hub of the overall interoperable apparatus, influences what is understood as relevant, what is considered a priority, and how those criteria are determined.

The spokes are everything that feeds the hub or draws from it. ELITE, another Palantir tool, draws from the hub. Itsuser guide lists sources including the Department of Health and Human Services and “CLEAR,” whichshares its name with a Thomson Reuters data product, a longtime ICE contractor. One officer testified that ELITE is “kind of like Google Maps,” showing agents how many potential targets live in an area and how likely they are to be present. In one Oregon town, an officer called an apartment complex “target rich” because vehicles there were registered to people “who had either a criminal or immigration nexus.”

On the ground, agents can turn to another spoke: Mobile Fortify, a facial recognition app that scans a face against a bank of 200 million images to identify a person and determine their immigration status—its outputs are treated as “definitive,” even though the app’s use technically requires human oversight. Recent reports suggest the app now pulls from a bank of 1.2 billion images, combining private image databases with massive government biometric databases.

ELITE and Mobile Fortify are private-sector applications, but they are only as valuable as the inputs other spokes can provide. Data brokers, companies that compile personal records from thousands of public and commercial sources and sell access to it, exist to be plugged into as many systems as can benefit from their information—functionally all of them. When ICE posted notice last month that it would pay LexisNexis $6.7 million for access to more than 82 billion records, the procurement papers specified that the database must be interoperable “with ICE applications, such as but not limited to, Palantir platform.” In other words, the purchase was conditioned on LexisNexis’s data flowing to the hub. Compatibility among federal systems has been a standing legal requirement for two decades. Now, the requirement extends to commercial hubs and spokes.

Modularity can make a system harder, not easier, to remove. Engineers make systems modular by building systems to common standards so that components can be swapped. If the replacement must fit the same socket as its predecessor, use the same sources, and feed the same hub, switching vendors does nothing to dismantle the architecture. For example, some cities replaced Flock with Axon, slotting identical technology under a different name into the same socket. Agencies do the same with contracts: ICE abandoned its plan for an exclusive $125 million Thomson Reuters agreement after public backlash, then sought a different procurement for related capabilities. Like the Ship of Theseus, every piece of the architecture can be replaced without the result looking any different from the original.

On the ground, the stack enables real violence. In Woodburn, Oregon, an ICE agent working to meet a daily target of eight arrests stopped a van of farmworkers after using Palantir’s ELITE to search its license plate. Then, an officer used Mobile Fortify to identify the passengers. The app returned two different incorrect identities for a woman, but she was detained anyway—one of at least three dozen people swept up in the town that day. Despite known error rates, agents report trusting the app’s outputs over physical birth certificates. The address tool can display 100 percent confidence and still be wrong. Nothing in the law requires anyone to tell her what the app concluded about her or gave her a way to contest it before being arrested. Although a federal judge has attempted to restrain ICE’s “casting dragnets” over farmworker towns, the technology that enabled the raid remains.

Built to Connect and Hard to Unwind

For as long as the United States has had immigration enforcement, it has been a negotiation between two parties. The federal government may decide whom to deport, but states and cities hold most of what enforcement needs—jail bookings, driver’s license photographs, arrest records, on-the-ground manpower—and decide whether to share it. The Constitution forbids DHS from directly conscripting state and local officers to make arrests. DHS can enlist them only with their governments’ consent, as it does through the 287(g) agreements discussed below. What’s emerged is a fissure in state posture: On one hand, we have sanctuary cities that limit their officers from holding people for ICE and sharing information with it. On the other hand, some cities are eager to cooperate. Immigration enforcement used to be the bargain struck through federalism.

But now, a third party sits at the table, and nobody elected it. Vendors do not broker the deal between Washington and the states, but their presence mediates the terms. They give the federal government a backdoor to the resources they need—private data and automation to replace state and local information and manpower, respectively—undercutting subfederal bargaining power. By reducing reliance on states, vendors pave the way for the federal government to execute its ideal version of immigration policy. What’s more: The private-sector tools built for the federal government that embed federal policies and priorities into their very design are repackaged and sold back to states and local governments that, pressed for resources themselves, readily adopt them. In doing so, they unwittingly feed the apparatus many of them so earnestly try to resist.

A town that buys Flock Safety’s license-plate camera network to catch burglars can, with one setting, make its cameras searchable by police departments across the country, partners in ICE’s 287(g) program—which is how Florida wildlife officers came to search thousands of other agencies’ cameras on ICE’s behalf.

A state that refuses to hand ICE its driver’s license records has not kept them from ICE if a data broker sells them. States and cities still hold real power at that table. What they lose is the ability to exercise it by saying no, because the yes has been built into the products they buy. After Oregon limited state data disclosures to ICE, its Department of Motor Vehicles signed agreements to sell driver’s license records to Thomson Reuters and LexisNexis: prohibited from sharing data with the federal government directly, Oregon sold the same data to a broker feeding the hub.

When a vendor’s system design and contract terms determine whether the data is searchable outside a jurisdiction, available to a federal platform, retained after the local contract ends, or used to improve the vendor’s next product, then subfederal immigration policies lose efficacy. The decision with the largest enforcement consequence may therefore occur before a local official ever encounters an ICE request, in the product and procurement choices that define what the system can do.

And after states and localities adopt these systems, the government’s surrounding infrastructure shapes to accommodate them, building reliance on the technology and undercutting their stated policies. Richmond, California, deactivated its license plate readers after learning that a national-search feature exposed local data; within months, after the police chief reported a 33 percent rise in auto thefts since the shutdown, a closely divided councilvoted to restore them anddirected the city attorney to negotiate a contract amendment prohibiting unauthorized data sharing. That is path dependence in practice: Tools, staff, budgets, and workflows grow around shared interfaces, and a later administration can reduce use without dismantling the capacity it inherits. The more compatible purchases a jurisdiction makes, the more expensive it becomes to refuse the next one. Policy that began as an administration’s priority can then outlast its political mandate as a legacy environment other institutions have learned to rely on.

Immigration Policy Written Into Code

This apparatus has bipartisan roots and reflects the post-9/11 national-securitization of immigration. Secure Communities, a federal program launched in 2008, turned a routine jail check—sending fingerprints to the FBI for a criminal record search—into an automatic DHS immigration check. When jurisdictions tried to opt out, the government said they could not benefit from the criminal history check without permitting the immigration one. States and localities lost the discretion over participation in immigration enforcement via data flows; now their only choice is whether to arrest in the first place.

Section 287(g) of the Immigration and Nationality Act, which lets DHS deputize state and local officers to do immigration work, caused a visible explosion in boots on the ground, but it’s the hidden installation of federal access to data and systems via interoperability that extends the program beyond the officers it deputizes. Deputized officers gain immigration authorities and privileges, including forms of federal immunity. But each agreement also puts a piece of the federal stack inside a local police department via subsidized software: logins to the federal immigration databases and biometric scanners—courtesy of the vendor Bi2 Technologies, the beneficiary of another sole-source contract.

Federal policy is often built into the architecture it uses and foists on deputized officials. Without any formal administrative procedures, such as public notice and an invitation to comment, ICE configured its software to determine whether detained individuals should be released or held in order to eliminate the possibility that the system would ever recommend release. From June 2017 to September 2019, the release rate for people whom ICE itself classified as low risk fell from 47 percent to 3 percent.

The capacity also travels easily to new purposes. Technically, these systems are built with purpose limits: Users are required to provide a covered justification for their searches. However, the available options and the monitoring (or lack thereof) for misuse are technical and procedural decisions that vendors determine. They leave a lot to be desired.

In Florida, fish and wildlife officers searched on ICE’s behalf, despite Flock promising not to work with ICE. The officers even admitted as much—justiying the search as “Immigration (civil/administrative) – I.C.E.” Flock, however, either did not notice or care. In Texas, officers used Flock to locate a woman suspected of having an abortion, dubiously justifying it as a matter of community safety, out of concern for her well-being—in a state that criminalized abortions.

The ability to locate and sort people is general purpose; the target list can change. Immigration is where the architecture is being perfected because it is where the federal government meets the least resistance: a population with the fewest legal protections and the fewest political defenders—in part because many cannot vote for the federal and subfederal officials who set enforcement policy—on terrain where courts, treating immigration as a matter of sovereignty and national security, have long deferred to the political branches. Immigration is a proving ground, not a containment zone.

No One Holds the Switch

This dispersed design also diffuses accountability. The government insists there is nothing to see: ICE’s acting director assured Congress in February that “we don’t have a database” tracking U.S. citizens. Read literally, the denial is hard to falsify. There is no single database. Instead, there is an architecture in which any database can be reached from any other, documented in pieces by the agencies that run it. A records request returns the whole, and no court order reaches it. Searches leave records, but the logs belong to the operator.

Concerned citizens and organizations file public records requests, and the answer is often that the details are a vendor’s trade secret or a law enforcement secret; ELITE has been in the field for more than a year, and the only privacy impact assessment—the public document an agency is supposed to publish describing what a system collects and why—was last updated in 2019 for a different system. Tools such as Mobile Fortify lack privacy assessments altogether. The public learns what it can through leaks and lawsuits, one at a time.

The people expected to supervise the apparatus sit in the department operating it, and internal oversight offices have been gutted or closed. The only federal rule requiring an agency to stop using an AI system that fails its safety standards is White House guidance that allows the agency itself to determine which systems are covered. ICE classified ELITE as “presumed high-impact but determined not high-impact,”reasoning that its outputs are limited to “normalized address data” and that officers “review and validate” them before acting. A federal court, citing officer testimony, wrote that ELITE’s leads are, “generally speaking,” “not accurate.” Yet agents have separately confirmed they treat system outputs, such as Mobile Fortify’s identifications, as definitive.

Vendors punt accountability back to democracy. Flock’s chief executive wrote that elected representatives should determine what is acceptable. The issue is that the decisions that matter never went through traditional democratic processes. A city can buy this software without holding a competitive bidding process at all, by ordering from a purchasing catalog that somebody else already negotiated. Without a city’s close attention, the contract renews itself unless somebody gives 30 days’ notice. The vendors set the defaults, delivering systems that share data with national networks automatically, and often obscure the fact that the setting can be turned off; the vendors have outsized power in dictating contract terms, resisting disclosure or audit requirements; the vendors dangle the threat of not renewing a contract to extract even more generous terms.

Interoperability entrenches what was built the less democratic way—through software design or contract—and once a jurisdiction depends on it, the ordinary democratic tools to undo it are aimed at the wrong part of the system. The apparatus continues to grow, even in the face of strenuous objections in the form of protests,tech worker campaigns,surveillance ordinances, andcongressional letters. The democratic debate may be happening, but the machine does not need to win it to survive.

Three Ways to Dismantle the Architecture

This section’s recommendations target subfederal entities because they are at the forefront of the resistance, and it is these states and cities’ position at the bargaining table that needs to be restored. But a strategy shift is warranted: If the pathology is architectural, the remedy must be as well.

Sanctuary laws remain important because they protect a state or city’s decision not to supply officers, custody, or data to immigration enforcement. But sanctuary laws do not reopen a choice already embedded in a federal repository or a vendor connection. Once a local jail booking enters a federal repository, or a local contract permits an outside platform to answer a federal query, the federal government no longer needs to compel a local official to act; it can simply use a system already in place. The same pipes survived policy reversals across three administrations, while the immigration detention population reached 65,765 on July 11. Use may decrease with a new administration; capacity waits at full scale for the next one.

The remedies below therefore shift from sanctuary policy to how the hub is built: the contracts that connect local systems to it, the data that feeds it, and the rights that can check it. First, states and localities should use procurement as policy to unwind the architecture in their jurisdictions. Begin with an integration map: an audit of every application programming interface (API), automatic feed, and outside recipient in the systems a jurisdiction already runs, which separates use from dependence. New York City ran one this past spring and recommended policies against sharing with federal immigration authorities, “including through technology vendors.” Then dictate contract terms that incapacitate the flow of information to the hub: no sharing by default, no secondary use of resident data, limited retention, independent audit rights, certified deletion at the end, and trade-secrecy refusals treated as a contractual breach.

Denver proved a city can demand such terms: Its Axon contract included city-owned data, a 21-day retention limit, no flow to national databases, and a vendor commitment to contest subpoenas. Criteria must describe what a system does, not whom its vendor serves, to survive inevitable challenges. The Constitution’s Supremacy Clause and intergovernmental immunity have already sunk rules that single out those who deal with the federal government.

Second, confer meaningful privacy rights to data subjects, such as bans on privacy-violating technology and due process for rights-impacting technology. Several states have started to cull the offending technologies and data flows: Maryland bars the sale of residents’ data for immigration enforcement and requires a warrant before its record custodians open their files; California lets a resident direct every registered data broker to delete their data with a single request; San Francisco barred its city agencies from using facial recognition. Residents should also be able to see, contest, correct, or delete a system output impacting their rights—a flag, booking transfer, plate hit, or risk score—before it flows back to the federal immigration hub.

Third, states should take advantage of their own constitutions to bestow and protect rights and remedies. Montana wrote electronic data into its constitution’s search protection and then barred its agencies from buying from brokers what would otherwise require a warrant to obtain. Illinois created a state cause of action, albeit one with legal vulnerabilities, against officers who violate the Constitution while conducting immigration enforcement; the Justice Department is suing to strike it.

Interoperability is not inherently unlawful or undesirable. A limited, documented request can resolve identity, prevent errors, and support ordinary public functions. The problem is a design that couples whole-population data flows to durable vendor integrations and supplies no reliable route to see and remove downstream copies. Resistance efforts should make the apparatus visible at the sites where public law can still reach it and dismantle the Hydra at the seams.

name: Policy
title: Trump Has Found a New Part of the Constitution to Abuse | The New Republic
authors: Matt Ford, Private Eyes Matt Ford, Hashed Out Matt Ford, Opening Day Matt Ford, Hafiz Rashid, Malcolm Ferguson, Ellie Quinlan Houghtaling
description:
In recent months, the Trump administration has leaned heavily on the clause to make extraordinary—and often dubious—claims about its own powers.
Earlier this year, the Trump administration sued New York City over its sanctuary jurisdiction policies.
California’s Constitution only allows U.S. citizens to cast a ballot in state and federal elections.
With sanctuary jurisdictions, the Trump administration was challenging a supposed clash between state and federal law.
But it also underscores the risks that the Trump administration takes when it makes unsupported supremacy clause claims in court.
text:
It’s been a big year for the supremacy clause. The important but rarely newsworthy constitutional provision has found itself at the center of multiple major legal battles. In recent months, the Trump administration has leaned heavily on the clause to make extraordinary—and often dubious—claims about its own powers.
