The clause declares that the Constitution, as well as the federal laws “made in pursuance thereof” and treaties signed under it, “shall be the supreme Law of the Land.” It further states that “judges in every state shall be bound thereby.” In other words, the supremacy clause does what its name suggests: It establishes that the Constitution is supreme over state legislatures and state courts, as is Congress when acting within its own spheres of authority.

The Trump administration has taken a much more aggressive view of the clause, wielding it as a tool to bludgeon Democratic-led state governments into compliance with its own policy agenda or, more accurately, self-serving desires. Naturally, this is not how the Constitution is meant to operate. There are also signs that the administration’s overreach could backfire.

The clause comes up most often in cases involving federal preemption. In short, when Congress enacts a constitutionally valid law, it narrows the states’ ability to regulate the same thing. A good example is environmental protection. The Clean Air Act and Clean Water Act limit states’ abilities to regulate some environmental issues while explicitly carving out other cases on which states can act. The Supreme Court has already heard a preemption case about climate litigation this term.

Earlier this year, the Trump administration sued New York City over its sanctuary jurisdiction policies. Like many other cities, counties, and states, New York City has a formal policy that forbids its local law enforcement agencies from cooperating with certain information requests from federal immigration officials. Trump and his allies have strenuously criticized these policies for hindering their mass deportation machine.

In court, the Trump administration also argued that these policies violate the supremacy clause because they are preempted by federal immigration laws. One law in particular, known as Section 1373, says that federal, state, and local agencies “may not prohibit, or in any way restrict,” federal, state, and local officials from sending the Department of Homeland Security, or receiving from it, information about immigration status and citizenship status.

Judge Ramon Reyes, a federal district court judge in New York, told the Trump administration that it was doubly wrong in a ruling last week. (It was actually triply wrong if you count standing, which I’ll skip here.) Reyes concluded that because the federal law in question did not regulate private actors—individuals, businesses, and the like—preemption did not apply. One important purpose of preemption is to break a tie when a person or business has to follow conflicting state and federal laws. Under the supremacy clause, the federal law wins. No such tie needed to be broken in this instance, he concluded.

Additionally, Reyes wrote, the Trump administration would lose even if its supremacy clause position was correct because that position would bring it into conflict with the Tenth Amendment’s anti-commandeering doctrine. That doctrine forbids the federal government from “commandeering” the states to enforce federal laws. States can voluntarily help the federal government enforce immigration laws, in other words, but they can’t be compelled to do it.

“If the challenged provisions were struck, while New York City would not be obligated to carry out federal immigration enforcement, they would be barred from prohibiting their agencies and employees from engaging in federal immigration enforcement,” Reyes wrote. He added that, “of course, there is nothing within federal law that obligates states to participate in federal immigration enforcement or compels states to comply therewith.”

The Trump administration might appeal this ruling, but it will be an uphill battle to ultimately prevail. The Supreme Court has favored a more rigid approach to the anti-commandeering doctrine in recent years, most notably in the 2018 case Murphy v. NCAA. In Murphy, the court struck down a near-total federal ban on sports betting because the law affirmatively prohibited states from enacting their own legalization regimes. Reyes extensively cited Murphy in his own ruling.

Trump attempted an even more audacious supremacy clause claim in California last week. The administration sued the state to stop it from counting mail ballots submitted in the upcoming midterm elections from what the Justice Department described as “likely noncitizens.” The administration claimed it had “sent relevant California officials a list of over 20,000 names” of “likely noncitizens” who had been sent a mail ballot.

There is good reason to doubt the underlying facts as presented by the Justice Department. The Trump administration, despite its most persistent efforts and frequent claims, has failed to identify or uncover any significant noncitizen voting in American elections. Similar allegations in neighboring Nevada also fell apart under scrutiny. DHS initially claimed, without evidence, that it had identified almost 16,000 noncitizen voters in the Silver State in July. It revised that number down to 185 names in August. In September, Nevada election officials announced that they had checked each name and found that they were all U.S. citizens.

In the California case, the Trump administration’s legal argument for preemption hinged on a provision known as Section 611(a). That provision generally makes it a federal crime for “any alien to vote in any election” for a federal candidate, with an exception for certain noncitizens who were raised in the United States under the mistaken belief that they were U.S. citizens. The Trump administration has brought a handful of criminal cases against defendants for violating the law in recent years. It also argues that Section 611(a) supports its supremacy clause claim, and thus its efforts to block the targeted 20,000 ballots from being counted.

There are a few flaws with this claim, including one big and obvious one: California law does not allow noncitizens to vote in federal elections. California’s Constitution only allows U.S. citizens to cast a ballot in state and federal elections. The California secretary of state’s office only allows U.S. citizens to become registered voters. While some cities like San Francisco allow noncitizens to vote in local Board of Education elections, the state does not conduct those elections. (Federal law does not affect them, either, so they aren’t relevant for the lawsuit.)

Where, then, is the supremacy clause claim? With sanctuary jurisdictions, the Trump administration was challenging a supposed clash between state and federal law. Here the laws do not even clash at all. Not to worry, the Trump administration said. The Justice Department instead claimed—again, without a shred of evidence—that California was intentionally allowing noncitizens to vote in federal elections anyway.

“Because California cannot pass a statute allowing noncitizens to vote in a federal election, it also cannot induce, encourage, promote, or knowingly facilitate noncitizen voting for a candidate who is running for a seat in the U.S. Senate or the U.S. House of Representatives,” the Justice Department argued in its complaint. “Nor can California allow a noncitizen to vote in the federal election when it has knowledge about the voter’s citizenship status, as noncitizens cannot vote in federal elections.”

California’s “actions” are preempted by federal law, the administration claimed—not a law or even a policy, but an “action” for which it provides no credible evidence. “The State knows that noncitizens might be registered to vote, and it knows the names of such individuals,” the complaint alleged. “But it still intends to count their vote without verifying the voter’s citizenship. California’s actions thus knowingly facilitate unlawful voting.”

In a better age, it would be considered shameful for the Justice Department to file a federal lawsuit of any kind—much less one intended to block lawful ballots from being counted—on conspiracy theories, let alone Trumpworld’s self-serving fantasies about widespread voter fraud. But both shame and competent lawyers are in short supply at Main Justice these days. By simply claiming that there are 20,000 noncitizen voters and demanding their ballots not be counted, the Trump administration is treating the supremacy clause as a nearly limitless source of power, apparently hoping a federal judge will infer it from the clause’s name instead of it substance.

This argument is even weaker in the context of a different federal court’s surprise ruling in Florida last month. In United States v. Cox, a Jamaican-born woman who unlawfully registered to vote had argued that Section 611—the provision invoked by DOJ in the California lawsuit—was unconstitutional as applied to her. Judge David Liebowitz, a federal district court judge, agreed with her interpretation.

“[Section] 611 is a voter qualification statute, and the Constitution does not authorize Congress to legislate voter qualifications for federal elections,” Liebowitz wrote. Except for a few limited cases not applicable here, he concluded, “Congress has no power to say who can vote or who cannot vote in federal elections—that foundational power is reserved for the States, and limits Congress.”

It may seem surprising that a law that criminalizes noncitizen voting could be unconstitutional. But two provisions of the Constitution suggest otherwise. The federal government does not actually run federal elections. The Constitution delegates that power to the states, though it allows Congress to regulate the “time, manner, and place” of those elections. It does not, however, allow Congress to set voter qualifications.

Under Article 1, for example, voters in House elections “shall have the Qualifications requisite for Electors of the most numerous Branch of the State Legislature.” In other words, if a state in the 1790s had only allowed free men with 10 acres of land to vote in state legislative elections, that would be the qualification for voting on federal representatives for that state, as well. Senators were not directly elected until the ratification of the Seventeenth Amendment in 1913, which also prescribes that voters “shall have the qualifications requisite for electors of the most numerous branch of the State legislatures.”

Article 2, which sets the rules for presidential elections, does not include that language. But it broadly delegates the power to choose presidential and vice presidential electors to the states. States are not constitutionally obligated to allow Americans to vote for president; state legislatures can choose the Electoral College delegation themselves, and have. (No state has done so since the early nineteenth century.) Put simply, Liebowitz wrote, “in Presidential elections, the States have the prerogative to establish whatever rules for selecting electors they see fit.”

Liebowitz framed his ruling in originalist terms. He noted that the Framers intentionally decided against letting Congress set voter qualifications and voted to reject a proposal that would have done so. “James Madison also objected,” Liebowitz wrote, “and elsewhere argued that the power to qualify electors was ‘fundamental’ to the Republican form of government, and should not be entrusted to the federal government, lest it use that power to ‘subvert the Constitution.’” The Reconstruction Amendments altered the federal-state balance of power and limited the states’ ability to deny suffrage, he explained, but did not reverse this basic allocation of power.

The Justice Department argued that Congress could enact Section 611 pursuant to its powers over immigration and foreign affairs, where it typically enjoys broad discretion. But Liebowitz declined to agree. Section 611 was drafted as a voter-qualification law, he wrote, and while it may be possible for Congress to write a statute that achieves this goal in other ways, it did not do so here. He also declined to strike down the law in all circumstances, noting that it may be constitutional as applied for D.C. elections, where there is no state legislature to set qualifications and Congress itself has plenary authority.

Liebowitz’s ruling does not mean that noncitizens may vote in federal elections—no state permits it, and states retain the power to criminalize voter fraud in any case. Federal appeals courts may also reach a different conclusion. But it also underscores the risks that the Trump administration takes when it makes unsupported supremacy clause claims in court. An ill-advised defeat only limits its ability to act in the future.

title: The court's third-country removal case has high stakes but will likely be decided on technical grounds
description:
For the third time, the Supreme Court will soon hear argument about the federal government’s power to send migrants to countries where they have no ties.
Last year, the Trump administration revamped the government’s third-country removal process to quickly send more migrants to countries where they have no ties.

text:
For the third time, the Supreme Court will soon hear argument about the federal government’s power to send migrants to countries where they have no ties. And for the third time, the justices are unlikely to focus on what matters most to the migrants who claim the Trump administration is violating the law – whether they will be persecuted, tortured, or killed. Instead, the court is likely to turn its attention to a much more technical issue: whether courts can force the government to let migrants explain why forced removal might mean almost-certain persecution.

In Department of Homeland Security v. D.V.D., scheduled for oral argument on Dec. 9, the court will review the Trump administration’s policy of removing migrants from the United States to any country that will accept them. The Immigration and Nationality Act permits so-called third-country removals under certain circumstances. After an immigration judge has ordered a migrant removed, immigration officials must first attempt to send the person to the country that they choose, where they hold citizenship, or last resided. If none of those countries accepts the migrant, officials can then send the person to a country that will take them in, so long as they are not sent to a country where they face likely persecution or torture.

Last year, the Trump administration revamped the government’s third-country removal process to quickly send more migrants to countries where they have no ties. Cuban citizen D.V.D., who receives treatment for a severe mental illness, and Honduran citizen M.M., who fled an abusive husband, represent a group of migrants who worry that the administration’s policy will send them into harm’s way. The policy – first announced in February 2025 and revamped in March 2025 – permits immigration officials to send migrants to any country whose government assures the State Department that it won’t persecute or torture anyone. If a government won’t provide that assurance, but will accept a migrant, the policy requires immigration officials to notify the migrant of its plans to send them to that country and give them “a reasonable opportunity” to consider whether they might face abuse there, “generally 24 hours, or after he has had a reasonable means and opportunity to speak with an attorney,” the U.S. solicitor general’s request for Supreme Court intervention explains.

The Trump administration hasn’t published a full list of countries that have assured it they won’t harm people, but, under the third-country removal policy DHS has attempted to send migrants to countries with documented records of mistreatment. An Immigration and Customs Enforcement official acknowledged efforts to transport migrants to South Sudan. News reports indicate that the administration has also tried sending people to Cameroon, the Central African Republic, and another three-dozen countries. The State Department warns people from visiting many of those countries.

Many have been sent closer to the United States. In coordination with the Mexican government, news reports suggest that more than 20,000 non-Mexicans have been sent there. One of the migrants suing DHS, a Guatemalan citizen identified as O.C.G., is among them. An immigration judge barred U.S. officials from sending him to Guatemala. Despite that, DHS “threw him on a bus to Mexico, where he had just been raped, and where he was quickly sent back to Guatemala, the place an immigration judge had just found he would likely be persecuted. And then [DHS] lied about it,” U.S. District Judge Brian Murphy wrote in February.

Indeed, Murphy, who sits in the Boston federal court, has repeatedly found the Trump administration’s legal position, as well as its litigation conduct, problematic. During the spring and summer of 2025, Murphy ordered DHS not to implement the policy citing concerns about its legality. The government nonetheless attempted to do so on multiple occasions. At least once DHS relied on testimony that a migrant purportedly gave to a government witness even though, according to Murphy, “there was no such witness.”

Murphy later concluded that the third-country removal policy is illegal. Without telling people where they are to be sent and giving them time to consider whether they might be harmed there, the administration’s policy violates the INA’s protection from persecution, Murphy concluded in February. The government’s view, he added, is that “‘as long as the Department [of Homeland Security] doesn’t already know there’s someone standing there waiting to shoot … that’s fine’.” But “[i]t is not fine, nor is it legal,” Murphy went on, before emphasizing that the government cannot deprive a person of their life, liberty, or property without due process of law. As a result, Murphy granted a request by a group of migrants who face the possibility of being sent to a third country to vacate the policy, ordering DHS to notify people before sending them to third countries.

The U.S. Court of Appeals for the 1st Circuit largely agreed with Murphy. Affirming most of Murphy’s decision, the appellate court explained in September that legal limitations on the government are meaningless if the people who the government targets can’t ask a court to intervene when they believe the government is violating the law. As the 1st Circuit summarized its position, “an individual’s right to contest removal to a country based on a fear of persecution in that country means little if one does not receive prior notice of the intended removal destination and a meaningful opportunity to contest that destination.”

Despite the high stakes of the administration’s policy, the Supreme Court is more likely to decide D.V.D. based on technical issues of judicial authority to consider the migrants’ claim. The solicitor general argued, in his petition for emergency relief, that a series of federal laws bar courts from hearing any claims that removal from the United States might result in persecution or torture. The one exception, the solicitor general contends, is for individual claims initially aired before a federal court of appeals. As a class action lawsuit first raised in the Boston district court, such federal courts thus have no authority even to consider the migrants’ claims, the solicitor general argues.

The migrants dispute the solicitor general’s view. Even though Congress has constrained judicial review of immigration-related claims, they argue that the INA allows courts to consider whether the federal government is acting illegally by sending people to countries where they are likely to be endangered. Congress has limited courts’ power to block immigration agencies through injunctions, but Murphy’s order vacating the policy, which is based in the Administrative Procedure Act, is not an injunction, they argue.

When it announced that it would hear arguments in this case, the court also invited the solicitor general to identify any reasons not previously argued for why it thinks the administration should win. That’s unlikely to prompt the government to focus on the risks that migrants face when DHS uses a hurried process.

For migrants who fear for their lives, the stakes couldn’t be higher: life or death. But, ultimately, this case is likely to turn on technical questions of judicial power.

title: Trump's Obsession With Somalia Isn't Just Racist. It's Been Lethal. - The Intercept
description:
Meanwhile, his administration has, largely without public knowledge, killed hundreds of people in Somalia, claiming they belong to terror groups.
The Trump administration reportedly launched the investigation to build a case to strip Omar of her U.S. citizenship and ultimately deport her.
During his second term alone, the Trump administration has conducted more than 200 airstrikes in Somalia, including close to 90 this year, claiming to target terrorists.
U.S. attacks in Somalia have skyrocketed during Trump’s terms in office.
Before Trump took office, in 2016, Islamist militants in Somalia killed 4,281 people, according to the Africa Center for Strategic Studies, a Pentagon research institution.
text:
The Trump administration is waging a multi-pronged war on Somali people, painting them as criminals, murderers, and terrorists and using multiple federal agencies to target them at home and abroad. The campaign includes military attacks in Somalia, as well as arrests, deportations, and the weaponization of federal law enforcement agencies against immigrants and the Somali American community in the United States, including the recent use of Homeland Security agents as a goon squad to target Minnesota congresswoman Ilhan Omar.

In his second term, President Donald Trump has routinely cast Somalia as lawless and Somalis as violent. Meanwhile, his administration has, largely without public knowledge, killed hundreds of people in Somalia, claiming they belong to terror groups. Trump personally ordered the death of a Somali man within days of regaining the White House, according to his counterterrorism czar Sebastian Gorka. The administration claimed, without offering any evidence, that the man was connected with the Islamic State terror group. Trump has sought to do the same with Omar.

Homeland Security agents raided Omar’s Washington, D.C., home last Monday, three weeks before the midterms, in which she is seeking reelection. The Trump administration reportedly launched the investigation to build a case to strip Omar of her U.S. citizenship and ultimately deport her. (Omar fled war in Somalia with her family when she was 8 years old, later immigrated to the U.S. as a refugee, and became a citizen in 2000.) The administration has also issued more than a dozen subpoenas, including to some of Omar’s relatives. On Monday, conservative media outlets reported that federal prosecutors obtained Omar’s DNA as part of their investigation.

“This is what happens in a dictatorship. The leader identifies his political, ethnic and religious enemies, and his agents scramble to do his bidding and make him happy,” Zaynab Mohamed, a Somali immigrant who represents Minneapolis in Minnesota’s state Senate, told The Intercept. “Representative Omar is the latest subject where Trump identifies the target and his minions go looking for a crime. The cases always fall apart, and this one will, too.”

Trump claimed not to have ordered the raid, but throughout his second term, his Justice Department has repeatedly targeted his political enemies — from New York’s attorney general, to the former head of the FBI, to members of the Federal Reserve. “I think she’s a terrible person, but that’s really up to the DOJ,” Trump said to reporters. “I have nothing to do with it.”

Omar called it “an attempt to target political enemies and weaponize federal law enforcement.” She added: “For ten years, Trump has targeted me with baseless lies and smear campaigns. This is just the latest escalation in his campaign of political intimidation.” Omar’s office did not respond to multiple requests for comment from The Intercept.

With the Somali community, Trump found a target that he could attack with Islamophobic, racist, and xenophobic rhetoric, without incurring much mainstream backlash, said Jaylani Hussein, the executive director of the Minnesota chapter of the Council on American-Islamic Relations.

“As immigrants, Muslims, and — most importantly — Black people, it’s the trifecta,” he told The Intercept. “None of us expected the scale and level of the vitriol. But despite this, it’s at the point that the traditional media almost ignore the attacks on the Somali-American community because it’s not a large constituency. Trump says these things, and people just move on.”

Trump’s War on Somalia

Over the last decade, Trump has overseen the killing of as many as 1,500 Somalis in more than 400 attacks, according to a count by New America, a D.C.-based think tank. During his second term alone, the Trump administration has conducted more than 200 airstrikes in Somalia, including close to 90 this year, claiming to target terrorists.

The U.S. military has been at war in Somalia for almost a quarter-century, conducting air attacks and commando raids aimed at the terrorist group al-Shabab as well as the Islamic State group, while the CIA and special operators created local proxy forces to conduct low-profile operations on behalf of America. At the same time, the U.S. has provided Somalia with billions of dollars in counterterrorism assistance.

U.S. attacks in Somalia have skyrocketed during Trump’s terms in office. From 2007 to 2017, under the administrations of George W. Bush and Barack Obama, the U.S. military carried out 59 declared airstrikes in Somalia. The Biden administration conducted 51 declared strikes over four years. During Trump’s six years in office, the U.S. has launched more than 400 attacks against purported militants.

The U.S. rarely offers any evidence that those killed are members of terrorist groups, much less leaders. A New America analysis found militant leaders comprised just 1.7 percent of those killed. Africa Command refused to provide requested evidence that any of those killed in airstrikes in Somalia this year were militants. “All U.S. strikes in Somalia are conducted in close coordination partners [sic] against designated terror groups,” an AFRICOM spokesperson told The Intercept by email.

“Trump has conducted more drone strikes in Somalia than Bush, Obama, and Biden combined. And so many civilians have died,” historian Elizabeth Schmidt, the author of “Foreign Intervention in Africa After the Cold War: Sovereignty, Responsibility, and the War on Terror,” told The Intercept. “They were often just young men living in an area where it was easy to label them jihadis. And it turns out they had nothing to do with terrorism.”

The U.S. claims that it has only killed six civilians over almost two decades of war in Somalia. A count by the airstrike monitoring group Airwars put the number at as much as 2,600 percent higher. A 2023 investigation by The Intercept determined, for example, that a drone attack in Somalia during Trump’s first term killed at least three, and possibly five, civilians, including 22-year-old Luul Dahir Mohamed and her 4-year-old daughter Mariam Shilow Muse. At the time of the attack, the U.S. announced it had killed “five terrorists” and that “no civilians were killed in this airstrike.”

Trump calls Somalia a “third-world” or “fourth-world nation,” says that it “stinks,” and disparaged Somalis who come to the U.S., saying “we’re going to go the wrong way if we keep taking in garbage into our country.”

His most xenophobic consigliere also claims Somalia is responsible for violence that has caused people to flee the country. “The entire Somali refugee program is predicated on a lie,” wrote Trump’s deputy chief of staff for policy and homeland security adviser, Stephen Miller, late last year. “Destroying your own country does not give you the right to become a citizen in ours.” But this faux history disregards America’s decadeslong role in fomenting violence in Somalia and destabilizing the country.

A casualty of the Cold War geopolitics that led to widespread conflict, political repression, and millions of deaths across the developing world, Somalia has experienced persistent political instability and strife since the late 1960s. In recent decades, the country has suffered civil war, famine, droughts, a longtime al-Shabab insurgency, and persistent humanitarian crises.

Over the last quarter century, the U.S. has intensified conflict in Somalia through direct attacks; training, funding, and running proxy forces; and funneling in weapons and other military assistance to one side of a civil war. As early as 2007, the Pentagon was aware that there were fundamental flaws with U.S. military operations in the Horn of Africa, and Somalia devolved into another forever war stalemate. This has continued, despite the record number of airstrikes in Somalia under Trump.

Before Trump took office, in 2016, Islamist militants in Somalia killed 4,281 people, according to the Africa Center for Strategic Studies, a Pentagon research institution. By August, this year’s total hit 6,731 deaths, a 57 percent increase. An analysis by the Costs of War project at Brown University found that instead of eliminating militant groups, the U.S. counterterrorism campaign in Somalia was “ensuring that the conflict continues in perpetuity.” An AFRICOM spokesperson said the command’s “operational focus remains on working with partners to degrade terrorist organizations to create the space required for Somali-led governance and stability.” But Trump claims Somalia has no government, no military, and is “not even a country.”

The Intercept interviewed people displaced by the forever war in a camp on the outskirts of Somalia’s capital, Mogadishu, in 2023. “We had to leave because of the drought and the conflict,” a mother of seven told this reporter. She was one of more than a dozen women from the Lower Shabelle region of southwest Somalia who spoke to The Intercept after fleeing the front lines of an offensive by the U.S.-backed Somali government against al-Shabab. Since Trump first took office, the number of Somalis forced from their homes has almost doubled from 2.4 million to 4.4 million.

“I don’t think most Americans realize that the presence of Somalis in the U.S. has a lot to do with U.S. wars in Somalia. U.S. military intervention made a bad situation worse. This led to a surge of refugees and asylum-seekers to the U.S.,” said Schmidt. “They weren’t coming because they wanted a better job. It’s because they feared for their lives and their children’s lives.”

During Trump’s first term, his administration acknowledged “the ongoing armed conflict” as a reason to extend temporary protected status — which grants legal status, work authorization, and protection from deportation — to Somalis in the U.S., noting the security situation was “fragile and volatile, with ongoing armed conflict among government forces, clan militias, African Union Mission in Somalia (AMISOM) troops, and al-Shabaab.”

Bringing the War Home

Despite the increase in violence, according to Pentagon statistics, the administration terminated Somalia’s TPS designation earlier this year. More than 1,000 Somali asylum-seekers have been ordered deported since February; more than half the deportation orders involve Somalis living in Minnesota, a nearly tenfold increase from 2025, according to a Minnesota Star Tribune investigation.

About 84,000 of the 260,000 people of Somali descent in the U.S. live in the Minneapolis–St. Paul area, according to the Census Bureau’s annual American Community Survey. The overwhelming majority are American citizens. Almost 58 percent were born in the U.S. and 87 percent of foreign-born Somalis are naturalized citizens.

The administration targeted that Somali community during a violent immigration crackdown in and around Minneapolis known as “Operation Metro Surge” during late 2025 and early 2026. “I don’t want them in our country,” Trump said in December 2025. The next month, he said: “Every one of them should be forced to leave this country, including Ilhan Omar.”

During Metro Surge, federal agents shot and killed protesters Renee Nicole Good and Alex Pretti. They, like Omar and hundreds of drone strike victims in Somalia, were labeled as terrorists by the administration without providing evidence.

During Trump’s second term, Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents have also arrested hundreds of Somali people, with reports of assault and mistreatment at the hands of federal agents.

Trump recently seemed to call for vigilante violence and threatened to back it with federal force. “The once Great State of Minnesota is being taken over by Somali Immigrants,” Trump posted on Truth Social earlier this month. “The Somalians should not be allowed to get away with what they are doing. They view you as weak and stupid people. Fight back Minnesota, fight back! If you need, the Federal Government will come to your rescue.” The White House did not respond to a request for comment.

Hussein, of CAIR-MN, said Trump’s rhetoric was endangering the Somali community. “Every few weeks, he’s literally going on a tirade. And I don’t think he’s ever spoken about other people the same way. He literally put out the message saying, ‘go fight them. I’ll come and help’ on social media,” he told The Intercept. “We’ve seen bullying. We’ve dealt with harassment. We’ve have some assaults.”

Trump has routinely demonized Somalis by tying the broader community to a high-profile fraud case: the alleged theft of $250 million from a pandemic-era program that provided food for children. The former leader of Feeding Our Future, the nonprofit at the center of the case, is white, although most of the defendants in the related cases are of Somali descent. “The Somalians, they’re crooked as hell,” Trump ranted at a Cabinet meeting in May, with the administration offering escalating and unverified claims, including reference to a “$19 billion Somali fraud scandal.”

The Trump administration’s effort to denaturalize and deport Omar is part of a broader push to strip naturalized Americans of their citizenship, with those of Somali descent specifically singled out. “I would do it in a heartbeat if they were dishonest,” Trump said in an Oval Office interview earlier this year. “I think that many of the people that came in from Somalia, they hate our country.”

Trump’s border czar Tom Homan said on Saturday that he had been “told they have a strong case” against Omar. “Of course, if you lie during the naturalization process, there is a process to denaturalize somebody. We’ve done it before,” he told Fox News. The rarely used denaturalization statute has been most famously employed to strip citizenship from Nazi war criminals, like John Demjanjuk, a former death camp guard and retired U.S. autoworker convicted on 28,060 counts of being an accessory to murder.

Mohamed, who in 2022 became the first Somali woman elected to the Minnesota Senate, called out Trump’s push to expel Omar as a grave threat to the country. “If the president can threaten to denaturalize and deport a member of Congress, no one is safe,” she told The Intercept. “This is a test of our democracy, and even Republicans should be speaking out about it. If we don’t defend the rights of Ilhan Omar, Somali-Americans, immigrants, and Trump’s political targets, we lose everything.”

text:
Loud ranchera music echoed off concrete walls as Rep. Gabe Evans watched a parade of black and white cows rotating on an automated milking carousel. Workers popped in and out of view, adjusting the equipment before leading the animals back to their pens.

Gary Henrickson explained to the congressman — his congressman — that Bella Holsteins, his dairy farm in Weld County, Colo., is an early adopter of technology that could one day require fewer human workers.

But not yet. In the meantime, this kind of work doesn’t qualify for agricultural work visas — and the cows need to be tended to every day, “even when it’s Christmas,” he emphasized.

The message during Evans’ visit last week was clear: Henrickson needs his workers. But immigration enforcement fears have “sent shivers” through his workforce.

“Our employees get extremely nervous,” Henrickson later told Bloomberg Law. “Even if their paperwork is in order, they still come and they feel like they’re visitors in the US.”

The farmer supports Evans, but his concern goes to an issue coursing through the race for Colorado’s 8th District, a battleground that could shape control of Congress.

Latinos comprise about 30% of the voters in the district, which sprawls from the Denver and Aurora suburbs to the oil and agricultural lands surrounding the meatpacking town of Greeley. But a growing number of them are unaffiliated, and both parties are scrambling to court their votes and get them to turn out next month.

“Latinos here in Colorado are becoming less and less sort of wed to a specific party,” said Dusti Gurule, president of the group Colorado Organization for Latina Opportunity and Reproductive Rights.

As a group, unaffiliated voters soared by 80% in the state from 2016 to 2026, outpacing Democrat or Republican registrations.

Evans, a first-term Republican, flipped the 8th District seat in 2024 by less than 1% — just a few thousand votes. Since then, the area has felt the brunt of an expensive economy and the reach of the Trump administration’s immigration agenda, which promised mass deportations and a focus beyond the border regions of the US.

That means a slowdown in the processing of immigration applications such as work permits. And more detention centers, like the one Immigration and Customs Enforcement has proposed opening in the district.

Immigration might have been a winning issue for Republicans in 2024, but this cycle both Evans and his well-funded Democratic challenger, former state Rep. Manny Rutinel, are grappling with how to make it their own.

“Now more than ever, the Latino vote is so important — so that politicians finally stop playing games with our community and start taking us seriously,” said Arturo Vargas, one of a dozen Hispanic faith leaders in Colorado who met last month with Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin.

A Paralyzing Fear

Immigrants comprise about 14% of the population in the 8th District, according to the immigration advocacy organization FWD.us. More than 90,000 either lack legal status or live with someone who does.

Michelle Santillanes, a small business owner, described the area as a place where multi-generational families have worked for years — and where it feels like everyone knows someone who has been detained. Colorado has avoided the high-profile ICE enforcement campaigns, but an existing detention center in Aurora, just east of Denver, increased its capacity.

Santillanes is a US citizen whose family is from El Salvador, but her husband, who’s from Mexico, was once without legal status. She runs a remodeling company in the area and, until recently, a restaurant. Immigration enforcement fears have affected both businesses, she said.

Customers “wouldn’t show up. They were afraid to go and eat. They just wanted to work and go home because they were afraid to get picked up anywhere,” Santillanes said last week as she sipped hot cafe de olla from a ceramic mug at a bustling Mexican restaurant in north Aurora. “Even people with green cards, they’re afraid.”

At her remodeling company, some workers declined to accept assignments out of fear of being detained.

Running a business is hard enough having to master marketing, staffing, permits, and taxes, Santillanes said. Then, she said, “on top of doing everything, guess what? Here you go, here’s immigration as well. Here’s the economy shutting down because of immigration.”

Santillanes said she’s still not sure who’ll get her vote in two weeks.

“It’s like we see the good in both sides and that’s where it’s hard to decide,” she said. “That’s why this time around I want to educate myself more — because I’ve seen what not voting does.”

‘Folks are Furious’

Rutinel has been among the progressive Democrats leaning into immigration as a campaign issue, primarily focusing on enforcement tactics.

“Folks are furious because they feel like they’ve been lied to,” he told Bloomberg Law during an interview Saturday, before talking with a dozen union members preparing for an afternoon of door-knocking.

A Yale Law School graduate and the son of an immigrant from the Dominican Republic, Rutinel said he would press for accountability for any enforcement officer who breaks the law. He also supports requiring judicial warrants for raids on homes and banning officers from covering their faces.

“We need to chart a new path forward,” he told the canvassers before they dispersed.

Door-knocking that day alongside the union members was Lucia Gomez, national immigration coordinator for Laborers’ International Union of North America. She helps union members get immigration defense and conducts know-your-rights training.

“We have a lot of mixed households,” she said of her work with the members. “This particular House race will allow another voice in Congress that begins to speak about individuals and about working families beyond just their production, but more about their contributions to their communities.”

Evans, meanwhile, has tried to paint his challenger as an “open-the-border radical,” criticizing his previous support for a state program to extend state healthcare for all residents regardless of immigration status.

Like other vulnerable Republicans this cycle — such as Rep. Monica De La Cruz in Texas and Sen. Roger Marshall in Kansas — Evans has a softened stance on immigration enforcement.

“We’ve helped over 100 people get or renew work permits or visas so that they can legally continue to work in the United States,” Evans told Bloomberg Law, adding that he believes he has pressured the administration to focus on enforcement against people with violent criminal records.

Publicly available data shows most people in ICE detention don’t have criminal convictions, and significant slowdowns in processing work permits have caused people to lapse in status across the country.

Evans also acknowledged industries in his district rely on people without legal status, citing a Department of Agriculture report that about 40% of the industry’s laborers are working without authorization.

“If you deport 40% of the ag workforce, you crushed the American farmer overnight and we’re all starving a week later when we can’t even make our own food,” said the former Army helicopter pilot and state representative. “I wish that wasn’t the case, but you got to play the hand you’re dealt, not the hand you wish you had.”

Evans also turns to his own heritage on the campaign trail, touting that he is the only Hispanic member of Colorado’s delegation. His mom, who is of Mexican descent, is featured in Spanish-language advertisements.

Pressing for Action

The Republican incumbent arranged last month’s meeting between Mullin and the pastors who shared concerns they hear regularly from their congregants.

“Under this new administration — and this also happened under previous administrations — I’ve had to help people who lost everything,” Adan Aguirre, one of the pastors, told Bloomberg Law.

He and two others who attended the meeting said Mullin told them ICE didn’t plan to target their community events, that the agency’s goal was to detain those with criminal records. But the DHS secretary also said officers who encounter someone without legal status will detain them; he said ICE is merely enforcing existing laws.

The faith leaders urged the administration to consider legislative proposals like the Dignity Act. The bill, introduced by Rep. María Elvira Salazar (R-Fla.), would provide a pathway to legalization for several groups of immigrants, including farmworkers, those who have lived in the US for a prolonged period of time, and recipients of Deferred Action for Childhood Arrivals.

Evans is a cosponsor of the bill. The pastors said they’re ready to work with whomever is elected on a solution.

“I know firsthand how difficult life can be when you lack stable legal status,” said pastor David Gramajo. “We are fighting hard to ensure they are given that opportunity. Because we know that if many of these individuals get that chance, it will help many families across the United States — especially in our own state.”

Vargas said the Mullin meeting was not his first with a public official. And despite attempts from the secretary to assure the group that there are legal pathways, he knows there are members of his congregation who cannot naturalize or seek legal status.

“In my church, I have people who have been living in the country for 30 years, who are grandpas and grandmas and who still can’t fix their status,” Vargas said.

He understands the fear: Even as a US citizen, Vargas carries a photo of his passport.

A Race to the End

About $47 million has already been spent on ads in the district, according to AdImpact, and campaign watchdog Open Secrets calls it Colorado’s most expensive House race. Campaign finance reports filed last week showed Rutinel with the money edge in the final stretch, but Evans has had the support of prominent GOP donors, including Elon Musk.

Evaristo Gómez, a civic engagement manager for the national turnout advocacy group Mi Familia Vota who is campaigning for Rutinel, said his group has been focusing efforts on the rural, northern areas of the district, which tend to lean Republican.

“It’s a really special place in Colorado’s political landscape. It’s amazing to see that it is such a competitive district because I think a lot of people are feeling disenfranchised or disillusioned,” Gomez said.

On the other side, Angel Merlos, with the center-right organization The Libre Initiative, boasts knocking on more than 30,000 doors for Evans since March.

Both sides see the Latino vote as a decisive factor in the outcome.

“The Hispanic community is growing and any politician who doesn’t consider and account for the Hispanic Latino vote, they’re only hurting themselves,” Merlos said. “We would love to see them come out in strong numbers.”

text:
The Pentagon has authorized the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) to test a military-grade heat ray and develop tactics for its potential use at the southern U.S. border, according to a memo signed by Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth and obtained by CNN.

Officially known as the Active Denial System (ADS), the system projects an invisible beam of millimeter waves that can reach a little more than half a mile, according to the military. The beam causes an intense burning sensation on the skin, which Pentagon officials have compared to the feeling of opening a hot oven. The tingling can last 10 to 15 minutes and creates an “instinctive and irresistible urge to run from the effect,” military officials have said.

The DHS request did not specify where or how the system would be tested or how it might eventually be used. The system has never been deployed at the U.S. border, though current and former Customs and Border Protection officials told CNN they have discussed using it to disperse crowds in areas with high numbers of crossings.

Officials previously considered whether the system could help agents deter people from crossing near a river. They raised concerns that people could be incapacitated or pushed into the water and need rescue, according to CNN. In 2018, then-Homeland Security Secretary Kirstjen Nielsen rejected a proposal to use the system against migrants. Officials also raised legal, use-of-force and sovereignty concerns, particularly if it were used on people who had not yet crossed into the U.S.

U.S. officials also considered deploying the system during periods of domestic unrest, including protests after George Floyd’s murder at the end of President Donald Trump’s first term, a former U.S. official told CNN.

The memo authorizes a “temporary loan” of one ADS system for seven months, starting in September. It says the system “shall not be operated by Department of War personnel” and makes DHS solely responsible for its use and for developing tactics and procedures. After the loan period, DHS can request further use of the system for border operations, a defense official told CNN.

“CBP is continually evaluating new technologies, especially those that enhance operational effectiveness and strengthen mission capabilities,” a Customs and Border Protection spokesperson said in a statement. The Pentagon referred CNN to DHS for comment.

text:
Relatives of gravely ill detainees at two Florida immigration jails say authorities are about to deport their loved ones to unknown countries in Africa despite worsening medical conditions.

Flights are scheduled as early as Wednesday, according to the families and the immigration advocacy group the Workers Circle, which has been monitoring conditions and speaking with detainees inside two Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) facilities in south Florida.

The group said multiple sick detainees with varying conditions have been targeted for imminent deportation, and learned about the operation only in the last few days.

“I received a call from several detainees letting me know that men were being pulled in to interviews with deportation agents, where they were being informed that because of their medical conditions, Mexico would not be accepting their entry, and they will be sent to Africa,” Arianne Betancourt, the group’s immigrant rights organizer, said at a Tuesday night press conference.

“We know that once they are deported and sent to these third countries, they are not receiving medical care in detention. They have difficulties getting medicine.”

The affected detainees are at the Krome North processing center in Miami, which was found to be experiencing severe overcrowding by a government inspector’s report last month, and the Broward transitional center in Pompano Beach. Both facilities are privately run on behalf of ICE.

Anisley Cortés, the wife of Noslén Sendra, a 41-year-old Cuban national, said her husband has been incarcerated since last November, first at the now closed “Alligator Alcatraz” immigration jail, and at Krome since April. She said he has uncontrolled diabetes and acute pancreatitis that resulted in a weeks-long hospital stay earlier this year.

“He lost over 50 pounds. They wouldn’t give him his medication, and they would not give him enough food. It was a nightmare of a time for all of us,” she said. “He is very sick and needs the right healthcare.

“Cuba will not accept him as a deportee, and we now have proof that Mexico will not accept him as a deportee because he is so sick. And so they told him that because he could not be accepted at either of those two countries, ‘Oh well, we’re going to have to send you to Africa’.

“They told him that Mexico would not accept him because he has too many medications that he requires, and so they said, ‘Well, we have to deport you anyway’. We’re left with the uncertainty of not knowing how he is, or if we’ll see him again.”

Shalyn Fluharty, an immigration rights attorney, said information from the detainees indicated deportation flights were imminent.

“We understand that just this week, within a couple of days, likely Thursday and Friday, there will be two flights going to Africa, in particular to the Central African Republic, and we also believe Burundi,” she said.

Fluharty said previously deported immigrants were shackled at their hands, ankles and waists during lengthy flights, and some who complained were placed in full body wraps with no ability to move.

“This is what we anticipate will be happening this week for these individuals, based upon what we’ve seen in the past,” she said.

“Travel can last sometimes up to 24 hours. What if you’re somebody who has a heart condition? Who has a high risk of stroke? Who is experiencing diabetes and requires regular access to food or insulin? These conditions take your already vulnerable medical state and make them, unfortunately, often life-threatening.”

Responding to a request for comment, a spokesperson for the homeland security department demanded to know the affected detainees’ personal information. The department did not respond further when provided with Sendra’s details.

Betancourt said families risked retaliation for their relatives by coming forward. “This is not a single one-off story,” she said.

“The inspector general’s report confirmed that there is a lack of medical care inside of the Krome detention facility. Families have been demanding oversight, and every day they are experiencing real fear to speak up and advocate for their loved ones.”

During two unannounced visits to Krome in May, government inspectors found multiple violations of noncompliance with detention standards, including severe overcrowding. Holding 1,102 detainees in a facility with a maximum capacity of 882, the report said, “jeopardizes the safe and orderly operations within the facility”.

Other listed violations included an inadequate number of operational toilets, sinks, and showers, and previous complaints included female detainees made to use toilets in full view of men, and arriving detainees held for more than 24 hours in a bus in the parking lot because of a lack of space.

Advocates say Donald Trump’s massive second term immigration crackdown has caused overcrowding in detention centers nationwide that DHS has attempted to alleviate by ramping up deportation flights to so-called third countries.

The controversial practice, approved by the US supreme court last month, has seen hundreds of detainees deported to at least a dozen African countries where they have no ties.

text:
The Pentagon has given the Department of Homeland Security permission to test a military-grade heat ray and develop tactics to potentially use it in operations at the southern US border, according to a memo signed by Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth last month and obtained by CNN.

The heat ray, officially known as the Active Denial System, is a nonlethal weapon that shoots an invisible beam of electromagnetic waves that can reach a little more than half a mile away, according to the US military.

The energy beam causes a burning sensation when it comes into contact with the human skin — which Pentagon officials have previously compared to feeling a blast of heat when opening a hot oven. Military officials have said the resulting “tingling effect” lasts between 10 and 15 minutes but also generates “an instinctive and irresistible urge to run from the effect.”

Deploying the heat ray at the US border would be an unprecedented step, even for the Trump administration, which has made border security and clamping down on immigration a top priority. The DHS request did not specify where or how the weapon would be tested and how it might eventually be used, but over the years, there have been internal discussions about potentially using it for crowd dispersal along the US-Mexico border, according to current and former Customs and Border Protection officials.

US officials had also considered deploying the system during moments of domestic unrest, including at the end of President Donald Trump’s first term when protests erupted over the murder of George Floyd, according to a former US official familiar with those discussions.

The memo authorizes the “temporary loan” of one ADS system for seven months, starting in September, and states that it “shall not be operated by DoW (Department of War) personnel,” appearing to absolve the Pentagon of any responsibility for how the directed-energy system may ultimately be deployed.

It also states that DHS is solely responsible for “system employment, use and development of tactics, techniques and procedures.” At the end of the seven-month loan period, DHS can submit an additional request for further use of the Pentagon system in border operations based on need, a defense official told CNN.

“CBP is continually evaluating new technologies, especially those that enhance operational effectiveness and strengthen mission capabilities,” a Customs and Border Protection spokesperson said in a statement to CNN.

The Pentagon referred CNN to DHS when asked for comment.

The US military briefly deployed the system to Afghanistan nearly two decades ago but ultimately declined to use it during active combat operations. The US military also considered using the system for crowd control purposes at US facilities abroad where terrorist detainees were being held at the time but ultimately declined to employ it for that purpose as well, according to a source familiar with those previous internal considerations.

Customs and Border Protection officials have previously entertained the idea of using the system in areas where there’s a high concentration of illegal crossings. Border officials have occasionally discussed potentially using the system as a crowd dispersal tool, but it has never been deployed.

Concerns over effectiveness and legality

Officials ran into hurdles over legalities, use of force, effectiveness, and potential issues over sovereignty, particularly if the system was deployed on people in Mexico who had not yet crossed into the US. Chief among those concerns, however, was whether people could be harmed, either directly or indirectly, by the weapon.

“Even if they’re chasing people back to the river, you don’t want them to go in and drown,” a former CBP official told CNN. “For the cost, for the training and for the policies you’re going to create, is the juice worth the squeeze?”

El Centro sector, which covers around 70 miles along the US-Mexico border, evaluated the system several years ago, when Rodney Scott, who now serves as CBP commissioner, helmed that sector, according to a CBP official.

At the time, officials were discussing whether the system might help agents with an influx of illegal crossings along the nearby river by discouraging people from trying to cross in that area or pushing them to get out of the water.

One of the considerations at the time was whether the system might result in more rescues if people were incapacitated by the technology, the official said, though it’s unclear why it wasn’t deployed.

In 2018, prior to midterms, CBP officials also weighed using it against migrants, but then-Homeland Security Secretary Kirstjen Nielsen shot it down.

“The issue was treating immigrants and citizens like enemy combatants,” a former DHS official familiar with previous discussions about using the weapon against migrants told CNN. “Thematically, inhumane treatments typically get rejected.”

Some Border Patrol agents have more recently cast doubt over whether they need the tool at all amid low border crossings and an increase in personnel, according to another former CBP official.

text:
The Donald Trump administration has done with Ukrainians and Sudanese this week what it did last month with Salvadorans: it has not terminated Temporary Protected Status (TPS), but it has not renewed it either. The program that provides legal immigration status to 101,000 Ukrainians and 1,800 Sudanese citizens was set to expire on Monday, but the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) has declined to comment, which for now leaves them protected from deportation.

The decision not to terminate TPS represents a 180-degree turn in the Trump administration’s immigration policy and comes amid the campaign for the midterms, to be held on November 3, in which the Republican Party is fighting for control of Congress. In a context expected to be unfavorable for the conservative party, some experts are speculating about the timing of this break with the trend of recent months, when TPS protections were ended for 13 of the 17 countries that had benefited from the program.

“I think it’s related,” says José Palma, national coordinator of the National TPS Alliance. “Republican strategists are trying to minimize the impact and confuse people into thinking they are changing course and will be more lenient in the future,” he says.

In an election in which all seats in the House of Representatives, one-third of the Senate and 36 governors’ offices are at stake, Trump’s falling popularity has become a burden for many Republican candidates. Only 37% of voters approve of President Trump’s performance, while 60% disapprove, according to the latest polls. In addition to the high cost of living, voters are concerned about the administration’s aggressive immigration policy. Most people believe the government has gone too far on immigration.

“Americans are very upset about the violence committed by U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) against U.S. citizens, and about ICE’s violence in general,” says Julia Gelatt, associate director of the Migration Policy Institute’s immigration policy program. Gelatt notes that it cannot be known for certain whether the policy change on TPS is due to the proximity of the elections, but she concedes it could benefit the Republican Party.

Todd Schulte, president of FWD.us, a migrant advocacy organization, shares the same view. “I can’t say exactly all the reasons they kept it, but we can say with certainty that maintaining TPS is the right thing to do and, moreover, it’s a measure with popular support; by contrast, ending it would have been extremely unpopular in places like Ohio, where we saw the public deeply disturbed by the termination of TPS for Haitians,” he says.

TPS is a program that allows citizens of countries experiencing a crisis due to armed conflict or natural disasters to live and work temporarily in the United States. In Ukraine’s case, TPS was granted in April 2022 after Russia’s invasion two months earlier. The Joe Biden administration extended it. The most recent extension was in January 2025, when DHS authorized an additional 18 months of protection, in effect until October 2026.

On Monday, when the program was due to expire, DHS merely said in a statement that “an announcement regarding TPS for Ukraine will be made in due course. Until that announcement is made, Ukrainian citizens in the United States under TPS remain protected.” A month earlier, on September 9, DHS issued a similar statement for Salvadoran citizens. Until then, the government had chosen to end TPS for Afghans, Venezuelans, Nicaraguans, Hondurans, Haitians and eight other nationalities.

In limbo

Ukrainians and Sudanese are now left in limbo, like Salvadorans. The uncertainty about their future is total. In theory, not terminating the program extends their stay by six months, but the government has reserved the option to make a decision at any time. “In real life, many families are suffering because of that lack of clarity in protection. What is happening is just another extension of the psychological torture the TPS community is enduring,” Palma criticizes.

The activist says that in practical terms, the failure to renew the program means, for example, that someone who needs to obtain a driver’s license cannot do so in states that require proof of immigration status, such as Texas. It also hurts them when looking for work, renewing a lease, or collecting retirement benefits, because federal databases are not updated pending a DHS announcement and they show no immigration status. Palma says that for many the anxiety caused by uncertainty about renewal is worse than the certainty of termination, and he criticizes that “they are using them as political pawns.”

TPS beneficiaries renew their permits every 18 months, when the government evaluates whether the country continues to suffer the conditions that led to the program’s creation. The last country whose TPS was not renewed was Haiti, leaving 170,000 Haitians on the brink of deportation despite the continued violence by criminal gangs that control parts of the Caribbean nation.

“The Trump administration has indicated that conditions in the country of origin are not a primary concern. They consider TPS is not aligned with the national interests of the United States,” Gelatt says.

In Ukraine’s case, however, it has always received preferential treatment because of the U.S. stance in the war with Russia, and it was also allowed to maintain a humanitarian parole program that was denied to other countries. Now, the recent agreement signed with Russian President Vladimir Putin for the export of diesel has prompted speculation about whether Washington’s support will continue.

Letter from senators

In September, 31 Democratic and Republican senators sent a letter to DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin and Secretary of State Marco Rubio urging renewal of TPS for Ukraine, calling it “a humanitarian imperative, but also a sound economic decision.” “In states such as Illinois, thousands of Ukrainian TPS beneficiaries strengthen our communities, not only through their valuable cultural contributions, but also through their participation in essential sectors such as transportation, health care and construction. Ending TPS for this group could destabilize those sectors and increase costs for American consumers by forcing thousands of experienced workers to leave their jobs,” the letter said.

As for Sudan, TPS was established in 1997 and successive U.S. administrations have continued to extend it because of the armed conflict and political instability that have plagued the African nation.

“The idea of returning people to these countries, falsely claiming it is safe to do so, is wrong; politically, it would be a totally mistaken approach at any time, and especially in the period leading up to elections,” adds Schulte.

The next country with TPS up for renewal is Lebanon, whose program expires on November 27, after the midterms.

title: Deported Haitians return to an unfamiliar country with no resources for them | International
description:
It was Saturday night and Jean, a Haitian who arrived in the United States nearly 20 years ago, had left his job in Broward, north of Miami, hours earlier.
“He told me that if he had his passport he could return [to Haiti].
“Haiti is not in a position to receive these people, whether they come from the United States, the Dominican Republic, Cuba, Chile or Brazil.
It is not a country with sufficient resources to support these people.” “Haiti is right now a humanitarian disaster.
And that if they leave Haiti it will be for another country that allows them to work, not for the United States,” she says.
text:
It was Saturday night and Jean, a Haitian who arrived in the United States nearly 20 years ago, had left his job in Broward, north of Miami, hours earlier. But he never made it home. He wasn’t answering his phone and the location of his AirPods remained in the same place. Around 1 a.m., his doctor—also a family friend—went out to look for him and found the car unattended in a parking lot. At that point, Jean himself called and said he had been detained by immigration and was at a Border Patrol station in Dania Beach.

The doctor went there to inquire. The place looked deserted. He pressed the intercom and an agent came out and confirmed that Jean was being held and, the agent told him, that he had two options: either he would be deported to Haiti within the next 48 hours, or he would be transferred to the Krome detention center, southwest of Miami, to appear before an immigration judge.

“He told me that if he had his passport he could return [to Haiti]. That they could make it a very simple process, that they could send him back with dignity. Those were the exact words he used: ‘We can send him back with dignity.’ That he wouldn’t be shackled or anything like that,” the doctor—who asked to remain anonymous—says. “But if he went to Krome, it would be a long process. He would be detained, essentially jailed, for three to six months, sometimes longer, depending on how long it took to see a judge. And even then there were no guarantees he could stay.”

The next day the doctor returned to the station with Jean’s passport, his prescription medicine and a Bible. “He had said they hadn’t given him a toothbrush, so I brought one. He had said it was cold there, so I brought a hat” and some socks, he says. Officials accepted the prescription medicines, the passport and the Bible, but not the other items.

By Monday afternoon Jean was already in Cap-Haïtien, in northern Haiti, a country mired in a severe crisis of food, medical care and infrastructure, without the resources to meet the basic needs of those already there, and where gang and paramilitary violence has forced millions to flee.

“Haiti is not in a position to receive these people, whether they come from the United States, the Dominican Republic, Cuba, Chile or Brazil. They are all arriving to a place that cannot support them,” Allie Pasieka of the International Rescue Committee (IRC) told EL PAÍS from Port-au-Prince. “Even if they can reach their families, assuming they can move around, they will probably face the same vulnerabilities as those families. It is not a country with sufficient resources to support these people.”

“Haiti is right now a humanitarian disaster. So sending anyone here contributes to that humanitarian disaster,” she added.

According to figures from Human Rights Watch (HRW), 749 people had been returned from the United States on nine flights since August 20, HRW’s senior researcher for the Americas, Nathalye Cotrino, told this newspaper. The researcher visited Cap-Haïtien in August and interviewed 44 deportees who had arrived on the first two flights since the Donald Trump administration ended Temporary Protected Status (TPS) for Haiti in July, a program that had allowed about 350,000 Haitians to live and work legally in the U.S.

A blow to remittances

The people Cotrino interviewed told her their biggest difficulty after returning was finding work. Some had left partners and children in the U.S. and now depend on the money that those relatives send them.

“The main thing they are saying is that they need money and job opportunities. And that if they leave Haiti it will be for another country that allows them to work, not for the United States,” she says. “They are thinking maybe of trying to go to Brazil, to Chile or to nearby Caribbean places, because it’s less costly to arrange that trip.”

Haitians who emigrate “are not fleeing only the violence but also a prolonged humanitarian, economic and political crisis,” Cotrino adds.

Pasieka says the deportations could destabilize families that depended on remittances sent by the person abroad. “Remittances are a very important part of Haiti’s economy. If those people are suddenly sent back, they may have been supporting a family that can no longer sustain them.”

Pasieka recently visited Artibonite, in the country’s north-central region, where the health system is on the brink of collapse. Only two hospitals in the region are still operating and only one is accessible without crossing gang-controlled territory.

“That hospital urgently needs beds, medicines, medical equipment and power. It is costing them more money to keep operations running, for example fuel for generators. Also, they are receiving many more people than before, and often those people cannot pay,” Pasieka explains, “not even the most basic fees.”

Forced displacement also disrupts education and leaves families homeless. Schools can be occupied by gangs, and some parents avoid sending their children to class because of the dangers of the journey.

“The gangs are trying to control crucial communication routes, like roads, where they set up checkpoints. That provides them with income, but it also lets them control exactly who enters and who leaves,” Pasieka says. For those returned to a place that is not their place of origin, reaching relatives is difficult.

That is the case with Jean, who is originally from Port-au-Prince but was deported to Cap-Haïtien. His family says they are trying to reach the capital.

Once in Haiti, the available aid is insufficient. “When you arrive at the places where people are sheltering, there is a very basic amount of assistance to help the most vulnerable. Not everyone,” Pasieka explains.

Cotrino is concerned about whether the deportees had the opportunity to defend their cases before being sent back. Most of those she interviewed were already detained before TPS ended, and told her they had no criminal records in the U.S., something she has not been able to verify. Some had deportation orders but said they did not know about them.

A Department of Homeland Security (DHS) spokesperson told this outlet that, under the Trump administration and with figures updated through August, they have “deported more than one million undocumented immigrants and arrested more than one million.” The spokesperson also noted that TPS is temporary and that “for too long” it has been allowed to function “as a de facto amnesty program, although Congress never intended it to be permanent.”

“What we would say now is that the time has come to close it: they don’t have to return to their country, but they cannot stay here,” the spokesperson added. He urged people to self-deport and accompanied his emailed response with a list of people deported to Haiti whom he attributed serious criminal records to.

Jean’s doctor says he does not know what Jean’s immigration status was when he was detained. “I don’t ask people about their immigration status. I take care of their medical problems,” he says. He often recalls that early-morning visit at the start of the month: the abandoned car and the items he brought to the station.

title: Immigration – Habeas corpus – Expedited removal order - Massachusetts Lawyers Weekly
description:
Because Congress, in the Immigration and Naturalization Act (‘INA’), has barred judicial review of such orders, see 8 U.S.C.
We affirm the district court’s dismissal of [the petitioner]’s petition for habeas corpus for lack of jurisdiction.
… “This appeal turns on whether this court has been deprived of jurisdiction over [the petitioner]’s amended habeas corpus petition.
[the petitioner] challenges the validity of her expedited removal order, not whether it has issued.
… “We affirm the district court’s dismissal of [the petitioner]’s petition for habeas corpus for lack of jurisdiction.” Alawieh v. Mullin, et al.
text:
Where a habeas corpus petitioner has alleged that Customs and Border Patrol officers invalidly issued her an order of expedited removal and wrongfully cancelled her H-1B visa upon her attempt to reenter the United States following her trip to Lebanon, the dismissal of the petition should be affirmed because (1) Congress, in the Immigration and Naturalization Act, has barred judicial review of such orders and (2) the petitioner does not fit within the statutory exception, 8 U.S.C. §1252(e)(2)(B).

“… [The petitioner], a Lebanese citizen, alleges that Customs and Border Patrol (‘CBP’) officers invalidly issued her an order of expedited removal and wrongfully cancelled her H-1B visa upon her attempt to reenter the United States at Boston Logan Airport following her trip to Lebanon. Because Congress, in the Immigration and Naturalization Act (‘INA’), has barred judicial review of such orders, see 8 U.S.C. §1252(a)(2), (e)(1), and [the petitioner] does not fit within the statutory exception, see id. §1252(e)(2)(B), (e)(5), we lack jurisdiction to review her claims. We affirm the district court’s dismissal of [the petitioner]’s petition for habeas corpus for lack of jurisdiction. …

“This appeal turns on whether this court has been deprived of jurisdiction over [the petitioner]’s amended habeas corpus petition. …

“We hold that we lack jurisdiction over [the petitioner]’s appeal. When [the petitioner] arrived at Logan Airport she was an ‘applicant for admission’ and subject to inspection by immigration officers. … Where, as here, ‘an immigration officer determines that an alien … who is arriving in the United States … is inadmissible under … section 1182(a)(7) of this title, the officer shall order the alien removed from the United States without further hearing or review unless the alien indicates either an intention to apply for asylum … or a fear of persecution.’ 8 U.S.C. §1225(b)(1)(A)(i).

“We are barred from reviewing [the petitioner]’s challenge to her expedited removal order by §1252(a)(2)(A)(i), which precludes judicial review of ‘any individual determination or … any other cause or claim arising from or relating to the implementation or operation of an order of removal pursuant to section 1225(b)(1),’ unless it fits within one of §1252(e)(2)’s three narrow exceptions in habeas cases. [the petitioner] challenges the validity of her expedited removal order, not whether it has issued. Only the second exception, §1252(e)(2)(B), is relevant here. Nothing in the text of §1252(e)(2)(B) gives us jurisdiction over [the petitioner]’s challenge. …

“We affirm the district court’s dismissal of [the petitioner]’s petition for habeas corpus for lack of jurisdiction.”

Alawieh v. Mullin, et al. (Lawyers Weekly No. 01-229-26) (14 pages) (Lynch, J.) Appealed from a decision by Sorokin, J., in the U.S. District Court for the District of Massachusetts. Sadaf Hasan, with whom Reem Subei, Muslim Advocates, Mark Fleming and National Immigrant Justice Center were on brief, for the petitioner-appellant; Christina Luo, Cynthia D. Vreeland and Wilmer Cutler Pickering Hale and Dorr LLP on brief for American Immigration Council, American Immigration Lawyers Association, Creating Law Enforcement Accountability & Responsibility, The National Immigration Project of the National Lawyers Guild, The National Immigration Law Center and Van Der Hout LLP as amici curiae supporting the appellant; Joshua A. Clem, with whom James J. Walker, Anthony P. Nicastro, Drew C. Ensign and Brett A. Shumate were on brief, for the respondents-appellees (Docket No. 25-2238) (Oct. 13, 2026).

title: Rwanda expected to become first host nation for EU migrant 'return hubs' - InfoMigrants
description:
According to AFP, the small African nation of Rwanda might be about to sign an agreement with a group of five EU member states, which are pushing for the establishment of migrant return hubs outside the EU.
