text:
[Episcopal News Service] A federal appeals court panel has ruled in favor of The Episcopal Church and 26 ecumenical and interfaith partners in a lawsuit contesting the Trump administration’s removal of “sensitive locations” protections for houses of worship in immigration enforcement.

The three-judge panel of the Court of Appeals for the D.C. Circuit ruled, 2-1, that a lower court judge erred in finding that the faith-based plaintiffs lacked standing to file their lawsuit. The plaintiffs have argued that the Trump administration’s intensified immigration enforcement actions have driven some worshippers to stay home.

The lower court judge ruled in April 2025 that The Episcopal Church and other plaintiffs had not sufficiently demonstrated an imminent threat. The Court of Appeals reversed that decision, sending the case back to the U.S. District Court to rule on the merits of the plaintiff’s arguments.

“Plaintiffs’ members likely face imminent harm from increased enforcement at their houses of worship,” the Court of Appeals opinion says. “That harm is traceable to the new enforcement policy.”

Presiding Bishop Sean Rowe and House of Deputies President Julia Ayala Harris issued a joint statement Oct. 20 after the appellate court ruling was handed down.

“As faith leaders who have borne witness to the harm of ICE enforcement on our congregations — and the impact of immigration in one of our families — we give thanks to God for today’s milestone in our multifaith effort to protect religious freedom,” the presiding officers said. “In The Episcopal Church, we cannot truly be ourselves when some cannot freely worship with us. Civic engagement is an important way Christians can demonstrate love for our neighbors, and with this litigation, we are challenging unjust policies that fall short of respecting the dignity of all people.”

The interfaith group of religious denominations and organizations sued the Department of Homeland Security in February 2025 after the Trump administration rescinded a policy that had protected houses of worship, schools and hospitals.

Since then, the Trump administration has escalated its campaign of immigrant detentions and deportations to include aggressive enforcement operations in targeted cities across the country. The deployment of Immigrations and Custom Enforcement officers, as well as Customs and Border Protection agents, has rattled communities, sparked protests and sometimes resulted in violent and deadly confrontations with both immigrants and U.S. citizens.

There have not been widespread reports of raids inside houses of worship, though in cities with a large federal presence, some churches have been joining efforts to assist immigrant families who are afraid to leave their homes to go to work or school or even to get groceries. One Episcopal church in Minnesota also was on a list of houses of worshiped where Homeland Security was reported to have spied on activists holding meetings there.

The Episcopal Church is one of 12 denominations that have signed onto the federal lawsuit, which also includes the Disciples of Christ, Mennonite, Methodist, Presbyterian and AME Zion churches. Other plaintiffs include regional denominational bodies and other religious associations.

The plaintiffs, represented by the nonpartisan Georgetown University Law Center, have argued the Trump administration is violating religious freedom protections in the First Amendment of the U.S. Constitution and the Religious Freedom Restoration Act of 1993.

title: Moderate Republicans fear being dragged down by Trump's unpopularity - EL PAÍS English
description:

The rising cost of living is complicating the efforts of Mike Lawler — a relatively popular politician — to hang on to his seat for another two years.
“Do you pledge your allegiance to Donald Trump?” Lawler was asked during a debate.
Lawler’s difficulties are also affecting other centrist Republicans who fear being dragged down by Trump’s shadow.
But all it takes is crossing a street to reach the 17th District, represented by Republican Mike Lawler.
text:
Dan Hanover has planted a sign in the front yard of his home in Tarrytown as if trying to ward off a curse. It bears just three words, “Mike Lawler for Congress,” but that is more than enough for everyone here to understand what it means: the retiree is determined to do whatever he can to help the Republican who represents this charming village north of New York City keep his seat in the House of Representatives after the November 3 election.

Above all, he fears that Democrats will end up controlling everything in a state where they already hold the governorship under Kathy Hochul, the mayoralties of the major cities and 19 of the state’s 26 seats in the House. “This is looking more and more like a one-party state. Someone has to offer an alternative. And that’s the Republicans,” Hanover says from his kitchen.

The 75-year-old retiree believes U.S. President Donald Trump is doing “a pretty good job,” especially compared with the “disaster” of his predecessor, Democrat Joe Biden.

The problem for Republicans is that Hanover’s positive view of Trump is not widely shared among his neighbors. In this part of the Hudson Valley, complaints about the high cost of living are constant, and many residents blame the Republican administration that came to power riding a wave of frustration over inflation during the Biden years.

The rising cost of living is complicating the efforts of Mike Lawler — a relatively popular politician — to hang on to his seat for another two years. Polls suggest a dead heat with his Democratic challenger, Army veteran Cait Conley.

Mike Lawler, like other Republicans desperate to create some distance from the top of the ticket, is running a campaign defined more by what separates him from Donald Trump than by what binds him to his supposed political ally.

His district is a good barometer of the national mood. It was one of only three congressional districts in the entire country that, in 2024, elected a Republican to Congress while simultaneously voting for Democrat Kamala Harris for president.

“Do you pledge your allegiance to Donald Trump?” Lawler was asked during a debate.

“I pledge my allegiance to my constituents, which I always have. It’s why I’ve been rated among the most bipartisan and effective members of Congress. I’ve been praised by presidents of both parties, including Joe Biden and Donald Trump [...] My best friend in Congress is a Democrat,” he replied.

“I’ve clashed with the president on numerous issues,” Lawler said on another occasion, after Democratic candidate Cait Conley blamed him for the economic difficulties facing local families because of his support in Congress for Trump-backed measures. According to an analysis by Congressional Quarterly, the Republican voted in favor of legislation proposed by the president 94% of the time.

On Monday, Lawler did break with Trump over the war in Ukraine. In an interview with CNN, after footage emerged of the U.S. president blaming Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskiy for the failure to reach a peace deal, the congressman responded: “Vladimir Putin, and Vladimir Putin alone, is responsible for this war.”

Perhaps because of what is at stake — it could help determine which party controls the House of Representatives — it has become one of the most expensive races in the country, with the two parties spending more than $40 million between them.

Each side is targeting the other’s vulnerabilities. Democratic ads highlight the ties between Donald Trump and Mike Lawler, while Republicans have closely scrutinized Democratic candidate Cait Conley’s links to artificial intelligence companies and have sought to associate her with the alleged antisemitism of Zohran Mamdani, the mayor of New York City.

Lawler’s difficulties are also affecting other centrist Republicans who fear being dragged down by Trump’s shadow. Among them is Senator Susan Collins, who is fighting to hold on to her seat in Maine by distancing herself from the Republican administration on issues such as the war with Iran, the sweeping tax package known as the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, which increased healthcare costs for many families, and tariffs on Canada.

“The president did not have a good plan,” Collins acknowledged during a debate last Tuesday.

A town split in two

Tarrytown has an unusual characteristic: it is split in two. One side of the town of 12,000 residents belongs to New York’s 16th congressional district, represented in Washington by a Democrat. But all it takes is crossing a street to reach the 17th District, represented by Republican Mike Lawler. Two ideologies sit side by side in this world of perfect lawns filled with professionals who spend their weekends mowing the grass.

Lawler says he has broken with Trump on issues such as lifting caps on tax deductions, extending temporary protections for Haitian migrants and expanding tax credits for health insurance. Taxes, immigration and healthcare are, in fact, among the issues that most concern residents of the Hudson Valley.

Faced with criticism over the excesses of Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE), local Republicans highlight crimes committed by immigrants in their campaign ads to underscore the need for tighter border controls.

“During Biden’s presidency, illegal entry got out of hand. Now, with Trump, there may have been some excesses, but the problem has been solved. Illegal immigrants have no place in this country,” says Hanover, the resident with the Republican campaign sign in his yard.

New York’s 17th District is particularly revealing because it shows how voting patterns shift depending on the makeup of local communities. Many residents moved here from New York City to escape increasingly unaffordable housing costs. As these generally more progressive families settled in the area, the district gradually became more Democratic.

The district’s diversity is evident from one town to the next. Home to about 780,000 people, it includes one of the largest Jewish populations in the United States as well as sizeable Haitian and Hispanic communities. Wealthy enclaves such as Chappaqua, home to Bill Clinton and Hillary Clinton, coexist alongside working-class communities.

People here are not fond of extremes. Lawler is a traditional Republican who steers clear of Trump-style bombast, while his opponent, Conley, is a centrist Democrat who highlights her military service, her support for Israel and her call to reform, rather than abolish, ICE — positions far removed from those of New York progressives such as Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez and Mamdani.

Peter Bartolacci is another Republican who lives in this landscape of family homes and manicured lawns. He is far from enthusiastic about the Trump administration’s performance, but says it was still the better option given the alternative.

“The Democrats haven’t presented a good candidate since Obama, whom I wasn’t a big fan of either. That’s when identity politics began, which hasn’t brought us anything good,” he says in his living room.

He is certain he will vote Republican on November 3. When asked if he likes what Trump is doing in Washington, Bartolacci answers with a line often used by former New York City mayor Ed Koch: “If you agree with me on nine out of 12 issues, vote for me. If you agree with me on 12 out of 12 issues, see a psychiatrist.”

title: What a Democratic Congress would mean, in spite of Trump's veto pen - USA Today

text:
WASHINGTON – With polls showing Democrats on the verge of winning a majority in the House and perhaps the Senate, congressional leaders from both parties are starting to map out their agenda after the Nov. 3 midterm elections.

Democrats are promising to focus on affordability and holding President Donald Trump and his administration accountable for alleged corruption and abuse of power, while Republicans are vowing to continue pursuing Trump priorities like border security and domestic fossil fuel production during his final two years in office.

But even if Democrats win back both chambers, they will quickly run into a pair of barriers – the Senate filibuster and Trump’s veto pen – that will make it hard for them to enact many of their plans.

Neither party has released a detailed agenda for the next two years, but their leaders have given hints about what Americans should expect.

House Democrats plan to focus on driving down the high cost of living, lowering the price of groceries, gas and housing, and fighting to make healthcare affordable for every American, House Democratic Leader Hakeem Jeffries of New York said in an interview with USA TODAY earlier this month.

"We are explicitly promising to fight for an affordable America, and we will have a responsibility to do everything in our power to make that happen," said Jeffries, who is almost certain to become House speaker if Democrats win a majority.

House Speaker Mike Johnson, a Louisiana Republican, has suggested voters could expect more of the same from the GOP if it defies the odds and hangs onto its slim majority after November.

"What we would do in the next two years is exactly what we have been doing already, and that is putting the conditions in place for a strong America again," Johnson said during a recent interview on CNBC, pointing to the party’s push for border security, energy dominance and pro-growth policies.

In the Senate, Democrats face tougher odds in the November midterms because they need to flip at least four seats, including at least three in states carried by Trump in 2024. But polls suggest their campaign to win back the majority is within reach, thanks to leads in North Carolina, Alaska, Ohio, and even surprising places such as Texas and Kansas.

Democratic Senate Leader Chuck Schumer of New York told reporters recently that, over the next two years, Democrats would focus on affordability and keeping Trump and his administration in check.

"We’re going to do everything we can to lower costs," Schumer said. "You’ve seen some of the things Trump has done that has raised costs. We’re going to do everything we can to clamp down on this horrible corruption and to end the chaos."

It won’t be easy.

Democrats will face Senate filibuster, Trump veto

Trump, a Republican, has two more years in office, meaning Democratic victories in the House and Senate would usher in a new era of divided government. Trump has said he would use his veto power to block many Democratic priorities and keep them from becoming law.

Democrats would be powerless to stop him. Overriding a veto requires a two-thirds majority in both chambers (290 votes in the House if all members are voting, 67 in the Senate). Even if there’s a blue wave in the midterms, Democrats are unlikely to come close to those numbers.

Just getting legislation through the Senate would be a challenge. Republicans could stall or even kill Democratic bills with a filibuster, a parliamentary maneuver allowing any member to delay or prevent a vote on a bill. Sixty votes are needed to overcome a filibuster, meaning Democrats would need help from a few Republicans to move forward – an unlikely prospect given the hyperpartisan climate in Washington.

Given those obstacles, "I don’t think Democrats are going to accomplish much legislatively," said Ron Bonjean, a political strategist with close ties to Republicans on Capitol Hill.

Democrats have pledged to end the eight-month-old war in Iran. But there's not a lot they can do to ensure it happens.

They could try to limit or cut off funding for the conflict by inserting provisions into must-pass bills, such as the Defense Department's budget, that would bar federal funds from being used in operations in Iran. Trump would probably veto such legislation, setting up a confrontation with Congress that could lead to another government shutdown – something that carries political risks for both parties.

Another option would be for Democrats to try to force a vote on the War Powers Resolution, which would restrict Trump’s ability to launch or expand military operations without congressional approval. House Democrats and a handful of Republicans have joined forces to pass the resolution three times since June. The Senate even passed the House-approved measure in June, but the Trump administration ignored it amid questions whether it carries the force of law.

Democratic strategist Josh Schwerin said that since Trump probably won’t allow most of their agenda to become law, Democrats should spend the next two years "blocking him from doing more harm and showing voters that Democrats have real answers to the country’s biggest problems."

What can Democrats do?

One way Democrats could rein in Trump is by blocking his appointees, which require Senate approval, and by launching investigations into Trump, his cabinet and his other allies.

Democrats have accused Trump and his allies of enriching themselves while in office, and Jeffries has vowed repeatedly to "hold the crooks accountable."

In the House, those accountability efforts would be led by Rep. Jamie Raskin of Maryland, the top Democrat on the House Judiciary Committee, and Rep. Robert Garcia of California, the top Democrat on the House Oversight Committee.

Raskin has already tangled with the Trump administration over tariffs, presidential pardons, and other issues. Garcia has pushed for the release of the files on convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein and has accused Immigration and Customs Enforcement and the Department of Homeland Security of misconduct and abuses against U.S. citizens.

Corporate donors to Trump's ballroom and participants in business deals brokered by Trump family members are expected to be among the first targets of investigations if Democrats take control of the House or Senate in the midterm elections, multiple Capitol Hill staffers, lawmakers and attorneys recently told Reuters.

Control of either chamber would give Democrats subpoena power and funding to bolster their investigative staff, enabling them to launch probes as early as February and potentially triggering lengthy legal battles that would place the Trump family business empire in the spotlight.

The investigations could dominate the second half of Trump's term after two years of dealmaking in which the Trump family expanded into crypto, drones, artificial intelligence and prediction markets, while the president's personal wealth grew by an estimated $2.2 billion.

Trump, who was impeached twice but acquitted by the Senate during his first term, could face other impeachment attempts if Democrats win the majority in either chamber. Top Democratic leaders have tried to tamp down such speculation, saying impeachment is not a priority for them. Jeffries told reporters in September that Democrats had not made any decisions about whether to pursue impeachment if they win the majority, but he refused to rule it out.

Democrats also could push to impeach members of Trump's cabinet, such as Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, who has faced criticism over the war in Iran and his decision to fire or sideline dozens of senior military officials, or Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., who has come under fire over his opposition to vaccines and for pushing out top health officials at agencies such as the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention.

'You make deals'

Will anything get done in the next two years?

Maybe. One area with bipartisan potential, Schwerin said, is artificial intelligence safety paired with guardrails against data centers – "more transparency, tech companies paying for grid and infrastructure upgrades, and tough clean air and water standards."

Establishing AI rules of the road has been a priority for years for the current Senate majority leader, Republican John Thune of South Dakota. Thune has worked for months with his Republican and Democratic colleagues to find common ground on the issue.

Trump has suggested he could work with Democrats on some issues.

"You know they’re going to want some stuff, and we’ll get – you make deals," Trump told Fox News’ Laura Ingraham in an interview Sept. 10.

Contributing: Reuters

Michael Collins writes about the intersection of politics and culture. A veteran reporter, he has covered the White House and Congress. Follow him on X: @mcollinsNEWS

Police say the group of clergy blockaded the door inside the White Cap Business Park in Williston on September 4. Part of the facility is leased to the Department of Homeland Security and the protesters refused to leave.

Rev. Karen Johnston of the First Unitarian Universalist Society of Burlington says she believes it’s her duty to stand up for migrants in the wake of the Trump administration’s increased immigration enforcement. “It is part of my pastoral, my clerical duties as an ordained clergy person to make sure that we stand for justice and protect the most vulnerable,” she said.

In total, seven clergy members pleaded not guilty Tuesday to unlawful trespass charges brought by the Vermont Attorney General’s Office.

“They were in court because our state attorney general decided to apply finite resources to prosecute these people of conscience who were protesting ICE’s brutality and racial profiling,” defense attorney Robert Appel said.

The Vermont State Police sent the charges straight to the AG after Chittenden County State’s Attorney Sarah George declined to prosecute similar arrests.

Attorney General Charity Clark released a statement last month saying she has a responsibility to uphold the law and she can’t apply the law based on whether she supports a political cause.

All seven clergy members were released on conditions. That includes not being allowed back on the Williston DHS property unless they’re there for religious reasons.

They also cannot contact the manager of White Cap Industrial Park, where the facility is located.

The Fairfax County Sheriff’s Office in Virginia ignored at least 1,670 immigration detainers from U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement between 2023 and 2025, releasing criminal illegal immigrants back into the community instead of transferring them to federal custody, according to a new House Judiciary Committee report.

The interim staff report – obtained by Fox News before its noon Tuesday release by the committee’s Subcommittee on Immigration Integrity, Security and Enforcement – also accuses Fairfax County Commonwealth’s Attorney Steve Descano of treating illegal immigrant defendants differently from similarly situated American citizens to limit their immigration consequences.

"This interim report provides evidence of the ways in which just one local jurisdiction has implemented policies that allow dangerous foreign nationals to reoffend and avoid deportation," the report, issued under House Judiciary Chair Jim Jordan, R-Ohio, and Subcommittee on Immigration Integrity, Security, and Enforcement Chair Tom McClintock, R-Calif., concluded.

"But Fairfax County and prosecutor Steve Descano are not outliers. They are indicative of a modern, radical, socialist Democrat Party that seeks to erase national borders and place illegal alien criminals ahead of law-abiding American citizens," the report added. "The policies supported by these Democrats, including sanctuary policies(link is external), will have negative and lasting consequences for Americans. The Committee and Subcommittee will continue to conduct oversight of these sanctuary policies to inform potential legislative reforms to better protect American communities."

The committee said a preliminary review of more than 1,100 criminal cases identified more than 100 previously unreported illegal immigrants who benefited from Descano’s prosecutorial decisions. The report said Descano’s office rarely pursued charges against illegal immigrants accused of crimes including driving under the influence, felony drug possession, felony grand larceny, shoplifting, fraud, trespassing, destruction of property and assaulting a law enforcement officer.

The committee accused Descano’s office of "de facto" decriminalizing some offenses and said most of the defendants reviewed went on to reoffend, in some cases escalating to violent crimes and murder.

The report, titled "Fairfax County, Virginia: The dangerous consequences of sanctuary policies," also alleges that Descano misled Congress about the scope of his policies.

"The Biden-Harris Administration worked to weaken the first Trump Administration’s efforts to hold sanctuary jurisdictions accountable for undermining immigration enforcement," the report read. "In addition to dropping federal litigation relating to sanctuary jurisdictions’ policies, the Biden-Harris Administration’s Justice Department(link is external), beginning in April 2021, no longer required jurisdictions to cooperate with ICE as a condition of receiving federal grant funding."

During testimony before the committee in May, Descano said his policy was "written with legal permanent residents in mind for minor crimes." But in a September letter, the committee said Descano acknowledged that prosecutors could consider immigration consequences in cases involving illegal immigrants as well.

Descano’s campaign website previously stated that when "possible," his office would "make charging and plea decisions that limit or avoid immigration consequences." He also argued that "if two people commit the same crime, but only one’s punishment includes deportation, that’s a perversion of justice and not a reflection of the values of Fairfax County."

The committee cited numerous cases in which it said criminal defendants benefited from reduced or dismissed charges. In one example, prosecutors allegedly reduced felony charges involving the sexual assault of a child to misdemeanor "consensual sex with a child" and offered a 90-day suspended jail sentence.

The report also said Descano’s office dropped more than 50 charges against a serial fraudster from China and allowed defendants charged with malicious wounding, strangulation, assault and battery and other violent offenses to "escape accountability and reoffend."

The committee detailed additional cases involving defendants accused of child pornography, rape, abduction, firearm offenses, drug possession and assault. In some cases, the report said, defendants were released despite ICE detainers and later arrested again.

One case involved Marvin Morales-Ortez, an alleged MS-13 member(link is external) whose charges were dropped before the Fairfax County Sheriff’s Office released him in December 2025. The report said Morales-Ortez allegedly murdered a man in Reston, Virginia, one day later.

Fairfax County Sheriff Stacey Kincaid blamed the release on the lack of prosecution, writing that "the system must work as a whole." She added: "When criminal defendants are prosecuted, authorities are better able to track court dates and monitor releases."

Kincaid has also previously criticized the county’s prosecution practices, stating, "It’s shameful the way things have not been prosecuted."

The report highlighted the case of Stephanie Minter(link is external), who was fatally stabbed in February. The suspect, Abdul Jalloh, is an illegal immigrant with more than 40 prior charges in Fairfax County. The committee said Descano’s office had dropped charges against Jalloh in almost every case and that police warned prosecutors before the killing that "it is not a question of if, but rather when [Jalloh] will maliciously wound — or worse — again."

Cheryl Minter, Stephanie’s mother, told the committee that "a system failed my daughter."

Chicago – Attorney General Kwame Raoul, as part of a coalition of 22 attorneys general, filed an amicus brief in support of litigation challenging the U.S. Department of Homeland Security’s (DHS) policy and practice of conducting unlawful warrantless civil immigration arrests.

In an amicus brief filed in the U.S. Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit in Escobar-Molina v. DHS, the coalition explains under federal law, immigration officers conducting warrantless civil immigration arrests must have probable cause to believe an individual is unlawfully present in the United States and is likely to escape before a warrant can be obtained. Federal law allows immigration officers to make an arrest without a warrant only when there is probable cause to believe a person is unlawfully present and is likely to escape before a warrant can be obtained.

“The Trump administration continues to instill fear and distrust within immigrant communities in Illinois and around the country with unnecessarily cruel and unlawful tactics,” Raoul said. “I will continue to stand with my colleagues and support the rights of all immigrants as we fight against the federal government’s immoral actions that disrupt our communities.”

In their brief, Raoul and the attorneys general argue the widespread harms of unlawful immigration enforcement practices disrupt communities and undermine public health, safety, education and local economies. The brief explains some of the disruptions have kept students out of school, disrupted agricultural work, discouraged people from seeking medical care, undermined families’ financial stability, and weakened the relationship between immigrant communities and local law enforcement.

This case challenges DHS’ policy and practice of conducting unlawful warrantless civil immigration arrests in the District of Columbia. In December 2025, the U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia granted in part a motion for a preliminary injunction.

text:
The Trump administration is sharply reducing the time refugees have to contest the termination of their status, a move advocates say could put as many as 186,000 people who fled persecution and war in their home countries on a path to deportation.

A new final rule reduces the time refugees have to challenge the revocation of their status from 30 days to 10. The rule took effect Wednesday and was published in the Federal Register just one day earlier, without going through the formal notice-and-comment period.

Refugees fleeing persecution have their claims processed outside the United States before entering the country under the bipartisan Refugee Act, passed by Congress in 1980. After one year, they become eligible to apply for lawful permanent residency, at which point they are no longer considered refugees.

The new policy targets refugees who have not yet obtained permanent residency or had their refugee status reviewed. U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services processes applications to adjust refugees' status to that of lawful permanent residents, and the policy comes as the agency faces significant backlogs. Between the second quarter of fiscal 2025 and the same period in fiscal year 2026, the number of pending I-485 applications, used to apply for permanent residency, rose 190%, according to a September analysis by the American Immigration Council.

The Department of Homeland Security has identified 186,000 cases involving "unadjusted" refugees who entered the United States between fiscal years 2015 and 2025. Data from the U.S. Refugee Admissions Program shows that about 30,000 refugees arrived in New York during that period.

Information from the Refugee Services program within the state Office of Temporary and Disability Assistance, which oversees services for refugees, shows that the majority of refugees in recent years were resettled in upstate New York.

Community-based organizations such as Albany's Refugee and Immigrant Support Services of Emmaus help support those new arrivals. A representative of the organization told the Times Union that the effects of delays in granting permanent residency are already being felt locally. Although applications for permanent residency have been filed on behalf of all refugees in the area, the new rule has heightened concerns about how long they will have to wait.

"It's always important to get those in as quickly as possible," said the representative, who requested anonymity because of concerns about retribution. "There are all these refugees nationwide who still haven't received their green cards. In Albany, we have submitted the applications for all of them, but it's a real vulnerability."

Processing an application for permanent residency and terminating refugee status are two distinct legal procedures under U.S. immigration law. Refugee status can be terminated if the federal government determines that an individual was never legally a refugee at the time of admission.

Although the new policy specifically addresses termination of refugee status, people whose applications for permanent residency remain unprocessed are vulnerable, the local refugee organization's representative said.

The rule comes as the Trump administration advances its immigration agenda and after refugees lost federal Medicaid coverage at the beginning of the month. It also comes just one week after a poll by the left-of-center think tank Data for Progress showed more than two-thirds of voters believe the U.S. should have a refugee program.

The largest numbers of refugee arrivals in the past decade were recorded in fiscal years 2024, 2016 and 2015, respectively. The new policy specifically references refugees admitted during President Joe Biden's administration, citing what it describes as an "alarming erosion of the integrity" of the refugee program.

Nationally, refugee advocates are raising concerns about the administration's actions, particularly the lack of due process under the new rule.

Laurie Ball Cooper, vice president of U.S. legal programs at the International Refugee Assistance Project, called the policy "an effort to strip lawfully present, lawfully admitted refugees of their status and deport them to persecution or worse."

"Now, it will be impossible for refugees to even fully understand the allegations against them, much less find counsel and contest those allegations, before their status is terminated," Cooper said. "Threatening the safety and stability of our refugee neighbors is an attack on the constitutional rights of every American."

Dorothea Lay, vice president of advocacy and policy with Jesuit Refugee Service, echoed those concerns, calling the removal of people who had been thoroughly vetted a "violation of dictates of fairness, due process and respect for human dignity."

​​​​​​​​​​​FOR IMMEDIATE RELEASE

BALTIMORE, MD – Attorney General Anthony G. Brown, as part of a coalition of 22 attorneys general, filed an amicus brief in the U.S. Court of Appeals for the D.C. Circuit in support of litigation challenging the U.S. Department of Homeland Security’s (DHS) policy and practice of conducting unlawful warrantless civil immigration arrests.

Under federal law, immigration officers conducting warrantless civil immigration arrests must have probable cause to believe that an individual is unlawfully present in the United States and is likely to escape before a warrant can be obtained. However, DHS officers routinely carry out warrantless arrests without determining if the individual is an escape risk. The brief highlights the widespread harms that unlawful immigration enforcement practices have inflicted on communities across the country, including in Maryland.

“ICE’s widespread unlawful arrests in Washington, D.C. do not just affect the people they take into custody; they affect entire families who live in our nation’s capital and its surrounding communities. A Maryland mother was afraid to join her asthmatic son in a D.C. hospital because she feared being detained, while a Prince George’s County educator reported a surge in students seeking mental health support following immigration raids,” said Attorney General Brown. “We are urging the court to ensure ICE follows the law, just like any other law enforcement agency.”

Across the country, federal immigration agents have escalated their enforcement activities, disrupting communities and undermining public health, safety, education, and local economies. Maryland has seen these harms firsthand, detailed in our amicus brief in Guzman, et al. v. DHS, as aggressive immigration enforcement tactics have disrupted students’ learning, endangered physical and mental health, separated children from their families, kept workers home and customers away from local businesses, and eroded the community trust that local law enforcement relies on to keep Marylanders safe. Federal agents’ use of masks and unmarked vehicles while carrying out operations has further contributed to fear and uncertainty in affected communities.

The brief was filed in Escobar-Molina v. DHS, a case challenging DHS’s policy and practice of conducting unlawful warrantless civil immigration arrests in the District of Columbia. On December 2, 2025, the U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia granted in part a motion for a preliminary injunction.

text:
On Oct. 14, 2026, the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) issued an interim final rule (IFR), effective immediately, cutting the time a refugee has to respond to a Notice of Intent to Terminate (NOIT) refugee status from 30 days to 10 days. 91 Fed. Reg. 65077. Comments are due Nov. 13, 2026 (Docket No. USCIS-2026-0397).

The same day, U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services (USCIS) finalized the October 2025 IFR ending automatic employment authorization document (EAD) extensions for certain categories, including refugees and asylees. 91 Fed. Reg. 65306.

Together, the rules leave refugees less time to defend their status and less protections to keep working.

What the IFR Does

The IFR amends 8 C.F.R. § 207.9 to shorten the refugee 10 days, down from 30 days, to respond and oppose termination. The basic termination standard is unchanged. There is no appealing the termination, and USCIS will process the individual under INA §§ 235, 240, and 241.

DHS grounds the rule to Executive Orders 14161 and 14163 and to Operation Post-Admission Refugee Reverification and Integrity Strengthening (Operation PARRIS). That initiative subjects refugee cases to renewed background checks and reinterviews and has already resulted in the issuance of NOITs.

Statutory, Regulatory Authority

DHS relies mainly on INA § 207(c)(4), 8 U.S.C. § 1157(c)(4), which allows termination when an alien “was not in fact a refugee” at admission and authorizes regulations governing the procedure. DHS also cites INA § 103(a), 8 U.S.C. § 1103(a), and Homeland Security Act § 102, 6 U.S.C. § 112. Key points:

Single ground. The only basis for termination is a finding the person did not meet the refugee definition at admission.

Principals and derivatives. The determination applies to principal refugees; a derivative’s status may be terminated if the principal’s is.

Timing. Termination is available only before adjustment to permanent residence or naturalization. A person whose LPR status is rescinded under INA § 246 reverts to refugee status and can again face termination.

Service. Under 8 C.F.R. § 103.8(b), three days are added when a notice is served by mail.

The Prior Process and How the IFR Changes It

Now, the NOIT still states the reasons, but the window is 10 calendar days, including weekends and holidays (a deadline on a weekend or holiday rolls to the next business day). The clock starts to run on the mailing date. With the mail rule, DHS calculates 13 days in total for mailed NOITs, which it will send by tracked express delivery. A timely interview request (rather than a full written rebuttal) counts as a timely response. Otherwise, the refugee “is considered to have forfeited his or her right to rebut the allegations,” and status is terminated.

Automatic Extensions

The refugee IFR does not address automatic extensions; refugee status has no expiration date to extend. The companion USCIS final rule ends the up-to-540-day automatic EAD extension for renewals filed on or after Oct. 30, 2025, in categories including refugees and asylees ((a)(3) and (a)(5)).

The effects build on each other. Refugees are work-authorized incident to status, but many rely on an (a)(3) EAD as proof; DHS reports about 113,000 refugees with approved (A3) initial EADs and pending Form I-485 applications. A refugee whose EAD expires during a pending renewal can no longer rely on a receipt notice, which can create Form I-9 reverification issues even though authorization continues. Termination of refugee status also ends work authorization immediately, which DHS acknowledges is “at least 20 days sooner than without this rule.”

Practitioners should file renewals early, keep other status evidence (such as the Form I-94) available, and advise employers on acceptable Form I-9 documents.

Due Process Concerns

DHS says the 10-day window “maintains adequate procedural safeguards.” Practitioners likely have reasons to disagree, including:

It is effectively the only chance to be heard. With no appeal, AILA observes, the notice period is “the only opportunity for a refugee to defend their status.”

Service and language barriers. Because the clock starts at mailing, refugees who have moved, have limited English proficiency, or lack counsel may lose valuable time before they understand the notice.

Scale. DHS identifies about 186,000 refugee cases from FY 2015 through FY 2025 that have not adjusted status, representing the maximum population potentially affected.

Procedural vulnerability. DHS invoked the APA’s good cause and foreign affairs exceptions (5 U.S.C. § 553(a)(1), (b)(B), (d)(3)) to bypass notice and comment. Good cause is narrowly construed, and related refugee policies have already been litigated, including the partial stay of the Feb. 18, 2026, ICE-USCIS detention memorandum in Jean A. v. Noem (D. Mass.).

DHS notes that individuals may still seek relief in proceedings under INA §§ 235, 240, or 241. Those proceedings, however, do not preserve refugee status and the path to adjustment under INA § 209.

text:
FRESNO, Calif. (KFSN) -- This month, ICE agents have shown up at Fresno County farms, construction sites, and have been making traffic stops across the city.

On Monday, Fresno City Councilmember Miguel Arias stood alongside activists to announce a response.

"The one way we can act, and we can help is by making resources available to those impacted by these immigration raids," said Arias.

Arias wants to bring back Fresno's immigration legal defense fund.

The city previously allocated $200,000 for the fund back in 2021.

If approved, the new resolution would allocate another $1 million to provide immigrants with outside attorneys for detention and deportation defense.

"These funds would be from the general fund, from salary savings of positions that are not filled," Arias said.

Arias wants to see those savings reallocated to the proposed defense fund during the city's midyear budget review in January.

Mayor Jerry Dyer says the proposal is premature because there's no way to know what the budget will look like until then.

While he understands the need for legal defense for immigrants, he says other local groups already provide those services.

"I try not to replicate or duplicate what other government entities are doing, like the county, the state or the feds, or nonprofits," Dyer said.

The city council will consider the proposal during their meeting Thursday.

title: Op-Ed: Biden said only Congress could fix the border; Trump proved him wrong | Opinion
description: Numbers can tell a story that no amount of partisan spin can erase.
text:
A U.S. Border Patrol vehicle sits in the desert near Sunland Park, N.M., on July 17, 2024. Photo: Glenn Fawcett / U.S. Customs and Border Protection via Flickr / United States Government Work

Numbers can tell a story that no amount of partisan spin can erase.

According to U.S. Customs and Border Protection data, southwest border apprehensions in fiscal year 2026 fell 95% from the Biden-era average, with fewer than 99,000 between ports of entry. Nationwide encounters totaled just 379,243 – the lowest in agency history and 88% below the 2.7 million annual average of the Biden years.

Fiscal 2026 also marked the first year with zero Border Patrol releases into the interior, a streak that reached 17 consecutive months by September. Drug seizures hit nearly 1 million pounds. These are not projections or aspirations. They are results.

Compare that to the record. In 2023, under President Biden, CBP recorded 3.2 million apprehensions – the highest on record – while encounters routinely exceeded 2 million a year. More than 2 million known gotaways entered without even being processed.

Catch-and-release was official policy, not the exception.

Cartels treated the border as a logistics corridor for fentanyl, human trafficking, and terrorism watchlist encounters. Border deaths climbed as migrants were funneled into remote, deadly routes. Interior cities absorbed the costs in overwhelmed shelters, strained schools, and elevated crime rates tied to released aliens. The contrast is not subtle. One administration treated the border as an open invitation. The other treated it as a sovereign boundary.

Biden and then-Vice President Kamala Harris spent years insisting this outcome was impossible without a sweeping new act of Congress. Biden repeatedly said he had “done all I can do” and needed “the power I’ve asked from the very day I got into office.” He claimed a bipartisan Senate bill would grant him “new emergency authority to shut down the border when it becomes overwhelmed,” and that legislation was “the only way to actually get the kind of system we have now that’s broken, fixed.” Harris pushed Biden’s narrative, blaming Republicans and then-candidate Trump for killing a bill that would have added agents and funding while accusing Trump of preferring to “run on a problem instead of fixing a problem.” The message was consistent: the executive branch was powerless; only Congress could restore order.

Fiscal 2026 demolishes that claim. President Trump did not wait for a comprehensive immigration overhaul. He did not invent new statutory authority. He restored and expanded enforcement of laws already on the books to the fullest extent as authorized by Congress – expedited removal, detention, and asylum restrictions – while ending the mass parole and release policies that had incentivized crossings. The deterrent effect was immediate and sustained.

When the message is clear that illegal entry results in apprehension, detention, and removal rather than a court date years later and work authorization, the migrant flow evaporates. New barrier construction resumed, but the decisive factor was policy posture, not concrete and steel alone.

This was not a near-impossible task requiring the invention of fresh statutes. Existing immigration law already authorizes the president to control entries, detain those who arrive illegally, and remove them. Prior administrations of both parties used those tools when they chose to. The Biden administration chose not to. It dismantled Remain in Mexico, ended Title 42 without a replacement plan, expanded parole programs, and directed agents toward processing rather than prevention.

The result was the largest illegal migration surge in modern history. The subsequent reversal under Trump demonstrates that the problem was not a lack of legislation. It was political will, the willingness of the chief executive to treat border security as a core duty of the office rather than a bargaining chip or a virtue-signaling gesture toward the rest of the world.

America does not owe the world an open invitation to enter at will, claim asylum on economic grounds, or remain indefinitely while courts grind through backlogs measured in years. Sovereignty is not a bygone concept. It is the prerequisite for any ordered liberty and any functional social contract. Nations that cannot or will not control who enters cease to function as nations. The costs of the alternative – fentanyl deaths measured in tens of thousands, unvetted noncitizens released into communities, cartel profits, and eroded public trust – are not abstract. They fall on American citizens first.

The historic lows of fiscal 2026 do not mean the work is finished. Gotaways still occur, cartels adapt, and interior enforcement remains contested. Yet the data establish a clear lesson: sustained executive enforcement of existing law produces rapid, measurable control. Claims that only new congressional legislation could achieve this were either mistaken or, more plausibly, an effort to lock in policies that maximized flows of illegal aliens while shifting blame.

The border is secure not because America discovered new legal magic, but because one administration decided that safeguarding the nation ranked above the idea that entry is a global entitlement. That decision, executed through ordinary presidential authority, is what the numbers now record.

Brian Lonergan is director of strategic communications and content at the Federation for American Immigration Reform in Washington, D.C., and co-host of the “No Border, No Country” podcast.

text:
A “catastrophic” tech blunder by Kristi Noem’s Department of Homeland Security put the public in danger by preventing ICE from using wiretaps to catch suspected criminals for months.

The extraordinary failure in April last year—which experts say will take “years” to recover from—followed an “inadvertent” change to the internet provider used by Homeland Security Investigations (HSI), ICE’s criminal investigative arm, according to information buried deep in an obscure government document uncovered by PunchUp.

The outage coincided with the number of wiretaps reported by DHS investigators collapsing by more than 80 percent under then-Homeland Security Secretary Noem, 54.

In admitting its mistake, DHS warned that losing wiretap capability for long periods can “severely cripple” ongoing high-stakes criminal investigations and pose a “direct, unquantifiable risk” to undercover agents and the public.

AndPunchUp, the Daily Beast’s sister investigations Substack, has also found that the failure could have had even wider ramifications because DHS records show HSI’s electronic-surveillance operation supports investigations involving other federal agencies, including the FBI and DEA.

Eric Balliet, a former Homeland Security Investigations agent who spent 25 years in federal law enforcement and used between 250 and 300 wiretaps, said he was astonished by the blunder.

“I cannot fathom a federal law enforcement agency not having the capability or capacity to legally intercept communications,” he told PunchUp. “When you lack the ability to intercept communications—phone calls, messaging apps and texts—the criminal networks win. Fentanyl, cocaine and heroin hit the streets. People are smuggled. People die.”

Balliet, who retired in July 2024, added, “I truly cannot comprehend how a law enforcement agency could drop the ball in such a catastrophic manner.”

Richard Marianos, a former assistant director with the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives (ATF), which used the HSI wiretap system, said the potential ramifications of wiretaps being out of action for such a prolonged period were massive.

“It becomes much more difficult to get intelligence against an organization and take out the high-value targets who are the decision makers on a telephone rather than those out on the streets committing crimes,” said Marianos, who teaches a master’s class on wiretapping at D.C.’s Georgetown University and is a protective intelligence expert at Kronus Intelligence Group.

“The longer those criminal kingpins are able to operate with impunity because wiretap tactics are unavailable, the more dangerous the organization will become because they are still operating on the street.”

Brandi Young, a federal prosecutor for 16 years who handled DHS wiretap cases and is now a partner at Texas law firm Keith & Lorfing, said an inability to use the technology could lead some of the most serious criminal investigations to “stall”—in some cases “forever.”

Balliet agreed, warning that even brief disruptions to surveillance capabilities could devastate complex investigations. “You lose track of who is talking to whom, the devices they are using, their nicknames,” he said, adding, “To not have that function for months is a dereliction of duty, malfeasance of what the American public expects from their law enforcement personnel.”

The potentially costly error only came to light in a procurement document DHS released late last month. The department appears to have disclosed its failure only to justify retaining its existing internet provider under a new sole-source contract.

Federal records show ICE awarded Cox Virginia Telcom a contract without competition on Sept. 25, potentially worth $702,884.56, to provide dedicated network circuits for HSI’s Title III and Linguistics Unit, the federal legal framework governing court-authorized interception of communications.

The episode also offers a rare glimpse inside the infrastructure used for wiretaps. The document says HSI uses static internet addresses to maintain connections with roughly 50 telecommunications providers. Those connections let intercepted content transfer into HSI’s own network.

But DHS admits a simple change caused that system to break down.

When HSI’s internet provider was inadvertently switched in April 2025, three months after Noem took charge at DHS, the agency was assigned a new internet address. Connections with providers then had to be rebuilt. DHS admitted the result was “months of downtime for wiretaps.”

The records do not say exactly how long the wiretap capability was out for, how many of HSI’s seven sites were affected, or how many investigations were disrupted. DHS declined to say.

But the Administrative Office of the U.S. Courts reported that DHS’s Investigations Office had just 23 wiretaps in 2025, compared with 133 in 2024—a fall of almost 83 percent.

DHS has given several other explanations for that slump, citing operational delays from government shutdowns, shifting enforcement and prosecutorial priorities, and staffing attrition and reorganization.

It has refused to say whether its months-long wiretap failure contributed to the extraordinary decline, how many court-authorized interceptions or criminal investigations were affected, whether evidence was lost as a result, who was responsible, or whether it undertook any review to prevent it happening again.

A DHS spokesperson told PunchUp, “We will not comment on law enforcement sensitive methods.”

Balliet illustrated the importance of maintaining wiretap capabilities with his experience investigating notorious Mexican drug lord Joaquín “El Chapo” Guzmán while working as an assistant special agent in charge in Nogales, Arizona.

“We had a team of 15 people doing nothing but working out who was going to change their device, their phone number, or their BlackBerry Messenger PIN,” he said. “That was their sole job because the criminal network was constantly changing its communications strategy to avoid detection.”

Balliet—who has published a book, Kingpins and Coyotes, about his career—added, “If we did not have that, he would not have been captured and would still be running the scene,” he said. “It really is that big a deal.”

Daniel Brunner, a retired FBI supervisory special agent who now runs a Spanish-language media platform on the bureau, says such a long delay would have been completely avoidable.

He told PunchUp: “DHS should have come to the FBI and said its system is down, and they needed help. Perhaps Kristi Noem didn’t want to show weakness or her systems were failing. There’s no reason why it was out for so long.”

For Balliet, the consequences could extend far beyond the outage itself. “It will take years to recover from something like this,” he said. “It’s laughable, but in an almost unbelievable way.”

Why the Final Rule Is a Harder Target The final rule changes the litigation in two ways.

Did the final rule change anything from the October 2025 interim final rule?
text:
Key Takeaways

What happened: On October 14, 2026, DHS published a final rule (91 FR 65306) ending the automatic extension of Employment Authorization Documents (EADs) for renewals filed on or after October 30, 2025. It took effect immediately.

No new change to work authorization: The final rule adopts the October 30, 2025 interim final rule (90 FR 48799) without any changes. These rules have applied for almost a year.

Who is affected: Adjustment of status applicants with (c)(9) EADs and H-4 spouses with (c)(26) EADs face the greatest risk of a work authorization gap.

Who is not affected: F-1 students filing for the STEM OPT extension still receive the 180-day extension, because it comes from a different regulation. L-2 and E spouses remain authorized to work incident to status.

Grandfathered filings: Renewals properly filed before October 30, 2025, keep the up-to-540-day automatic extension, subject to the applicable eligibility conditions and the 540-day maximum.

Litigation: A federal court in California granted relief to seven H-4 spouses who challenged the interim rule. The final rule has a fuller record, but strong arbitrary and capricious arguments remain.

What Does the New DHS Final Rule Do?

On October 14, 2026, the Department of Homeland Security published a final rule titled “Removal of Automatic Extensions for Certain Employment Authorization Documents” in the Federal Register (91 FR 65306). The rule ends the practice of automatically extending an expiring EAD while USCIS processes a timely filed renewal application. It became effective the same day it was published.

If that headline sounds familiar, it should. The final rule does not create a new policy. It adopts, without a single change, the interim final rule DHS issued on October 30, 2025.

What the final rule does change is the legal landscape. A permanent rule backed by a full comment record is a different target in court than a rule issued without public input. Below, we explain what the rule does, who is affected (and who is not), and where we think the litigation goes from here.

When Did Automatic EAD Extensions End?

Automatic EAD extensions ended for renewals filed on or after October 30, 2025, not on October 14, 2026.

For most of the last decade, an applicant who timely filed an EAD renewal could keep working past the card’s expiration date while USCIS processed the renewal. A 2016 rule set that bridge at 180 days. Temporary measures in 2022 and 2024 stretched it to 540 days, and a final rule published December 13, 2024, made the 540-day extension generally available on a permanent basis, subject to eligibility requirements.

Less than a year later, on October 30, 2025, DHS reversed course with an interim final rule (IFR) titled “Removal of the Automatic Extension of Employment Authorization Documents” (90 FR 48799). An interim final rule takes effect immediately and asks for public comment afterward, rather than before. DHS invoked the Administrative Procedure Act’s “good cause” and “foreign affairs” exceptions to skip the normal notice and comment process. The IFR:

Added a new 8 CFR 274a.13(e), providing that a renewal EAD application filed on or after October 30, 2025, does not automatically extend an expiring EAD or the underlying employment authorization.

Revised the heading of 8 CFR 274a.13(d) so the up-to-540-day extension applies only to renewals properly filed before October 30, 2025.

Preserved extensions provided by statute or by a Federal Register notice for Temporary Protected Status (TPS).

The final rule “reaffirms and finalizes” those provisions and states that DHS adopts the IFR “without any changes.” DHS also adopted the IFR’s preamble reasoning. Because nothing changed, DHS waived the usual 30-day delayed effective date, reasoning that affected people had already been on notice for almost a year.

What Is Different About the Final Rule Compared to the Interim Final Rule?

The regulatory text is identical to the IFR. What is new is dozens of pages of preamble responding to public comments. That preamble matters for two reasons.

First, it finalizes the policy. There is no longer an “interim” rule awaiting revision after comments. A final rule can still be amended or rescinded, but only through further rulemaking or a court order. Employers and employees should not plan around the possibility that the 540-day bridge returns on its own.

Second, it builds the record DHS will rely on in court. DHS responded directly to the arguments challengers raised against the IFR: the lack of evidence for the security rationale, the existence of continuous vetting tools, the reversal of the 2016 and 2024 rules, reliance interests, and the availability of narrower alternatives. DHS rejected every alternative, including shorter extensions and carve outs for H-4 spouses and employment-based adjustment applicants.

DHS also put numbers on the harm. Its own analysis estimates that 20,000 to 33,000 EADs will lapse in a single 18-month window starting in May 2027, affecting roughly 1,700 to 2,800 employers. DHS projects $312.1 million in labor turnover costs to U.S. employers and $138.1 million in lost productivity over that period. 91 FR at 65308. DHS concluded that its security concerns outweigh those costs.

Who Is Affected by the End of Automatic EAD Extensions?

The exposure depends on one question: does the employee’s right to work come from the EAD itself, or from an underlying immigration status? For most business immigration clients, the risk is concentrated in two groups.

Adjustment of Status Applicants with (c)(9) EADs

Employees with a pending Form I-485 who work on a (c)(9) EAD are directly affected. If a renewal filed on or after October 30, 2025, is not approved before the current card expires, the employee must stop working until the new card is approved. The rule’s own example makes the point: an applicant whose EAD expires May 30, 2026, cannot work on May 31 if the renewal is still pending.

Two practical notes. Adjustment applicants who independently maintain valid H-1B or L-1 employment authorization may continue working pursuant to that authorization, notwithstanding expiration of their (c)(9) EAD. The employee must actually remain authorized for that employment under the applicable petition and status, which is one reason we often recommend maintaining nonimmigrant status during a pending adjustment. And for combo cards, the advance parole portion was never covered by the automatic extension, so travel planning was already tied to the printed date.

H-4 Spouses with (c)(26) EADs

H-4 spouses of H-1B workers are among the most exposed. Their work authorization comes from the EAD, not from H-4 status, so a pending renewal no longer bridges any gap. Commenters told DHS that H-4 EAD renewal processing times frequently exceed the 180-day early filing window, which means many H-4 spouses face a gap even when they file at the earliest possible date. DHS acknowledged that risk and declined to create an exception.

The H-4 timeline is also tied to the H-1B principal. A late H-1B extension can shorten the runway for the spouse’s renewal. The automatic extension was also never unlimited for H-4 spouses. Under the prior framework, it depended on an unexpired Form I-94 showing H-4 status and ended when that I-94 expired. A spouse whose I-94 had already expired, with the H-4 extension still pending, did not qualify at all, while a spouse whose I-94 expired partway through the 540 days received a shorter extension.

L-2 and E Spouses

L-2 and E spouses are employment authorized incident to status. Their right to work continues as long as their status remains valid. For Form I-9 purposes, the acceptable evidence depends on the documents presented; an unexpired Form I-94 bearing the appropriate spousal designation (for example, L-2S) can document that authorization.

Does the Final Rule Affect STEM OPT?

No. The final rule does not affect the F-1 STEM OPT extension. The 180-day extension that lets a student keep working after timely filing a STEM OPT application comes from a separate regulation, 8 CFR 214.2(f)(11)(i)(C), with the corresponding work authorization provision at 8 CFR 274a.12(b)(6)(iv).

The IFR and final rule amended only 8 CFR 274a.13, which governs renewals of an EAD in the same category. A STEM OPT application is not a renewal of the post-completion OPT EAD. It is an extension with its own regulatory bridge. Students who timely file for STEM OPT continue to receive the 180-day extension.

Can the Final Rule Be Challenged in Court?

Short answer: VERY LIKELY

The Interim Final Rule Has Already Lost Once

On January 8, 2026, seven H-4 spouses filed Jane Doe 1 v. Department of Homeland Security in the U.S. District Court for the Central District of California before Judge David O. Carter. Their complaint argued that DHS lacked good cause to skip notice and comment, that the security rationale was pretextual, that DHS ignored the reliance interests created by the 2016 and 2024 rules, and that the IFR never addressed DHS’s existing continuous vetting programs.

On September 10, 2026, the court granted preliminary relief to the seven plaintiffs, restoring the automatic extension for them. That order covers only those plaintiffs, and no court has blocked the rule for anyone else.

Other challenges have followed different paths. In Doe v. USCIS, No. 1:26-cv-01336 (D.D.C.), Public Citizen challenged the IFR on behalf of a single worker; after the plaintiff moved for a stay and preliminary injunction, USCIS processed her renewal and the case was dismissed.

Why the Final Rule Is a Harder Target

The final rule changes the litigation in two ways.

The procedural argument weakens. The strongest claim against an interim final rule is that the agency skipped notice and comment without good cause. DHS has now taken comments, responded to them, and issued a final rule. Courts generally treat that process as curing the procedural defect going forward, though challengers can still argue that DHS did not approach the comments with an open mind, given that it changed nothing. The final rule does not necessarily cure any procedural violation retroactively, which could matter for claims involving lapses that occurred between October 30, 2025, and October 14, 2026.

The record is fuller. Many of the arbitrary and capricious arguments against the IFR were “failure to consider” arguments: DHS did not address continuous vetting, did not weigh reliance interests, did not consider alternatives. The final rule’s preamble now addresses each of those points, at least on paper.

That said, an agency does not win simply by responding to comments. Under Motor Vehicle Manufacturers Ass’n v. State Farm, the agency must show a rational connection between the facts found and the choice made. Under FCC v. Fox Television Stations and DHS v. Regents of the University of California, an agency reversing a prior policy must acknowledge the change and account for the reliance interests it upsets. We see three arguments that the expanded record does not fix. Each targets a gap in DHS’s reasoning, which matters: a court cannot set aside a rule merely because it considers the policy unwise or the costs too high.

What Should Employers and Employees Do Now?

File renewals as early as possible. Most EAD renewals can be filed up to 180 days before the current card expires. Every week of delay increases the risk of a gap.

Know when the card’s expiration date is a hard stop. For an employee whose only work authorization is an EAD renewed on or after October 30, 2025, a Form I-797C receipt notice does not extend that authorization, and reverification is due by the printed expiration date. That is not necessarily true for an employee with independent authorization or a qualifying statutory or regulatory extension.

Track expiration dates consistently. An internal system that tracks work authorization expiration dates from completed Forms I-9 is appropriate, and early notice helps employees plan. Reverification and document requests must follow the Form I-9 rules, and employers should not single out employees for different treatment based on citizenship or immigration status.

Look for an independent basis to work. Adjustment applicants who can maintain valid H-1B or L-1 employment authorization should do so. For key H-4 employees, consider whether H-1B sponsorship makes sense.

File the H-1B extension early. Filing the H-4 extension and H-4 EAD together with the principal’s H-1B extension gives the family the longest runway.

Decide on a gap policy in advance. Work with counsel on how to handle an employee whose authorization lapses, such as an unpaid leave of absence where permitted by employment law and company policy, and apply it consistently.

Consider federal court. Depending on the circumstances, a mandamus or APA unreasonable delay lawsuit may provide a means to challenge USCIS’s failure to adjudicate a pending renewal within a reasonable time. Our litigation team handles these cases for H-4 spouses and adjustment applicants across the country.

Frequently Asked Questions

Is the 540-day automatic EAD extension still available?

Only for renewal applications properly filed before October 30, 2025, and only if the applicable eligibility conditions are met. Renewals filed on or after that date receive no automatic extension, except where a statute or a TPS Federal Register notice provides one.

When did the final rule take effect?

October 14, 2026, the date it was published at 91 FR 65306. The same policy has applied since the interim final rule took effect on October 30, 2025.

Did the final rule change anything from the October 2025 interim final rule?

No. DHS adopted the interim final rule as final without any changes to the regulatory text. The final rule adds DHS’s responses to public comments.

Can I keep working on my (c)(9) EAD while my renewal is pending?

Not if you filed the renewal on or after October 30, 2025. You must stop working when the current card expires unless you have another basis for employment, such as independently valid H-1B or L-1 employment authorization.

Are H-4 EAD holders affected?

Yes. H-4 spouses who filed (c)(26) renewals on or after October 30, 2025, lose work authorization when the current card expires if USCIS has not yet approved the renewal.

Does the rule affect the STEM OPT 180-day extension?

No. The STEM OPT extension is governed by 8 CFR 214.2(f)(11)(i)(C) and 8 CFR 274a.12(b)(6)(iv), which the rule did not change.

Has a court blocked the rule?

Not generally. In Jane Doe 1 v. DHS (C.D. Cal.), the court granted relief on September 10, 2026, but only to the seven H-4 plaintiffs in that case.

What can I do if my EAD renewal is delayed?

File as early as permitted, maintain any independent status, and talk with counsel about whether a mandamus or APA unreasonable delay lawsuit makes sense in your situation.

Talk to Our Team

If you have questions about how the final rule affects your employees or your family, contact Reddy Neumann Brown PC. Our business immigration and federal litigation teams will continue to monitor the litigation and share updates on the firm blog and on our Visa Vibes podcast.

We work with employers, employees and investors helping them navigate the immigration process quickly and cost-effectively.

text:
In Brief

Mahmoud Khalil has asked the U.S. Supreme Court to let him continue challenging his detention and potential deportation while immigration proceedings continue.

The case tests whether federal judges have authority to order the release of immigrants before removal proceedings are completed.

Khalil’s supporters argue the government targeted him for pro-Palestinian speech, raising free speech and due process concerns.

A Supreme Court ruling could shape future challenges involving immigration detention, deportation, and First Amendment rights.

Mahmoud Khalil, the former Columbia University graduate student and activist who has been fighting his deportation, asked the Supreme Court on Monday to allow him to continue to contest his immediate detention and possible removal from the United States while his separate immigration proceedings continue to play out.

It is unclear whether the high court will choose to hear the case and when it might decide that. Khalil’s request comes during a court term already packed with high-profile cases involving President Donald Trump’s immigration agenda, such as whether the administration can send migrants to countries that are not their own.

Khalil, who is out of custody, brings his case to the Supreme Court amid a closely watched saga that has raised fundamental questions about free speech and due process rights in the United States.

“Our question is simple: Can the government weaponize immigration laws to punish someone’s speech — then tell the federal court that they have no power to step in?” Khalil said Monday during a virtual news briefing.

“If the Trump administration can punish someone for their pro-Palestine speech, this or any future administration can punish anyone for any speech, whether it’s pro-Palestine, pro-Israel or anything,” he added.

Federal immigration officials in March 2025 arrested Khalil, a legal permanent resident, on charges that he had helped foster a hostile environment for Jewish students.

Secretary of State Marco Rubio had said in a court memo that the presence of Khalil and another student would “undermine U.S. policy to combat antisemitism.”

The U.S. government alleged Khalil was a threat to national security, but his arrest prompted an outcry from people who viewed it as a targeted attack on an activist with views disliked by the government.

His arrest was the first of multiple attempted deportations of pro-Palestinian protesters last year, and he became a symbol of the Trump administration’s crackdown.

Khalil was held in detention in Louisiana for months, far from his home and his wife in New York, and he missed the birth of their first child. He was released after a federal judge barred the administration from detaining him in June 2025.

Khalil has since wound through a labyrinth of court proceedings that could either result in his remaining in the United States or his deportation to Algeria, where he is a citizen, or Syria, his native land. He has remained out of detention as appeals courts have reviewed his challenges to his arrest and deportation proceedings.

Khalil’s attorneys are asking the Supreme Court to decide a relatively narrow question with large implications: whether a federal judge had jurisdiction to order his release before the conclusion of his separate immigration proceedings.

If the high court sides with Khalil, he probably will remain out of detention. If the justices side with the federal government, Khalil could be arrested and deported.

The Trump administration has argued that the federal court’s order to release Khalil was an “unprecedented” intrusion into immigration proceedings conducted by the executive branch.

Federal judges have “no authority to micromanage ongoing removal proceedings,” Alanna T. Duong, a senior Justice Department attorney, wrote in a filing to the U.S. Appeals Court for the 3rd Circuit, where until recently Khalil’s case was being litigated.

Federal immigration agents in March 2025 arrested Khalil in his apartment building and detained him for months. A federal judge in New Jersey later ordered his release, finding that the government’s stated “foreign policy” interest in detaining and possibly deporting Khalil was probably unconstitutional.

In January, a panel on the 3rd Circuit reversed that order, making Khalil again vulnerable to deportation. It also reversed an order blocking an immigration court from considering the government’s claim that Khalil’s presence in the United States would have “potentially serious adverse foreign policy consequences.”

Khalil remained out of detention as he appealed that ruling to the full 3rd Circuit. But in May, Khalil lost that appeal, prompting his request to the Supreme Court.

His attorneys estimate that if the high court agrees to take the case, it will hear arguments in the spring and make a decision in June.

text:
Congresswoman Mary Gay Scanlon, D-5, Swarthmore, spent Thursday morning assisting Delaware County nurse Monica Ryadi as she checked in with federal immigration officials in Philadelphia.

Ryadi was detained at Los Angeles International Airport and separated from her from her husband and 3-year-old son during a trip to Disneyland in September.

Ryadi spent two weeks in a California immigration detention center after being taken into custody by Immigration and Customs Enforcement on Sept. 15. She came to the United States as a child from Indonesia and believed she was legally protected from deportation.

The Department of Homeland Security disputes the legality of being in the country, saying she overstayed her authorization to remain in the United States and was issued a final order of removal in 2010.

“She’s a solid member of our community,” says the Congresswoman.

Scanlon said they are trying to get an ankle monitor Ryadi must wear removed. Scanlon said the ankle monitor can interfere medical equipment such as MRI’s, which she uses in her work as a nurse.

“She had to check in this morning. She was a little nervous about what would happen so we went with her lawyer,” Scanlon said Thursday. “This is a woman who has permission to be here. She has been here for decades. She’s a nurse. She has work authorization, pays taxes and follows all the rules,” Scanlon said. “They picked her up and threw her in a detention center for two weeks and now they are saying they want to deport her to a third country because the court has already said she can’t be sent back to the country her family came from.”
