text:
The Manhattan Immigrant Welcome Center opened its doors in West Harlem on Sept. 29, offering services to connect immigrants with legal aid and healthcare.

The center, located at 431 W. 125th St., describes itself as a direct response to the targeting of immigrants in cities across the country by President Donald Trump’s administration. Immigration and Customs Enforcement arrests in New York City increased by 71 percent in the first 15 months of the Trump administration compared to the last 15 months of the Biden administration, according to a May 2026 audit by the mayor’s office. On Oct. 8, the shooting of Marble Hill resident Oscar Belgal provoked outrage from New Yorkers, who flooded the streets calling for the abolition of ICE.

Amid the citywide uptick in ICE presence, Manhattan Borough President Brad Hoylman-Sigal announced the opening of the Immigrant Welcome Center in late September. The center will work in tandem with various volunteer organizations to provide legal and health services, including New York Legal Assistance Group, New York Cares, and Cabrini Immigrant Services, to immigrant community members.

The center has served over 70 constituents seeking its services in its first three weeks of operation, according to Holyman-Sigal. At the ribbon cutting ceremony, he said the Welcome Center was inspired by the Queens Immigrant Welcome Center, opened by Queens Borough President Donovan Richards in summer 2021. Hoylman-Sigal noted that, in addition to being the site of the borough president’s northern Manhattan office, West Harlem is a historically immigrant-rich community.

“Harlem has historically served as a melting pot for immigrants of different cultures for decades, including Puerto Rican, West African, and other immigrant communities,” Hoylman-Sigal wrote in a statement to Spectator. “Immigrants have contributed to Harlem’s evolving cultural identity seeking opportunity and belonging, making it a meaningful place for a center dedicated to helping immigrant New Yorkers navigate life in the city.”

34 percent of West Harlem’s population is “foreign-born,” according to data collected by the U.S. Census Bureau.

“What makes our community rich in diversity is our immigrant community,” Holyman-Sigal said at the Sept. 29 ribbon cutting ceremony for the center.

In 2024, President Donald Trump promised to launch “the largest domestic deportation operation” as part of his presidential campaign,and he has specifically targeted sanctuary cities such as Los Angeles, Chicago, and New York City since assuming office. .

“In the face of Donald Trump’s lawless targeting of immigrants, Upper Manhattan has seen neighbors from across the community come together hand-in-hand to protect the rights of those most vulnerable,” City Council Majority Leader Shaun Abreu, CC ’14, wrote in the press release.

Over the summer, the New York Immigration Coalition reported an increase in ICE presence in northern Manhattan, including the neighborhoods of Washington Heights and Inwood. Federal agents have been reported as impersonating construction workers and police officers in order to perform arrests.

“Manhattan is central to ICE’s campaign and presence in the City,” Hoylman-Sigal wrote in a statement to Spectator.

New York Legal Assistance Group, one of the organizations which will partner with the center, is a nonprofit organization that provides free civil legal assistance to New Yorkers in need. The organization will bring its “Mobile Legal Help Clinic” van to the center monthly to provide residents with “information, resources, and access to justice,” according to Lisa Rivera, the organization’s CEO and president. The services of the Manhattan Immigration Welcome Center are not limited to recent immigrants.

“We are proud to forge this vital partnership and ultimately make legal services accessible whether someone arrived yesterday or over a decade ago,” Rivera wrote in a statement to Spectator.

For Hoylman-Sigal, the center aims to aid immigrants navigating social service systems.

“With so many rules shifting, families need someone who can give them accurate answers in their language about their rights and which resources are available to them,” the borough president wrote. “Our staff can help eligible New Yorkers enroll in social services resources such as food assistance and in NYC Care, which provides free to low-cost medical care regardless of immigration status.”

Javier Ramirez Baron, executive director of Cabrini Immigrant Services, a nonprofit that provides free legal and social services to immigrants across New York City, believes that the Welcome Center is timely and significant.

“Especially for the time that we live in right now, and in my opinion, our community living here, the community needs to hear from the elected officials that they are working with,” Ramirez Baron said.

According to Ramirez Baron, Cabrini has a history of working in collaboration with the borough president’s office, but the recent partnership between the Welcome Center and his offices has brought “more referrals, especially for people who want to have a lawyer or a creditory representative to review the cases.”

“I’m proud that so many immigrant New Yorkers already know about our Immigrant Welcome Center, and encourage all New Yorkers to take advantage of the free legal, casework, and social services assistance our office can provide,” Hoylman-Sigal wrote.

Deputy Editor Franka Etkin can be contacted at franka.etkin@columbiaspectator.com. Follow Spectator on X @ColumbiaSpec.

The organizations are holding a press conference today at LULAC Headquarters, 150 W. Parker, fifth floor, to formally declare a “State of Emergency” in response to a series of incidents involving ICE that they say have caused irreparable harm to immigrant families and the broader community.

Two young girls left alone after mother detained

The girls were present at the press conference and made themselves available for interviews.

Calls for accountability following death, injury of immigrants

“After the killing of Lorenzo Salgado Araujo by ICE this summer, the inhumane treatment continues without any sign of accountability or of recognizing the consequences of their unconstitutional actions and the horrendous suffering on families and our communities,” organizers said in a statement.

text:
By The Associated Press

WASHINGTON (AP) — Palestinian activist Mahmoud Khalil asked the Supreme Court on Monday to let federal judges quickly determine the legality of immigration-related detentions so that people cannot be held for months or years without judicial oversight.

In papers filed with the high court, Khalil asked it to overturn a ruling earlier this year by the 3rd U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals in Philadelphia that found federal courts do not have jurisdiction to review the legality of the detentions until immigration courts had fully considered each case.

Khalil, a lawful permanent U.S. resident, was detained by immigration authorities last year because of his participation in pro-Palestinian demonstrations at Columbia University in the spring of 2024.

The U.S. government argued at the time that Khalil’s presence in the U.S. was harmful to the country’s foreign policy interests.

As a result, the former Columbia graduate student spent over three months in detention before a federal judge in New Jersey ordered him freed after finding that the federal government had acted unconstitutionally.

Khalil told a remote news conference Monday that the appeal was “bigger than just my ability to stay here.” He said he wanted to ensure that thousands of immigrants, documented or not, can challenge the Trump administration’s “unlawful” attempts to stop protected speech.

He said the administration knows “all too well its baseless allegations and smears against me cannot survive the slightest scrutiny in federal courts,” so it wants to channel it into “kangaroo” immigration courts where it can control the outcome.

In a statement Monday, the U.S. Department of Homeland Security said: “It is a privilege to be granted a visa or green card to live and study in the United States of America. The Trump Administration acted well within its statutory and constitutional authority with respect to Khalil, as it does with any alien who advocates for violence, glorifies and supports terrorists, harasses Jews, and damages property. We would encourage him to use the CBP Home app and self-deport.”

The 3rd Circuit has put its ruling on hold so that Khalil could appeal to the Supreme Court. He remains free.

Although the Supreme Court typically agrees to grant only a small percentage of appeals requests, the U.S. government has already asked the high court to overturn a federal appeals court decision that upheld a judge’s decision to release Georgetown University scholar Badar Khan Suri. That ruling by the 4th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals in Richmond, Virginia, directly conflicted with the 3rd Circuit decision in the Khalil case.

Sometimes, conflicting appeals court rulings can increase the chances that the Supreme Court agrees to hear a case. If it does, oral arguments before the justices would likely occur sometime next year.

text:
(Hartford, CT) – Attorney General William Tong, as part of a coalition of 22 attorneys general filed an amicus brief in the U.S. Court of Appeals for the D.C. Circuit in support of litigation challenging the U.S. Department of Homeland Security’s (DHS) policy and practice of conducting unlawful warrantless civil immigration arrests.

Under federal law, immigration officers conducting warrantless civil immigration arrests must have probable cause to believe that an individual is unlawfully present in the United States and is likely to escape before a warrant can be obtained. However, DHS officers routinely carry out warrantless arrests without determining if the individual is an escape risk. The brief highlights the widespread harms that unlawful immigration enforcement practices have inflicted on communities across the country, including in Connecticut.

“Trump said he was going to deport violent criminals. Instead, he’s terrorizing communities with error-riddled warrantless and meritless arrests that have separated parents from children and crippled local businesses. His hyper-aggressive, rushed, and chaotic actions have caused needless deaths and injuries. There is a reason basic due process exists in the United States of America, and Trump needs to learn to follow the law,” said Attorney General Tong.

Across the country, federal immigration agents have escalated their enforcement activities, disrupting communities and undermining public health, safety, education, and local economies. Connecticut has seen these harms firsthand, as aggressive immigration enforcement tactics have kept students out of school, disrupted agricultural work, discouraged people from seeking medical care, undermined families’ financial stability, and weakened the relationship between immigrant communities and local law enforcement. Federal agents’ use of ski masks, dark sunglasses, plainclothes, and unmarked vehicles, and refusals to identify themselves while carrying out operations, has further contributed to fear and uncertainty in affected communities.

Today’s brief was filed in Escobar-Molina v. DHS, a case challenging DHS’s policy and practice of conducting unlawful warrantless civil immigration arrests in the District of Columbia. On December 2, 2025, the U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia granted in part a motion for a preliminary injunction.

In filing the brief, Attorney General Tong joins the attorneys general of Arizona, California, Colorado, Delaware, District of Columbia, Hawaii, Illinois, Maine, Maryland, Massachusetts, Michigan, Minnesota, Nevada, New Jersey, New Mexico, New York, Oregon, Rhode Island, Vermont, Virginia, and Washington.

text:
BURLINGTON, Vt. (WCAX) - Seven clergy members faced a judge Tuesday after they were arrested during an ICE protest in Williston last month.

Police say the group of clergy blockaded the door inside the White Cap Business Park in Williston on September 4. Part of the facility is leased to the Department of Homeland Security and the protesters refused to leave.

Rev. Karen Johnston of the First Unitarian Universalist Society of Burlington says she believes it’s her duty to stand up for migrants in the wake of the Trump administration’s increased immigration enforcement. “It is part of my pastoral, my clerical duties as an ordained clergy person to make sure that we stand for justice and protect the most vulnerable,” she said.

In total, seven clergy members pleaded not guilty Tuesday to unlawful trespass charges brought by the Vermont Attorney General’s Office.

“They were in court because our state attorney general decided to apply finite resources to prosecute these people of conscience who were protesting ICE’s brutality and racial profiling,” defense attorney Robert Appel said.

The Vermont State Police sent the charges straight to the AG after Chittenden County State’s Attorney Sarah George declined to prosecute similar arrests.

Attorney General Charity Clark released a statement last month saying she has a responsibility to uphold the law and she can’t apply the law based on whether she supports a political cause.

All seven clergy members were released on conditions. That includes not being allowed back on the Williston DHS property unless they’re there for religious reasons.

They also cannot contact the manager of White Cap Industrial Park, where the facility is located.

authors: ALEXX ALTMAN-DEVILBISS | The National News Desk, ALEXX ALTMAN-DEVILBISS, The National News Desk
description:
California officials are calling for an investigation after a man was reportedly injured while being detained by federal immigration agents in Long Beach over the weekend.
Long Beach Mayor Rex Richardson said he filed a formal complaint with the Department of Homeland Security, demanding accountability for the agents’ actions.
Richardson called on DHS and ICE to remove the agents involved from field enforcement duties while an independent investigation is conducted.
“Long Beach will not stay silent when our neighbors are harmed.
Federal agents also denied that its officers hit a person riding a bike.
text:
California officials are calling for an investigation after a man was reportedly injured while being detained by federal immigration agents in Long Beach over the weekend.

In a video shared by StopICE.net, agents appear to pin the man against a curb as he yells for help and repeatedly says his arm is broken.

Long Beach Mayor Rex Richardson said he filed a formal complaint with the Department of Homeland Security, demanding accountability for the agents’ actions. Richardson identified the man as Ricardo Gonzalez, a “Long Beach resident, father, and former City employee.”

The complaint alleges Gonzalez was repeatedly tased, forcibly restrained and seriously injured during Saturday’s incident. Richardson called on DHS and ICE to remove the agents involved from field enforcement duties while an independent investigation is conducted.

“Long Beach will not stay silent when our neighbors are harmed. A federal badge is not a license to brutalize people or disregard their constitutional rights,” Richardson wrote on Facebook. “If you are entrusted with enforcing the law, you must answer to it.”

Long Beach police officers who responded to the scene said they saw “a large group disturbance” involving ICE agents and found a handcuffed man who was bleeding, according to a police department release.

Officers took him to a nearby fire station, removed his handcuffs and transported him to a hospital, police said.

LBPD said ICE called for emergency assistance because of vehicle vandalism and a person needing medical aid. The department said its officers found a handcuffed, bleeding man and took him to a nearby fire station before he was transported to a hospital. The department said its officers were not involved in immigration enforcement and made no arrests.

ICE described the encounter as a targeted operation to arrest what it called an “at-large criminal illegal alien.” The agency said demonstrators tried to impede the operation, threaten officers and damage government vehicles despite being given lawful commands. ICE said its officers followed their training and used the minimum amount of force necessary.

Federal agents also denied that its officers hit a person riding a bike. According to officials, the man was arrested after smashing the mirror of a government vehicle, and that resisting arrest can result in injury. ICE said he was transferred to local police custody and that it is investigating potential charges over the vehicle damage.

The agency cited increases in assaults, vehicle attacks and death threats against law enforcement and said violence and efforts to obstruct officers must end.

text:
Security camera footage obtained by the Watchdog shows the moment an ICE agent uses his unmarked vehicle as a weapon to stop Ricardo Gonzalez.

Gonzalez, a U.S. citizen, is seen riding an e-bike and turning left onto a one-way street. Then, an ICE vehicle can be seen speeding down the street in the wrong direction and striking Gonzalez.

The agent exits his vehicle and immediately draws a weapon before approaching Gonzalez and yelling for him to "get on the ground."

"Fuck you. You hit me with your fucking car," Gonzalez shouts back. "I'm a fucking U.S. citizen."

View this post on Instagram

A post shared by Long Beach Watchdog (@lbwatchdog)

The incident, originally reported by the Watchdog Sunday, occurred on Ellis Street at Locust Avenue in North Long Beach at noon on Saturday, according to the video timestamp.

Gonzalez’s daughter Leslie on Monday told the Watchdog her dad is “doing well and still healing.”

“We can see him getting better slowly,” she said in a text message.

According to Leslie, after the agent hit her dad with the vehicle, they tased him twice. Video taken by Sherman Austin, founder of stopice.net, shows agents handcuffing Ricardo while he lays face down in the gutter yelling that his arm is broken.

Leslie organized the GoFundMe to raise money to cover the cost of Ricardo’s hospital bills as well as any legal expenses that may arise as a result of the incident. As of 12:30 Monday, the campaign had received $16,600 in donations, exceeding its initial goal of $6,500.

Gonzalez, 40, is a U.S. citizen born in Hanford, CA, Leslie told the Watchdog. For the past eight or so years, Gonzalez worked for the City of Long Beach — first in the health department and then the utilities department, a position he left in September, she said.

In a statement to the Watchdog Sunday, Mayor Rex Richardson said he was “outraged” by the incident.

“Federal immigration agents are not above the law,” Richardson wrote. “These aggressive enforcement tactics are creating fear and putting our residents at risk. This is unacceptable, and it must stop.”

Richardson said he is “demanding answers” from the Department of Homeland Security and working with congressional representatives to “seek transparency and accountability.”

In a post on X Sunday, Rep. Robert Garcia said the incident is “horrific and should concern not just our community but the whole country.”

“I’m proud of the neighbors who documented and stood up for the family being terrorized by ICE,” Garcia, the former mayor of Long Beach, wrote. “Donald Trump and his inhumane and illegal deportation machine must be stopped. Long Beach stands with our community and our immigrant families. ICE is not welcome in Long Beach. Abolish ICE.”

The Department of Homeland Security has not responded to questions from the Watchdog.

Numerous videos show LBPD vehicles blocking streets, with numerous people asking why the police department is assisting in a federal immigration operation, which is against city and state law.

The department released a statement clarifying its presence, saying ICE personnel “requested emergency assistance from LBPD and LBFD due to vehicle vandalism taking place and a subject in need of medical aid.”

According to the department, an officer located Gonzalez, handcuffed and bleeding. Fire department personnel were unable to reach the scene due to trash cans — placed there by residents to obstruct federal vehicles — blocking the street, so LBPD officers transported Ricardo to a nearby fire station, where they removed the handcuffs.

LBFD personnel then took Ricardo to a local hospital.

“LBPD left the area and some ICE agents followed LBPD personnel to a secure parking lot in the police station,” the department continued. “The ICE agents were subsequently directed to leave the station.”

The department said it made no arrests and added that, while it does not assist in immigration enforcement, it also “cannot legally obstruct or interfere with federal enforcement operations.”

Many residents do not accept the department’s explanation, saying that crowd control during federal immigration operations still constitutes assisting ICE.

“What the heck, [Long Beach]?” one commenter wrote. “Why are you collaborating with ICE terrorizing the neighborhoods?"

text:
Pro-Palestine activist Mahmoud Khalil has petitioned the United States Supreme Court to review a court ruling that could pave the way for his re-arrest and deportation.

On Monday, Khalil’s lawyers filed an emergency application to the high court, seeking an immediate stay of a decision from Philadelphia’s 3rd Circuit Court of Appeals.

Recommended Stories

list 2 of 4Mahmoud Khalil calls for deportation to be halted in light of new evidence

list 3 of 4Why is pro-Palestinian activist Mahmoud Khalil suing Columbia University?

list 4 of 4US court hands Trump victory against pro-Palestine activist Mahmoud Khalil

end of list

That court had ruled that federal law should have prohibited lower courts from ordering Khalil’s release from immigration detention in June 2025.

Instead, the appeals court said that Khalil’s detention should have been weighed first in an immigration court — a system overseen by the executive branch of the US government — and not in district court, which is part of the judicial branch.

In March 2025, Khalil became the first student protester known to be targeted for his pro-Palestinian views under the second administration of President Donald Trump.

A permanent US resident and former Columbia University graduate student, Khalil was arrested inside the student housing complex where he lived with his wife, a US citizen.

The push to deport Khalil has become a flashpoint in the debate over free speech on US campuses.

His petition to the Supreme Court could result in a major legal showdown that determines whether federal courts can intervene when noncitizens face retaliatory detention for speech protected under the First Amendment of the US Constitution.

Khalil’s lawyers have asked the Supreme Court to rule that noncitizens do indeed have the right to sue if immigration officials detain them as a reprisal for exercising free speech.

“If the Trump administration can punish someone for their pro-Palestine speech, this or any future administration can punish anyone for any speech,” Khalil said during a news conference on Monday.

Trump campaigned for re-election in 2024 in part on a pledge to crack down on the pro-Palestinian student protest movement, which had erupted in 2023.

Columbia University in New York became an epicentre for such activism. Khalil, who was born in a Palestinian refugee camp in Syria, had served as a spokesperson for the protest groups.

The Trump administration, however, has characterised pro-Palestinian activism as a threat to US foreign policy interests. It has argued it has the legal right to deport noncitizens who engage in such protests as a result.

After his arrest, Khalil was quickly moved to immigration detention centres in New Jersey, then Louisiana, where he remained in custody for more than three months.

Khalil faces deportation to Algeria or Syria if the 3rd Circuit Court’s decision holds.

In May, the 3rd Circuit narrowly voted six-to-five against reconsidering his case, but its decision will not go into effect until Khalil has exhausted his appeals.

He has fought his deportation both in the immigration court system and in the federal district court system, where he has filed a habeas corpus case. Both cases remain ongoing.

In April, the Board of Immigration Appeals denied his appeal in the immigration court system and issued a final order of removal in his case.

On Monday, faculty and staff at Columbia University held a silent vigil outside one of the school’s gates to protest what they described as “abducted students”, taken by Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE).

Placards with portraits of Khalil and fellow student protester Mohsen Mahdawi, among others, were hoisted into the air. Demonstrators called for solidarity with the students facing deportation and pushed for Columbia University to reopen its gates to the public after their closure during the protest movement.

text:
U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement arrests have spiked this year in Butler County, where the agency is working in partnership with the sheriff's office. But instead of deporting criminals, the construction industry says they're arresting longtime workers with no criminal record, disrupting home building and driving up costs.

Deputies from the Butler County Sheriff's Office have joined ICE agents in arresting immigrants as part of what's called a 287(g) cooperation agreement.

"If you're here illegally, you need to come to our country legally," said Butler County Sheriff Slupe. "For those that choose not to self-deport, enforcement is an opportunity to get these illegal immigrants back to their country."

Since November, the sheriff's deputies have assisted ICE in arresting 150 immigrants in Butler County — many of them taken from construction sites. Recently, representatives of those building and construction firms met with the sheriff complaining that longtime workers, some here as long as 10 or 20 years, are being detained and deported, disrupting the industry.

"Our industry relies on immigration labor," said Jim Eichenlaub, the Builders Association of Metropolitan Pittsburgh's executive director, whom construction companies designated as their spokesperson. "Let them alone, let them work, let them be gainful contributors to our society."

The construction companies working in Butler County declined to be interviewed but privately say ICE agents surveil job sites and randomly check papers of their workers, oftentimes following them home and pulling them over for alleged traffic infractions. They say ICE enforcement is highest in Butler County because of its partnership with Slupe, resulting in a climate of fear.

"There are raids coming onto construction sites, ICE enforcement teams coming onto the sites, pulling folks out of their job duties, checking papers," Eichenlaub said.

"Those who are even here legally are fearful of going out for fear that they're going to get swept up and detained," he added.

To work with federal agents, the sheriff has designated 13 deputies, and the Department of Homeland Security pays his office $15,000 a quarter for each one — a total of $780,000 a year — which Slupe says goes to the purchase of information technology upgrades and new equipment like language translators.

In a statement to KDKA, the Department of Homeland Security said through these partnerships, "ICE is not arresting people here legally. We are targeting the worst of the worst of the worst criminal illegal aliens. If we do encounter someone illegally in the country, we will arrest them. We do not pick and choose which laws to enforce."

According to KDKA's analysis of data from the Deportation Data Project, there have been 231 total ICE arrests in Butler County this year and last. Thirty are listed as convicted criminals, 23 are listed as having pending criminal charges, but 178 are listed just as immigration violations.

Slupe concedes he has mixed feelings about arresting someone with no criminal record who has been working here for years.

"Yeah, I'm a human being," Slupe said. "I have feelings. I get it. But unfortunately, if they're here illegally, something needs to be made right."

"I do empathize with them, I really do," he added. "But at the end of the day, Congress needs to work on a law better than what we have maybe."

The builders association supports something called the Dignity Act — a new bipartisan bill that would grant protection to workers who entered the country before the major influx during the Biden administration, whether they came in legally or not.

"If everyone's really serious about the affordability of housing, they have to consider that labor and immigration reform is a key component of that," Eichenlaub said. "It's extending our timeframes, it's driving up costs and it's disrupting the industry."

In working with ICE, Slupe concedes he sometimes has mixed feelings, but until the law changes, he says he will continue to help ICE enforce it.

title: Trump's obsession with Ilhan Omar has reached a dangerous new level - The Guardian
description:
What do you think it is about Ilhan Omar, exactly, that seems to get under Donald Trump’s tangerine-tinted skin?
However, the extent of his animus towards Omar, the first Somali American in Congress, suggests there’s more to it.
The president has plenty of enemies, but few have been attacked as ferociously and consistently over the years as Omar.
Now Trump’s obsession with Omar has reached a dangerous new level.
“Certainly, if the evidence points that way, that could happen,” Tom Homan, Trump’s “border czar”, told Fox News over the weekend when asked about Omar being deported.
text:
What do you think it is about Ilhan Omar, exactly, that seems to get under Donald Trump’s tangerine-tinted skin? The president has claimed he has a problem with the progressive Democratic congresswoman because she is “unpatriotic” to the US and “disrespectful … to Israel”. However, the extent of his animus towards Omar, the first Somali American in Congress, suggests there’s more to it. Trump has insisted he is “the least racist person there is anywhere in the world”, so I’m sure it has nothing to do with the fact that she’s brown and Muslim. Truly, it’s a mystery.

Whatever the reason, Trump’s not a fan. The president has plenty of enemies, but few have been attacked as ferociously and consistently over the years as Omar. He’s called her “garbage”, among other nasty names, suggested (without evidence) that she married her brother, and said she “should be thrown the hell out of our country”. His supporters have echoed his calls to deport Omar, who fled war-torn Somalia as a child and became a naturalised US citizen at 17.

Now Trump’s obsession with Omar has reached a dangerous new level. Trump isn’t just throwing out insults any more; his administration seems intent on stripping the congresswoman of her US citizenship and deporting her. Last Monday, 22 days before the November midterms in which Omar is seeking re-election, federal agents raided her house in Washington DC. Her phone was seized and grand jury subpoenas were reportedly issued to some of her relatives as part of an investigation concerning her immigration paperwork. Trump, by the way, denied any involvement. Just a curious coincidence that one of his biggest nemeses is now being treated like a criminal.

As House Democratic leaders have said, the raid on Omar’s house “raises serious questions about the continued corrupt weaponisation of the federal government against Donald Trump’s adversaries”. But it also raises another question: is this “just” a stunt designed to embarrass and intimidate Omar before the midterms? Or is there a real possibility that the congresswoman could be denaturalised and deported?

“Certainly, if the evidence points that way, that could happen,” Tom Homan, Trump’s “border czar”, told Fox News over the weekend when asked about Omar being deported. “We’ll let the evidence lead where it leads, but she’ll be held to the same standard you and I are held: if she violated the law, then she’ll be held accountable,” Homan added.

Oh, please. I know the Mar-a-Lago set are big on Botox, but I can’t believe Homan was able to preach about accountability with a straight face. Not many people are convicted of 34 felonies and face no jail time. Trump, however, is in the White House rather than prison because the supreme court’s conservative majority (which he helped create) found that former presidents are entitled to a degree of immunity from criminal prosecution.

The US government has every right to uphold its immigration laws, but its appetite seems to vary considerably depending on the person. If Homan really is so keen on accountability, may I suggest he take a look at the Trump megadonor Elon Musk? The tech mogul’s brother, Kimbal Musk, has publicly joked about the fact that the brothers briefly worked in the US without proper documentation in the 1990s. (Elon said it was a “grey area”.) And then there’s Melania Trump: in 2016, the Associated Press reported the first lady was paid for 10 modelling jobs in the US before she had legal permission to work in the country. (Melania has denied ever violating the terms of her immigration status.)

Omar was just a teenager when her father filled out the paperwork that led to them both being naturalised. I obviously have no idea if there were any errors in that. But I can tell you that this “investigation” is not about accountability. It is a terrifying abuse of power that reflects the way in which the Trump administration is weaponising the immigration system to stamp out dissent. We’ve already seen Trump deport noncitizen student activists to crack down on pro-Palestinian speech. Now he’s applying that strategy to Omar, a sitting congresswoman. As Barack Obama warned at the weekend, “If this becomes the new normal, there’s no reason to believe it will stop with her.” Indeed it won’t; Trump is just getting started.

Arwa Mahdawi is a Guardian columnist

title: Attorney General Bonta Supports Litigation Challenging Unlawful Immigration Arrests
description:
Circuit in support of litigation challenging the U.S. Department of Homeland Security’s (DHS) policy and practice of conducting unlawful warrantless civil immigration arrests.
The brief highlights the widespread harms that unlawful immigration enforcement practices have inflicted on communities across the country, including in California.
“The Trump Administration has engaged in an aggressive, militaristic mass deportation program with no regard for people’s humanity and dignity,” said Attorney General Bonta.
Attorney General Bonta has consistently fought against unlawful federal immigration enforcement practices across the country.
In filing the brief, Attorney General Bonta, District of Columbia Attorney General Brian Schwalb, and Colorado Attorney General Phil Weiser lead the attorneys general of Arizona, Connecticut, Delaware, Hawaii, Illinois, Maine, Maryland, Massachusetts, Michigan, Minnesota, Nevada, New Jersey, New Mexico, New York, Oregon, Rhode Island, Vermont, Virginia, and Washington.
text:
OAKLAND — California Attorney General Rob Bonta today co-led a multistate coalition in filing an amicus brief in the U.S. Court of Appeals for the D.C. Circuit in support of litigation challenging the U.S. Department of Homeland Security’s (DHS) policy and practice of conducting unlawful warrantless civil immigration arrests. Under federal law, immigration officers conducting warrantless civil immigration arrests must have probable cause to believe that an individual is unlawfully present in the United States and is likely to escape before a warrant can be obtained. However, DHS officers routinely carry out warrantless arrests without determining if the individual is an escape risk. The brief highlights the widespread harms that unlawful immigration enforcement practices have inflicted on communities across the country, including in California.

“The Trump Administration has engaged in an aggressive, militaristic mass deportation program with no regard for people’s humanity and dignity,” said Attorney General Bonta. “Federal immigration agents are arresting people without the requisite probable cause determination, often while masked, wearing armor, and carrying lethal weapons. California will not stand by while this Administration creates fear in our immigrant communities. We will continue to fight back, defend our neighbors, and stand up for the rights and dignity of every person.”

Across the country, federal immigration agents have escalated their enforcement activities, disrupting communities and undermining public health, safety, education, and local economies. California has seen these harms firsthand, as aggressive immigration enforcement tactics have kept students out of school, disrupted agricultural work, discouraged people from seeking medical care, undermined families’ financial stability, and weakened the relationship between immigrant communities and local law enforcement. Federal agents’ use of ski masks, dark sunglasses, plainclothes, and unmarked vehicles, and refusals to identify themselves while carrying out operations, has further contributed to fear and uncertainty in affected communities.

Today’s brief was filed in Escobar-Molina v. DHS, a case challenging DHS’s policy and practice of conducting unlawful warrantless civil immigration arrests in the District of Columbia. On December 2, 2025, the U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia granted in part a motion for a preliminary injunction.

Attorney General Bonta has consistently fought against unlawful federal immigration enforcement practices across the country. Earlier this month, he filed a lawsuit challenging the Trump Administration’s policy and practice of carrying out civil immigration enforcement in and around state courthouses. He also supported challenges to unlawful federal immigration enforcement practices in several cases:

United Farm Workers v. Noem: He filed an amicus brief in support of a challenge to DHS’s “Operation Return to Sender” in Kern County, where roving patrols and warrantless arrests kept children out of school and workers at home.

Vasquez Perdomo v. Noem: He led a multistate coalition in filing an amicus brief challenging suspicionless stops during “Operation at Large” in Los Angeles, which disrupted local businesses and led to the cancellation of community events.

Ramirez Ovanda v. Mullins: He co-led a multistate brief in support of plaintiffs challenging ICE’s policy and practice of carrying out unlawful warrantless arrests in Colorado.

In filing the brief, Attorney General Bonta, District of Columbia Attorney General Brian Schwalb, and Colorado Attorney General Phil Weiser lead the attorneys general of Arizona, Connecticut, Delaware, Hawaii, Illinois, Maine, Maryland, Massachusetts, Michigan, Minnesota, Nevada, New Jersey, New Mexico, New York, Oregon, Rhode Island, Vermont, Virginia, and Washington.

text:
Texas Border Business

By Valentina Guerra-Gonzalez

A teenage kid wakes up and steps out of his bedroom. His dad tells him he’s home from work on an “extended leave.” But the kid knows there’s more to it. He tells his parents his stomach hurts, but both say going to the doctor is too risky. So he goes to the door and into his family’s car, whose AC has been broken for the past few months. The 100-degree sun passes through the windows, and he prays another part won’t break down. His family can’t afford another loss. Since the 2026 USMCA renewal negotiations stalled, families living along the U.S.-Mexico border have felt such rampant consequences.

The renewal negotiations began in July 2026, prompting the U.S. to decline to extend the deal. The United States and Mexico face questions about market access, tariffs, and immigration; the negotiations’ greater impact is on border communities. As the stalemate continues, the U.S. and Mexico should recognize the effects of this ongoing economic and political uncertainty on an area defined by both cultures and sustained by bilateral trade and tourism.

A major tension surrounding the current renewal is the U.S. Section 232 national security tariff. In March 2025, the Trump administration imposed a 25% tariff, and by June 2025, the steel and aluminum tariff had risen to 50%. From Mexico’s perspective, this is seen as a threat to free trade with its largest market, the United States. On the other hand, the U.S. views this as a way to promote national security and protect domestic producers and manufacturers. While both countries aim to address their economic priorities, they are ignoring the interconnected trade that supports border communities. This places financial burdens on consumers, especially those who already struggle to afford daily necessities and may now be unable to afford rising auto repair prices.

In this stalemate, the U.S. also needs to recognize the dependence U.S. consumers have on Mexico’s market. Because of Mexico’s ideal climate for produce, most U.S. grocery stores carry brands like “Avocados from Mexico” and “Driscoll” strawberries. These brands, along with other natural produce, are grown or manufactured in Mexico, making them highly dependent on stable U.S.-Mexico trade and underscoring the countries’ interconnected dynamic. With the stalemate and continuing tensions, the possibility of tariff increases places another financial burden on consumers. If an agreement fails to preserve tariff-free agricultural trade, grocery prices would rise even higher, and some may no longer be able to afford this produce.

Border cities also serve as manufacturing hubs for U.S.-Mexico trade, with maquiladoras, or factories, located in northern Mexico and employing both U.S. and Mexican workers. Their low-cost labor and proximity to the U.S. and Mexico allow the United States to manufacture its products in these places and export them across the border, both domestically and internationally. Maquiladoras employ thousands of Mexican and U.S. workers, who cross the border every day to work as managers, specialists, or engineers. The stalemate, however, threatens the jobs of these workers. Amid current trade instability, foreign businesses avoid investing in these maquiladoras because the future market remains uncertain. Without foreign business investments, maquiladoras could face shutdowns, and workers from both sides of the border could lose their jobs.

The Trump administration’s immigration policies have also complicated the treaty’s socio-political negotiations. Many people immigrate to the U.S. hoping to start anew and find jobs in transportation, agriculture, and maintenance, which support American facilities that produce goods for trade. However, since Trump’s first presidential campaign in 2015, he has advocated stricter policies toward immigrants, including the construction of a border wall, and has expanded the authority of government agencies, such as the Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE).

Stricter border security enforcement has also led to longer inspections of trade, causing delays and additional costs for businesses. Furthermore, it has led to an increasing number of immigrant detentions. Immigrant workers’ jobs are a pillar of the U.S. economy and contribute to the supply chain that the U.S. economy runs on. Without them, manufacturing and production industries face the risk of losing workers, which would disrupt the production of goods and hinder a smooth U.S.-Mexico trade relationship.

Trump’s administration’s security measures at the border have already strained U.S.-Mexico relations. In January 2025, he declared a national emergency on the southern border, allowing the deployment of military personnel to the border. In February 2025, he issued Executive Order 14194 titled “Imposing Duties To Address the Situation at Our Southern Border.” While some goods were negotiated to receive protections under the USMCA, imported goods from Mexico received an additional 25% tariff. Mexico’s president, Claudia Sheinbaum, has pushed for cooperation by providing humanitarian aid to those turned away at the border or sent back to Mexico. Still, the Trump administration persists in asserting that Mexico’s government is weakly handling illegal immigration, thereby increasing drug trafficking. These events have heightened tensions ahead of USMCA renegotiations and are factors in the continuing stalemate. As this review remains unresolved, free trade becomes more uncertain, and the border economy faces greater threats.

It is essential for both countries to understand the interconnected lives of those at the border, whose stability now rests in the hands of negotiators in Washington and Mexico City. As the review continues, Mexico must reduce its dependence on the U.S. market while continuing to advocate for free trade across North America. Similarly, the United States must recognize its dependence on Mexico for many goods. Ultimately, given both countries’ geographic proximity and integrated communities, the border economy and dynamics should be the top priority. If both administrations recognize their mutual reliance and see that the stalemate is destabilizing trade and affecting the daily lives of their citizens, an agreement that prioritizes people and protects national sovereignty is possible.

Written by Valentina Guerra-Gonzalez, a 17-year-old senior at St. Andrew’s Episcopal School in Austin, Texas, and a former Rio Grande Valley resident whose interest in U.S.–Mexico relations inspired her research on the economic challenges facing border communities.

text:
As federal immigration authorities continue their nationwide enforcement campaign, state-held data — including driver’s license records and license plate information — has become a key tool. But laws in some states intended to restrict federal access to that information fall short of preventing it, according to a new report.

The report from the University of Washington examined four methods by which federal immigration agencies can obtain state DMV data: direct database access, the Nlets interstate law enforcement network, data brokers and local law enforcement agencies. Researchers also examined patterns of immigration arrests in Maryland, Minnesota, New York and Washington — all states that have enacted some type of law geared toward restricting this type of sharing.

However, the report found that immigration agents with Immigration and Customs Enforcement and Customs and Border Protection continue to query state-held vehicle data in these states, with some searches linked to immigration arrests.

Angelina Godoy, a professor at the University of Washington and director of its Center for Human Rights, said that though these pathways are established and widely used, they’re often unknown to the state and local administrators of certain public data, such as DMVs or state comptroller offices.

“I think that in many cases, state and local leaders may even be unaware that this is happening, and it’s far too late for them to be waking up to it. But better to wake up today than tomorrow,” she said.

The researchers pointed out that while public awareness efforts about the technologies powering immigration enforcement — such as Flock Safety’s automated license plate readers — are generating deserved scrutiny, the use of less-visible systems such as Nlets and state DMV databases can facilitate immigration enforcement with equally serious consequences, despite receiving far less public attention.

Of particular concern is the Nlets system, Godoy said, which is a nonprofit computer network that allows state, local, federal and international law enforcement agencies to share criminal justice and public safety data. It appears to be the most common pathway used by federal authorities, she said. Agents can enter or scan a license plate in Nlets, and the issuing state’s DMV returns vehicle registration data, including the registered owner’s name, which agents can then cross-check against immigration databases.

Though states can block queries of their own data from certain federal agencies, as Washington did for ICE, Godoy noted that political will to extend restrictions to other agencies such as Border Patrol varies from local agency to agency. And, restricting one route may shift use to another.

“States that have, for the most part, relatively recently decided to open pathways for noncitizens to obtain driver’s licenses or to register their vehicles, they’ve done that out of an interest of being more inclusive or keeping roads safer,” she told StateScoop. “But I think in many cases, they did so without realizing all the various pathways through which federal immigration agencies can obtain folks’ data through the Department of Motor Vehicles, and the way in which that access can then be sort of weaponized against communities, essentially.”

Restricting the use of state-held data for immigration enforcement is a public safety and civil rights issue, the researchers argued in the report. Aggressive traffic stops made by ICE have resulted in injuries and deaths, and safeguards against federal agencies accessing this data — which can be perceived as seemingly routine — can help initiate an enforcement encounter with potentially deadly consequences.

To establish the holes in the law, the researchers documented examples in four states by starting with known immigration arrests and using public-records requests to trace preceding DMV queries. Godoy said the records often showed a query was followed by an arrest within minutes. The total number of arrests cannot be quantified, she said, and many states including Massachusetts and California denied the records requests researchers made to the query records. These state denials and additional missing query records prevent a reliable total count, Godoy said, adding that the findings should not be read as limited to those four states.

In fact, she called the data-sharing problem “widespread.”

“They’re not only arresting people who are undocumented, but people who are maybe on a student visa, or have a work permit, or are in all different stages of the immigration process,” Godoy said. “And this all takes place just within seconds that they get a response to their query, and in minutes, they make a determination about whether they’re going to arrest the person or not.”

While vendor-contract limits, downstream-use audits, and public audit results can help stop some access to state-held data, Godoy warned they may fail when agencies require their data vendors to anonymize who conducts the searches for security purposes.

Another conundrum is that who has authority to safeguard this data varies by method of access and the state individually; the DMV holds the data, governors typically direct restrictions, and legislatures can require safeguards.

Despite these policy conversations and questions of authority on data, Godoy hopes that the “human safety piece” is not lost.

“There’s real cases — and the report highlights many of them — of both families being separated as a result of these mechanisms, but then also the violence that we’re seeing now in ICE enforcement,” Godoy said. “It was really striking to me when we undertook this research that while we’re hearing a lot about the ICE shootings… one of the things that’s often lost in those stories is that the overwhelming majority of those shootings are taking place precisely in these traffic stop arrests.

“So, the DMV data is really important,” she continued, “and the rapid way in which it’s winding up in their hands while they’re still at the wheel performing these high-risk operations, and then suddenly surrounding a car in ways that have caused crashes, let alone shootings, is really worrisome.”

title: Security camera footage shows immigration enforcement in San Francisco's SoMa - KTVU
description:
Security camera video shows immigration enforcement in San Francisco Monday morning.
"San Francisco law enforcement does not participate in federal civil immigration enforcement, and our city stands with our immigrant communities," Lurie wrote.
The San Francisco Police Department reiterated this message when we reached out to them.
If anyone is having an interaction with federal immigration enforcement and needs immediate legal support, that is the number they should call, he said.

text:
Security camera video shows immigration enforcement in San Francisco Monday morning. Mayor Daniel Lurie says his office has been in contact with the Rapid Response Network (RRN) about the detainment of a man on 360 6th Street in the SoMa neighborhood.

The RRN says the man seen in the video being detained by officers wearing military fatigues and a plainclothes officer has been identified and is in touch with San Francisco's Public Defender's Office on his immigration case.

What do we see in the video?

There are several WYZE video clips shared by a witness, who wishes to remain anonymous, that show a man in a suit being backed, first against a metal grate, and then a wall as he repeats, "I'm not doing anything," while as many as four men struggle to detain him.

The clip is time stamped at 8:47 a.m.

One of the men attempting to detain the man asks for his ID as other immigration officers with SRT patches search his pockets. SRT is the acronym for ICE units' special response teams. According to the ICE.gov website, ICE special response teams execute "high-risk criminal arrest and search warrants" in addition to handling "dangerous or violent alien removals."

Another video clip shows the moment the unidentified person was first approached by the officers. One in plainclothes, wearing a red flannel shirt and a badge around his neck, is brandishing a gun. The man who was detained says, "I don't know who you guys are," as he is being ordered by the officers to get on the ground.

The three officers, who are in tactical gear, all have neck gaiters which obscure their faces. The man being detained can be heard saying, "I'm an American citizen" and "I know my rights. I'm a U.S. citizen. You're not supposed to touch me," and "Don't touch me." The man asks to see the officers' badges. The plainclothes officer who was not wearing one at first then puts his badge on.

A crowd of bystanders starts to gather as the enforcement operation continues. Some bystanders appear to be recording video of the ordeal on their phones.

At the end of the series of WYZE clips, it appears the man is taken down to the ground and detained. One of the final clips shows him being walked away in handcuffs. The entire ordeal on video lasts about five minutes.

Rapid Response Network

The Rapid Response Network thanked the community for alerting them to this immigration activity. KTVU reached out to ICE for comment but has not heard back. It is not clear where the detainee is being held, if at all.

The mayor's office referred us to his post on Instagram where he thanked RRN for their quick action. He offered a poignant reminder of city policy.

"San Francisco law enforcement does not participate in federal civil immigration enforcement, and our city stands with our immigrant communities," Lurie wrote. The San Francisco Police Department reiterated this message when we reached out to them.

Lurie listed the RRN hotline, 415-200-1548. If anyone is having an interaction with federal immigration enforcement and needs immediate legal support, that is the number they should call, he said.

Public Defender's Office statement

What they're saying:

By Monday evening, the public defender's office told KTVU in a statement that it is "outrageous for a plainclothes ICE agent to pull a gun on someone walking down the streets of our city."

They said their Immigration Defense Unit is working to get the man seen in the video legal representation. In addition, they said they would not be releasing this person's name.

"We are part of a robust network of Bay Area immigrant rights advocates who will not tolerate violence by ICE agents in our communities," the public defender's office said.

On social media, State Sen. Scott Wiener alluded to his No Secret Police Act, signed by Gov. Gavin Newsom, which requires officers to show their face while on duty.

"Reminder to ICE agents: Our law that the Governor just signed is in effect, and you can now be sued for violating people's constitutional rights. Your impunity is over," Wiener wrote.

The Department of Homeland Security, which ICE is a part of, has said it will not comply with this California law, after a federal judge ruled in the federal officials' favor.

Rally for immigrant services

An emergency rally for immigrant services is being held in San Francisco on Tuesday at noon on the steps of City Hall in light of increased ICE enforcement, according to Supervisor Jackie Fielder's office, who represents the city's Mission District. Speakers at the rally will include fellow supervisors, Connie Chan, Shamann Walton, as well as organizations - La Raza Centro Legal and the San Francisco Immigrant Legal and Education Network (SFILEN).

text:
The Department of Justice (DOJ) claimed its recent California lawsuit to block the state from counting ballots from 20,000 people it suspects are noncitizens does not violate a previous court order for one simple reason: It was merely acting on findings from the Department of Homeland Security (DHS).

The DOJ’s argument comes in response to a claim from the pro-voting group Common Cause, which previously sued to stop the administration’s broad effort to build a national voter database with private data from every state. U.S. District Judge Sparkle Sooknanan barred Trump’s DOJ from carrying out its “list maintenance project,” which sought to obtain Americans’ confidential voter information and compare that against federal immigration data to cull state voter rolls.

Common Cause said the DOJ’s recent California actions violated Sooknanan’s court order and asked to hold a status conference on the matter.

DOJ’s response: We don’t need a conference because we were merely acting on DHS’s findings.

The department said its recent California lawsuit “cannot be construed as part of the same purported policy that this Court vacated,” — and even claimed that the voter list maintenance project Sooknanan blocked doesn’t exist.

Because, as DOJ argued, its recent actions in the Golden State stemmed from DHS’s “independent analysis under its own authority based on a voter roll that it received through a lawful purchase,” which then resulted in DHS’s lawsuit against California.

In response to the department’s nationwide voter roll grab, Common Cause sued the department in April, arguing that its effort amounts to an attempt to federalize voter list maintenance. On Oct. 9, Sooknanan said the DOJ unlawfully exceeded its authority and violated privacy laws and blocked the DOJ from continuing its voter roll project.

Common Cause wasn’t the only one to claim the DOJ violated a court order.

California Secretary of State Shirley Weber (D) made a similar claim in response to the DOJ last week.

“In that order, the court vacated the DOJ’s policy of, among other things, comparing state voter roll information ‘against a federal database to identify purportedly ineligible voters,’ in collaboration with DHS, ‘and demanding that states remove voters from their rolls based on the results of those comparisons,’” Weber said. “It appears that your letter may utilize a policy that a federal court has already deemed unlawful.”

Pro-voting intervenors in the DOJ’s recent California lawsuit also made a similar claim.

But the DOJ held firm that they did no such thing since the basis of the lawsuit came from a DHS — not DOJ — investigation.

“To be part of the supposedly ‘comprehensive effort to request the voter rolls from all states and the District of Columbia’ that this Court vacated, the California lawsuit must at least originate from the DOJ’s request for California’s voter roll,” the department said in its Monday response.

text:
PELHAM PARKWAY, The Bronx (WABC) -- Alex Nilaj, a longtime leader of the Open Hand food pantry in the Morris Park and Pelham Parkway neighborhoods, was taken into Immigration and Customs Enforcement custody last week after being detained at 26 Federal Plaza during an immigration hearing.

Nilaj is known locally for his work with the Open Hand food pantry, which serves 8,000 people a month. Residents line up on Thursday and Saturday mornings for fresh produce and other staples.

"A lot of people really need that right now, especially in like a lot of hard times," neighbor Geraldine Callejas said.

Since Nilaj was taken into custody, neighbors say the food pantry on Lydig Avenue has been noticeably quieter.

Rep. Richie Torres, D-N.Y., said he has known Nilaj for years.

"Every elected official in the Bronx knows, Alex. Every civic association knows Alex. Every member of the local community board knows Alex. He's no stranger. He's one of us," Torres said.

The Department of Homeland Security described Nilaj as an undocumented immigrant from Albania who entered the United States 20 years ago and overstayed. In a statement, the agency said, "He received due process and was ordered removed by an immigration judge on July 22, 2008. This administration will not ignore the rule of law."

Nilaj is not accused of any offense other than the immigration violation. He is being held at Delaney Hall, where Torres said he has visited him.

"Delaney has about a thousand inmates. None of them are serious offenders or violent offenders. None of them. As far as I'm concerned, Delaney Hall should not even exist," Torres said.

Neighbors described Nilaj as a valued member of the community.

"Very good person. Very friendly," neighbor Samia Bouzeria said.

Residents have launched a petition seeking Nilaj's release, saying the Open Hand food pantry needs him to remain open and that the community depends on its services.

"We want him back. We really want him back," Bouzeria said.

"I never liked ICE to begin with, I don't know why people would support it to begin with," Callejas said.

Torres argued that federal immigration enforcement should focus elsewhere.

"The federal government should be focused on the most violent, serious offenders, not public servants like Alex," he said.

Nilaj has an attorney who is filing a formal habeas petition seeking his release. He also has a wife and children. No information was available about their citizenship status or what he was hoping to accomplish at Federal Plaza last week.

Torres said Nilaj told him he has attended multiple immigration hearings over the years and has made every effort to follow the rules while pursuing the American dream.

text:
The Legal Landscape

The Legal Landscape is a monthly Policy & Advocacy report that provides a deeper dive into legal topics so that you can understand the law as it changes. Against a shifting legal landscape, USCRI hopes these updates will be helpful to newcomers and communities who want reliable and timely information.

Due Process Risks for Refugees

Effective October 14, 2026, the Department of Homeland Security announced that refugees would be afforded only 10 days to respond to a Notice of Intent to Terminate refugee status. In the interim final rule, the Department cast doubt on the refugee admissions of the prior administration, yet evidence of widespread fraud or exploitation has not been provided.

Refugees who receive a Notice of Intent to Terminate may either respond in writing or request an interview. Failure to respond will lead to termination of refugee status and referral to immigration court for removal proceedings. Rather than guarantee proper service or require a response, silence is taken as admission.

The Refugee Convention, which the United States acceded to in 1968, requires due process before the removal of a refugee. Article 32 states that refugees must be afforded the right to present evidence, the right to appeal, and the right to legal assistance. According to international law, the United States is prohibited from deporting a refugee to a country where they would face persecution or torture.

U.S. caselaw on appeal rights after refugee status termination is developing. On October 5, 2026, in Mukantagara v. Noem , the Tenth Circuit Court of Appeals reversed a district court finding that federal courts do not have jurisdiction to review an agency decision to terminate refugee status. The court noted that terminating refugee status requires a mandatory and nondiscretionary finding that an individual was not a refugee at the time of admission. A nondiscretionary finding is subject to judicial review and can be challenged in federal court. Currently, the opinion does not have precedential weight outside of the Tenth Circuit.

While due process rights are usually guaranteed by governments, termination of refugee status also throws into question what procedural protections a refugee will be guaranteed by the international system. Refugee resettlement is a global, coordinated effort between refugee host countries, other resettlement countries, and international organizations, including several United Nations organizations. Many refugees are first identified by the United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees as individuals eligible for international protection under the Refugee Convention. Termination of refugee status by the Department would not automatically terminate an individual’s eligibility for international protection. Yet, the lack of clarity on what protections a refugee could rely on and what other safe options are available may test the current international system, at a time when funding support are at historic lows.

Stripping Back the Temporary Protected Status Statute

In January 2025, 17 countries were designated for Temporary Protected Status. Today, only four designations remain—three of which are in limbo. The expiry dates for El Salvador, Sudan, and Ukraine have passed without formal decisions on whether Temporary Protected Status will be extended, re-designated, or terminated. The future of Temporary Protected Status is uncharted, and the past 21 months have highlighted the weaknesses of the original statute.

In 1990, Congress created Temporary Protected Status to close a gap in U.S. law regarding humanitarian protections for individuals who are already in the United States facing dangerous conditions if forced to return to their home country. Asylum protection, enacted by the Refugee Act of 1980, is afforded to individuals who fear persecution. Because exposure to conflict, environmental disaster, and other dangerous conditions does not always rise to the level of individual persecution, the executive branch offered safe haven through Extended Voluntary Departure. This tool was used ad hoc to grant temporary protection to nationals from 16 countries, including Iran, Afghanistan, Cuba, and Nicaragua.

Disapproval of the discretionary nature of Extended Voluntary Departure came to a head when the executive branch refused to grant protections to nationals of El Salvador after civil war broke out in 1980 between U.S.-backed government forces and guerilla groups. In 1990, Congress passed the Immigration Act, formalizing Temporary Protected Status and designating El Salvador. Congress formalized the process to move away from the ad hoc approach. Yet in doing so, Congress never fixed the problem it had with Extended Voluntary Departure in the first place: the discretionary nature of it.

text:
Community advocates and elected officials are amplifying Know Your Rights information and rapid response networks as an increase in immigration enforcement once again hits California.

On Saturday, neighbors in North Long Beach rushed out of their homes and blocked federal immigration agents from detaining a man they violently knocked to the ground.

Unión del Barrio has shared video footage of immigration agents spotted in Inglewood, Koreatown and East LA in recent days and is urging residents “to be cautious during this wave of deportations” and to “not surrender to fear.”

With just weeks before the Nov. 3 election, community and labor organizations, including InnerCity Struggle, have hosted voter-protection trainings to ensure voters understand how to protect their votes and what they can do in the face of any interference.

While there are no known examples of Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents at California polling places, organizers at a recent training said even rumors can create fear and urged trainees to encourage voters to stay in line and to observe and document what’s happening.

The Boyle Heights Immigrant Rights Network last week said it is continuing its rapid response efforts and seeking volunteers to spread the word about what people can do when they spot ICE agents.

“Sharing this information and encouraging people to commit to these different opportunities is the best thing we can do to help protect our community,” said Ken Campa, director of programs at Proyecto Pastoral.

Here’s who to call if you spot ICE:

My background: I was part of the team that launched De Los, a new section of the Los Angeles Times exploring Latino identity. I’ve been a local reporter for The Press-Enterprise in Riverside, The San Gabriel Valley Tribune, and The Orange County Register. You can find my writing on religion, food, and culture in The Atlantic, Eater, the Associated Press, the Washington Post, and Religion News Service. My upbringing spans South Central, El Monte, and Pomona.

What I do: A Report for America corps member, I write about how decisions surrounding immigration, city hall, schools, health, religion and culture impact Boyle Heights and East LA. title: Ecuadorean man decries detention, second immigration arrest involving Ogden police officers
description:
OGDEN — An immigrant from Ecuador is crying foul over his detention by federal immigration agents last month and the involvement of an Ogden police officer, who assisted as the ICE agents struggled with the man.
Another officer helped with the Sept. 3 detention of Alcivar as a second Ogden officer looked on.
The video from an Ogden police officer's body camera shows the detention of Dennys Alcivar Torres in Ogden on Sept. 3, 2026.
Both Paredes and Alcivar were placed in immigrant detention facilities but have since been released, though their respective immigration cases remain unresolved.
The Ogden officer arrives with Alcivar on the ground, and the agents cuff the man.
text:
OGDEN — An immigrant from Ecuador is crying foul over his detention by federal immigration agents last month and the involvement of an Ogden police officer, who assisted as the ICE agents struggled with the man.

"It changed my life, 360 degrees," Dennys Alcivar Torres said, saying the incident took an economic toll and affected him emotionally and psychologically. "I'm afraid."

He addressed the Ogden City Council during the public comment portion of the body's Oct. 13 meeting and later spoke with KSL, charging that his detention amounted to a physical attack.

"I demand that this blow to my human rights and physical integrity be reviewed," he said at last week's meeting, addressing the body in Spanish. "I'm asking that the city implement a policy that the police department accepts police reports from anyone attacked by ICE officials."

Alcivar's detention by Immigration and Customs Enforcement officials is the second local case that Weber County immigrant advocates have seized on in their push for a clearer Ogden Police Department policy outlining the role police officers may have in ICE actions. The department doesn't have a formal accord with ICE, unlike some other law enforcement agencies, but a police officer happened upon the Aug. 25 detention of Jonathan Paredes Rodriguez, originally from Venezuela, spurring the debate. Another officer helped with the Sept. 3 detention of Alcivar as a second Ogden officer looked on.

On both occasions, Ogden officers interacted with ICE officials and the respective men targeted by immigration authorities. Video of the Sept. 3 detention shows an officer assisting as two ICE agents were cuffing Alcivar on the ground of an Ogden parking lot, the man already largely under control. In the Aug. 25 incident, also on video, Paredes surrendered to an ICE agent after seeking assistance from the Ogden officer, there on an unrelated issue.

The video from an Ogden police officer's body camera shows the detention of Dennys Alcivar Torres in Ogden on Sept. 3, 2026. Two ICE agents were already subduing the man when the Ogden officer arrived:

Numerous immigrant advocates addressed the City Council on Sept. 1 in the wake of Paredes' detention, pressing the city to spell out what sort of interaction police may have with ICE agents. Kim Haslam, active in Ogden United, which has advocated for immigrants on the issue, said so far she hasn't heard any specifics, though officials say they are working on an updated plan.

"Many of us have asked repeatedly at every council meeting when the timeline is, and they have not told us," she said. The advocates have largely blasted the ICE crackdown on illegal immigration in Ogden and beyond as heavy-handed and targeted chiefly at immigrants who don't have major criminal records.

In a statement Monday, Ogden Police Capt. Matt Ward said authorities are mindful of Alcivar's comments from last week's City Council meeting, but not much more. Both Paredes and Alcivar were placed in immigrant detention facilities but have since been released, though their respective immigration cases remain unresolved.

"We are conducting a review of the incident. As we've stated in the past, we are looking at a policy for the department regarding interactions with ICE. Because we're actively reviewing the incident, we can't provide any further comment on the September 3rd interaction," Ward said.

'Vital signs were low'

Alcivar, who ran a marketing business in Ecuador and is trained as a lawyer, had plenty to say. He had been living in Kaysville before he was detained, but since his release from an immigrant detention center in California in early October, he has been finding lodging at varied locations, most recently at the Riverdale home of some friends.

He said he came to the United States from his home in Guayaquil, Ecuador, on a tourist visa and had been in the process of trying to secure a student visa to study English when agents detained him on Sept. 3. He had just left Ogden Justice Court, where he had a court date stemming from tickets he received in an Aug. 2 traffic case, one a class C misdemeanor for failing to keep a proper lookout for others while driving, the other for driving without a license, an infraction.

"I paid all the fees to be able to make the change in status, presented the documents and everything was going well," he said, referencing his request for a student visa. He maintains that U.S. law permits him to remain in the United States while his application for the student visa remains unresolved.

In a statement to KSL on Monday, though, the Department of Homeland Security offered another take.

"Alcivar Torres entered the United States legally on June 8, 2025, but violated our nation's laws by refusing to depart by the required date. His pending application was denied in September 2026 for abandonment, and he has no lawful status to remain in the United States," the department said.

As for the Sept. 3 detention, Alcivar said he was cooperative with the ICE agents as they descended on him to arrest him and that he asked them to look up his case. He was seated in a parked car, which was not turned on.

"I show him my passport, and he tells me my visa expired. I tell him no, that I've made a change in status and that I've done it legally," Alcivar said. One of the agents told him he was in the country illegally, he said, and Alcivar said that can't be.

Video of the encounter from a bystander, supplied by Haslam, shows the two ICE agents subsequently pulling Alcivar from his car, unsuccessfully attempting to cuff him and forcing him to the ground. The Ogden officer arrives with Alcivar on the ground, and the agents cuff the man.

"Alcivar Torres refused to comply with officers' lawful commands to exit his vehicle and continued to resist arrest. Officers relied on their training to gain control of the situation. The Ogden Police Department arrived on scene to assist officers with safely making the arrest," the Department of Homeland Security said in its statement.

Alcivar said paramedics called to the scene reported that his "vital signs were low" and he was eventually taken to a hospital. There, one of the medical officials said the man "was on the point of dying," Alcivar maintains. He said he tried to call Ogden police to the hospital so he could file an incident report against the ICE agents stemming from their handling of him.

An officer never spoke to him, though, which prompted his call to City Council members at the Oct. 13 meeting that Ogden police allow reports by people alleging they've been attacked by ICE agents.

"I call police and explain to them and clearly tell them that I was unnecessarily attacked by a police officer and two ICE agents. I need to make my report. Police never arrived or I don't know if they arrived," he said.

Alcivar has consulted a lawyer and is weighing his alternatives, but isn't sure what comes next.

"I can't do anything because they haven't given me a work permit, nothing. I can't do anything," he said.
